messages.body_plain:
I’d just suggest doing directly what I suggested below:
- First fit the 7 models separately.  Use these to get point predictions for each data point.
- Write a new Stan program with data vector[N] y; matrix[N,y] y_pred; and parameter simplex[7] lambda; to minimize the sum of squared prediction errors.
- Then feed in the data and the Nx7 matrix of predicted values and run Stan-optimize on this new program to estimate lambda.
- Voilà, your new model:  a weighted avg of your original 7 models with weights lambda_1,…lambda_7.

No marginalizing discrete parameters is necessary here.

I agree that this is not the same as fitting a mixture model, but I think the above makes sense as a form of model averaging.  As I said, I’m curious how it works out.

> On Feb 7, 2016, at 3:43 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> If we had "cut", you could do that model mixture optimization directly
> in Stan in one go.  But it's not a Bayesian procedure.
>
> If you literally built up a mixture model in Stan, you'd get a different
> result, because each mixture component could fit the data its responsible for
> rather than making each component fit all the data equally weighted.
>
> You want to check out the marginalizing discrete parameters section of
> the manual to figure out how to write that new model Andrew's suggesting.
> Normal with fixed scale gives you a density proportional to the sum of square
> errors because we work on the log scale.
>
> - Bob
>

>>
>> My advice:
>>
>> Forget reversible jump.
>>
>> Instead, fit the 7 models separately—actually, you’ve already done that, so you’ve done all the hard work.  For each of the 7 fitted models you get a predicted value for each data point.  Call these y_hat_{nk} for data points n=1,…,N and models k=1,…,7.   Now just create a new model that is a mixture of the 7, with mixture fractions lambda_1,…,lambda_7 which are simplex-constrained (i.e., nonnegative and sum to 1).  You can estimate the lambdas that minimize the sum of the squared prediction errors (that’s just constrained least squares, but it’s easiest to do via a simple Stan model.)
>>
>> You should be good to go.
>>
>> Please let us know how this works.
>>
>> A

On Sat, Feb 6, 2016 at 2:30 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Saturday, February 6, 2016 at 2:35:09 PM UTC-5, Tyler Blazey wrote:
> > This generally works fine. If K is 30 or larger, however, Stan starts to throw this error:
> >
> >
> >  [1] "Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : "
> >
> >  [2] "  model2107116f846c_fc55120bf3759a2d9575c7b8f269b9c5_namespace::write_array: y is not positive definite:"
> >
> >
> > I can make the error go away by replacing corr_matrix[K] with matrix[K,K]. Does this mean that the correlation matrix generated by multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L_Omega) is not a valid correlation matrix? If so, is this something I should be concerned about?
>
> You shouldn't be concerned about it, except insofar as it is really difficult to get a large correlation matrix to be numerically positive definite. If L_Omega is a cholesky_factor_corr then multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L_Omega) is positive definite by construction, even if it fails is subsequent positive definiteness check, which is why you should not bother to check it, which is why you should declare it as a matrix[K,K] rather than a corr_matrix[K]. Also, this is why you should parameterize your model in terms of Cholesky factors rather than covariance or correlation matrices if at all possible.
>
> Ben
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Discrete parameters...again!
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Discrete parameters...again!
messages.body_plain:
We can't do the efficient sampling with only the
total log density because there's no way to pull out the
Markov blanket for each discrete parameter to compute its
conditionals efficiently.

But if the "objective function" can be extended to include
conditionals for discrete parameters, we could do it efficiently.
(Yes, I know it's the wild West for discrete parameters; I'm just
talking about efficiency relative to other systems like BUGS).

- Bob

>> a Stan model, which would be run.   A graphical mdoel with
>> discrete parameters would be able to generate all the conditional
>> densities we need to run Gibbs on top of that.  We could
>> allow other ways to set those conditionals, like just using
>> the full densities.
>>
>> - Bob

>>> We talked about various options, the simplest of which was to allow the user to tag the program or divide it into blocks to tell it which lines of code needed to be evaluated when updating each discrete parameter.  I think that if we felt it was important to allow Stan to work with discrete parameters, we could come up with various reasonable solutions.  But we were never convinced it was such a big deal, so we never decided to do it.  I _don’t_ think the solution is to go to graphical modeling.  I mean, yes, I do want a graphical modeling wrapper for Stan, but I don’t like the idea that Stan internally would use graphical models.  To me, that’s too limiting.

messages.body_plain:
I think there's a big gap between doing the proper mixture modeling,
Andrew's half-way solution that cuts the inference on each model from
the mixing, and the typical Bayesian model averaging that weights by
model posterior (an aggregated cut-based solution):

  http://www.stat.colostate.edu/~jah/papers/statsci.pdf

Often in machine learning (as in the 4th author of the above
paper's work winning the Netflix Prize!) you optimize on held-out
or cross-validated data rather than in-training-sample data, often
running a logistic regression with further predictors for items in
addition to an intercept:

  http://www.netflixprize.com/assets/ProgressPrize2007_KorBell.pdf

- Bob

P.S.  By "cut" I just mean running a model and gathering its results to
      use downstream rather than allowing "feedback" in the model.  It's
      a "feature" of BUGS :-)

I took a look at the references that Bob sent, and my mixture-modeling optimization does seem pretty much the same as the “stacking” idea from the statistics literature.  I did some quick googling and also found this paper from 2003 that seems relevant to this discussion:
http://delivery.acm.org/10.1145/970000/964281/4-683-clarke.pdf
This idea seems so natural, I don’t know why I’d not thought of it before, or why it doesn’t seem to come up much in the Bayesian model averaging literature.

messages.body_plain:
Here’s the reference:
http://dl.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=964281
What we’re talking about _does_ appear to be stacking, and I have no idea why this is not a standard approach in Bayesian statistics.  And why is it not in chapter 7 of BDA3?  I’ve seen so much wasted effort going into attempts to compute marginal likelihoods for Bayesian model averaging, and this idea seems much better.

I guess it didn’t used to be so feasible.  Now that we have pointwise loo at our fingertips, this stacking thing seems like the right way to go.

I prefer the term “mixture model” to “stacking,” though.

messages.body_plain:
I think overloading "mixture model" here's going to be confusing
(not that "stacking" really helps matters).  A standard mixture
model puts a prior on the simplex and estimates it along with the
individual model's parameters.  You'll get a different marginal
posterior for the model parameters that way than if you fit the
models separately and then combine them after the fact.  At least
I'm pretty sure you will.

How about "pseudomixture"?  Or "postmixture"?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Following Christian Robert and Judith Rousseau’s language, it’s a mixture model conditional on the hypotheses. The hypotheses are the estimated predictive posteriors. Mixture modeling makes sense in that it’s all about the decision to condition on the models or to infer them jointly with the mixture weights.

Dustin

> On Feb 7, 2016, at 11:19 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> I think overloading "mixture model" here's going to be confusing
> (not that "stacking" really helps matters).  A standard mixture
> model puts a prior on the simplex and estimates it along with the
> individual model's parameters.  You'll get a different marginal
> posterior for the model parameters that way than if you fit the
> models separately and then combine them after the fact.  At least
> I'm pretty sure you will.
>
> How about "pseudomixture"?  Or "postmixture"?
>
> - Bob
>
>> On Feb 7, 2016, at 8:31 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>
>> Here’s the reference:
>> http://dl.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=964281
>> What we’re talking about _does_ appear to be stacking, and I have no idea why this is not a standard approach in Bayesian statistics.  And why is it not in chapter 7 of BDA3?  I’ve seen so much wasted effort going into attempts to compute marginal likelihoods for Bayesian model averaging, and this idea seems much better.
>>
>> I guess it didn’t used to be so feasible.  Now that we have pointwise loo at our fingertips, this stacking thing seems like the right way to go.
>>
>> I prefer the term “mixture model” to “stacking,” though.
>>

>>> @Andrew, the link you wrote is broken.
>>>
>>> Why not just use the evaluation criteria (normalized) as weights? Since Ben already has all the numbers to calculate LOO-CV, it’d be easy to weight based on these estimates of the log pointwise predictive density. I have no idea if this works, maybe the scaling is off. However it already sounds less sensitive than using the marginal likelihoods/Bayes factors as the loss function to weight things on, which is the more traditional thing to do.
>>>
>>> Dustin

>>>>
>>>> I took a look at the references that Bob sent, and my mixture-modeling optimization does seem pretty much the same as the “stacking” idea from the statistics literature.  I did some quick googling and also found this paper from 2003 that seems relevant to this discussion:
>>>> http://delivery.acm.org/10.1145/970000/964281/4-683-clarke.pdf
>>>> This idea seems so natural, I don’t know why I’d not thought of it before, or why it doesn’t seem to come up much in the Bayesian model averaging literature.
>>>> A
>>>>

>>>>>

>>>>>

>>>>>> Cheers
>>>>>>
>>>>>> Roy
>>>>>>
>>>>>>
>>>>>> On 08/02/16 10:14, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>>>>>>> I’d just suggest doing directly what I suggested below:
>>>>>>> - First fit the 7 models separately.  Use these to get point predictions for each data point.
>>>>>>> - Write a new Stan program with data vector[N] y; matrix[N,y] y_pred; and parameter simplex[7] lambda; to minimize the sum of squared prediction errors.
>>>>>>> - Then feed in the data and the Nx7 matrix of predicted values and run Stan-optimize on this new program to estimate lambda.
>>>>>>> - Voilà, your new model:  a weighted avg of your original 7 models with weights lambda_1,…lambda_7.
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> No marginalizing discrete parameters is necessary here.
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> I agree that this is not the same as fitting a mixture model, but I think the above makes sense as a form of model averaging.  As I said, I’m curious how it works out.
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> On Feb 7, 2016, at 3:43 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> If we had "cut", you could do that model mixture optimization directly

>>>>>>>> If you literally built up a mixture model in Stan, you'd get a different
>>>>>>>> result, because each mixture component could fit the data its responsible for
>>>>>>>> rather than making each component fit all the data equally weighted.

>>>>>>>> errors because we work on the log scale.
>>>>>>>>

>>>>>>>>>

>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>> Instead, fit the 7 models separately—actually, you’ve already done that, so you’ve done all the hard work.  For each of the 7 fitted models you get a predicted value for each data point.  Call these y_hat_{nk} for data points n=1,…,N and models k=1,…,7.   Now just create a new model that is a mixture of the 7, with mixture fractions lambda_1,…,lambda_7 which are simplex-constrained (i.e., nonnegative and sum to 1).  You can estimate the lambdas that minimize the sum of the squared prediction errors (that’s just constrained least squares, but it’s easiest to do via a simple Stan model.)
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>> You should be good to go.
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>> Please let us know how this works.
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>> A
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> On Feb 6, 2016, at 10:57 PM, Ben Lambert <ben.c....@googlemail.com> wrote:
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> Hi,
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> I have currently fit about 7 different quite highly-dimensional hierarchical models for a particular problem using Stan; all the fits, as well as convergence diagnostics (Rhat, n divergent, and all the other Shiny Stan diagnostics) are ok. The individual models take about an hour to run individually.
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> The models each have different parameterisations, with differing numbers of parameters. I would ideally like to do some sort of mixture modelling, where I assign priors on the probability of each model a priori, but then let the data decide the ultimate weights given to each model. (I know that BDA section 7.5 suggests that it is preferable to do more of a continuous model-type expansion, but as far as I can tell this is not possible in this paper, since its point is to compare the results obtained across existent models in the literature, where there is a considerable lack of consensus on model choice).
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> Since each model has different numbers of parameters, I would normally need to do reversible jump MCMC here. Firstly, I want to check - is this possible in Stan? (I think from this discussion that it is not: https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups#!searchin/stan-users/reversible$20jump$20mcmc/stan-users/CXAT_XUTfwE/Nxgqjm_Zx1AJ0).
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> Secondly, does anyone know of any approximate results that could be used to average across all the models? (I have kept the log-likelihood in order to calculate LOO-CV, and WAIC, and was wondering whether this could be used.) I suspect that there isn't really anything I can do here, other than coding up the models myself in another language, but I wanted to tap the community brain before I begin this (arduous) process.
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> Best,
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayesian model averaging without reversible-jump MCMC on highly-dimensional models
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Bayesian model averaging without reversible-jump MCMC on highly-dimensional models
messages.body_plain:
1.  Computational

2.  Robustness to specification of priors within the separate models.  For problems with pure Bayes model averaging, see my 1995 paper with Rubin, also this is discussed a bit in chap 7 of BDA3.

> On Feb 7, 2016, at 11:44 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> Is the motivation for not doing full Bayes purely computational?
> Or is it about fitting the models independently before mixing?
>
> - Bob
>
>> On Feb 7, 2016, at 11:30 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>
>> Bob:
>>
>> No, it is a mixture model.  It’s just not _full Bayes inference_ for the mixture model.
>>
>> A
>>> On Feb 7, 2016, at 11:19 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> I think overloading "mixture model" here's going to be confusing
>>> (not that "stacking" really helps matters).  A standard mixture
>>> model puts a prior on the simplex and estimates it along with the
>>> individual model's parameters.  You'll get a different marginal
>>> posterior for the model parameters that way than if you fit the
>>> models separately and then combine them after the fact.  At least
>>> I'm pretty sure you will.
>>>
>>> How about "pseudomixture"?  Or "postmixture"?
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>
>>>> On Feb 7, 2016, at 8:31 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>>>
>>>> Here’s the reference:
>>>> http://dl.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=964281
>>>> What we’re talking about _does_ appear to be stacking, and I have no idea why this is not a standard approach in Bayesian statistics.  And why is it not in chapter 7 of BDA3?  I’ve seen so much wasted effort going into attempts to compute marginal likelihoods for Bayesian model averaging, and this idea seems much better.
>>>>
>>>> I guess it didn’t used to be so feasible.  Now that we have pointwise loo at our fingertips, this stacking thing seems like the right way to go.
>>>>
>>>> I prefer the term “mixture model” to “stacking,” though.
>>>>
>>>>> On Feb 7, 2016, at 8:27 PM, Dustin Tran <dustinv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>>
>>>>> @Andrew, the link you wrote is broken.
>>>>>
>>>>> Why not just use the evaluation criteria (normalized) as weights? Since Ben already has all the numbers to calculate LOO-CV, it’d be easy to weight based on these estimates of the log pointwise predictive density. I have no idea if this works, maybe the scaling is off. However it already sounds less sensitive than using the marginal likelihoods/Bayes factors as the loss function to weight things on, which is the more traditional thing to do.
>>>>>
>>>>> Dustin
>>>>>> On Feb 7, 2016, at 8:08 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>>>>>
>>>>>> I took a look at the references that Bob sent, and my mixture-modeling optimization does seem pretty much the same as the “stacking” idea from the statistics literature.  I did some quick googling and also found this paper from 2003 that seems relevant to this discussion:
>>>>>> http://delivery.acm.org/10.1145/970000/964281/4-683-clarke.pdf
>>>>>> This idea seems so natural, I don’t know why I’d not thought of it before, or why it doesn’t seem to come up much in the Bayesian model averaging literature.
>>>>>> A
>>>>>>
>>>>>>> On Feb 7, 2016, at 5:25 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> Aki and I have discussed this approach.  I’ve talked about it a lot but have never done it, hence my curiouity about how well it might work on this particular example.  I don’t recall seeing the method in the literature but it could well be there.  It’s also related to a recent paper by Christian Robert and Judith Rousseau.
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> On Feb 7, 2016, at 4:32 PM, Roy <royco...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> Hi Andrew
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> That sounds like an interesting idea as it could be applied to any set of fitted models, even Frequentist ones, right? Are there any references in the literature of model averaging you are basing your suggestion on? I'm just curious :)
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> Cheers
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> Roy
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>> On 08/02/16 10:14, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>>>>>>>>> I’d just suggest doing directly what I suggested below:
>>>>>>>>> - First fit the 7 models separately.  Use these to get point predictions for each data point.
>>>>>>>>> - Write a new Stan program with data vector[N] y; matrix[N,y] y_pred; and parameter simplex[7] lambda; to minimize the sum of squared prediction errors.
>>>>>>>>> - Then feed in the data and the Nx7 matrix of predicted values and run Stan-optimize on this new program to estimate lambda.
>>>>>>>>> - Voilà, your new model:  a weighted avg of your original 7 models with weights lambda_1,…lambda_7.
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>> No marginalizing discrete parameters is necessary here.
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>> I agree that this is not the same as fitting a mixture model, but I think the above makes sense as a form of model averaging.  As I said, I’m curious how it works out.
>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> On Feb 7, 2016, at 3:43 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> If we had "cut", you could do that model mixture optimization directly
>>>>>>>>>> in Stan in one go.  But it's not a Bayesian procedure.
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> If you literally built up a mixture model in Stan, you'd get a different
>>>>>>>>>> result, because each mixture component could fit the data its responsible for
>>>>>>>>>> rather than making each component fit all the data equally weighted.
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> You want to check out the marginalizing discrete parameters section of
>>>>>>>>>> the manual to figure out how to write that new model Andrew's suggesting.
>>>>>>>>>> Normal with fixed scale gives you a density proportional to the sum of square
>>>>>>>>>> errors because we work on the log scale.
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>> - Bob
>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> On Feb 7, 2016, at 12:09 AM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> My advice:
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> Forget reversible jump.
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> Instead, fit the 7 models separately—actually, you’ve already done that, so you’ve done all the hard work.  For each of the 7 fitted models you get a predicted value for each data point.  Call these y_hat_{nk} for data points n=1,…,N and models k=1,…,7.   Now just create a new model that is a mixture of the 7, with mixture fractions lambda_1,…,lambda_7 which are simplex-constrained (i.e., nonnegative and sum to 1).  You can estimate the lambdas that minimize the sum of the squared prediction errors (that’s just constrained least squares, but it’s easiest to do via a simple Stan model.)
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> You should be good to go.
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> Please let us know how this works.
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>> A
>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>> On Feb 6, 2016, at 10:57 PM, Ben Lambert <ben.c....@googlemail.com> wrote:
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>> Hi,
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>> I have currently fit about 7 different quite highly-dimensional hierarchical models for a particular problem using Stan; all the fits, as well as convergence diagnostics (Rhat, n divergent, and all the other Shiny Stan diagnostics) are ok. The individual models take about an hour to run individually.
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>> The models each have different parameterisations, with differing numbers of parameters. I would ideally like to do some sort of mixture modelling, where I assign priors on the probability of each model a priori, but then let the data decide the ultimate weights given to each model. (I know that BDA section 7.5 suggests that it is preferable to do more of a continuous model-type expansion, but as far as I can tell this is not possible in this paper, since its point is to compare the results obtained across existent models in the literature, where there is a considerable lack of consensus on model choice).
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>> Since each model has different numbers of parameters, I would normally need to do reversible jump MCMC here. Firstly, I want to check - is this possible in Stan? (I think from this discussion that it is not: https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups#!searchin/stan-users/reversible$20jump$20mcmc/stan-users/CXAT_XUTfwE/Nxgqjm_Zx1AJ0).
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>> Secondly, does anyone know of any approximate results that could be used to average across all the models? (I have kept the log-likelihood in order to calculate LOO-CV, and WAIC, and was wondering whether this could be used.) I suspect that there isn't really anything I can do here, other than coding up the models myself in another language, but I wanted to tap the community brain before I begin this (arduous) process.
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>> Best,
>>>>>>>>>>>>
>>>>>>>>>>>> Ben

Thanks.  2 makes sense.  The mixture weights are like data weighting --- that's
why the mixture component won't get same parameter estimates as full model.
And now that I think about priors, of course they'll be affected --- there's
less overall data weight, and the weight there is comes from where the model's
the best at fitting, so it's not even a random subsample.

- Bob

Hi,

I have been changing the model a bit from the last one. I’ve fixated a class to always have coefficient = 0, to avoid identifiability problems.

When I run the model, it seems to run quite fast in the start (~50 samples per day). However, when it reaches about ~200 samples, it slows down dramatically, and only draws about 1 sample per day. I’m wondering if I’ve unintentionally come up with a problematic posterior. I fixed one of the classes, so that K[6] = 0, which should fix the identifiability problem with softmax. I have tried to set wide priors, to give Stan some room to explore. As I have understood it, multinomial regression coefficients can be interpreted as a relative risk. The priors I have specified now should give each coefficient a value -+3, which would give risks in the interval exp(+-3) = [0.05, 20], which are perfectly reasonable relative risk values.
I do have a rather large number of data points, 7,493,720 to be exact. They are, however, split over 187,343 combinations. This is because there are 40 combinations of discrete covariates per data point ( 2 sex and 10  age). There are 6 different outcomes.

Could there be any other problems, or bad specifications?

I have uploaded the model to https://gist.github.com/demodw/84e46c6bac8eb1e55d99. Any pointers on how to improve the efficiency would also be much appreciated! I could not find a multi_logit function, and softmax only takes vectors, so I had to do the log likelihood increment per data point.

Also, when I am running diagnostics, should I look at Rhat values for the raw (K-1) coefficients, or for the K coefficients? And can I somehow exclude the (K-1) coefficients from the output?

Variable names might be a bit silly, but it helps me keep track of where in the hierarchy I am. :-)

Thanks in advance!

David

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayesian model averaging without reversible-jump MCMC on highly-dimensional models
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Bayesian model averaging without reversible-jump MCMC on highly-dimensional models
messages.body_plain:
> That would be great.  The whole “Bayesian model averaging” thing has been a useless time sink for decades.

I wouldn’t go that far — I agree that it’s a mess in the social sciences, especially
when models are hierarchical, but it has its use in applications with strong
generative/causal models.  Although even in those applications where BMA
is useful the predictive performance should still be good!

The way I like to think about it is that _conditioned on the assumptions_ BMA
is the mathematically self-consistent and conceptually elegant right answer.
But in practice it’s almost impossible to build an analysis with the assumptions
held constant and BMA becomes highly vulnerable to overfitting and we need
some predictive diagnostics.

Anyways, there’s a nice write up of Mike West’s approach in http://arxiv.org/abs/1601.07463.
Basically if you assume that your individual models are exchangeable then
de Finetti’s theorem holds and any model weighting has to take the form of
a hierarchical model*.  The individual weights could be marginal likelihoods,
in which case you recover BMA, or they could be sensitive to predictive
structure and the whole process can be iterated with new measurements.
Andrew’s two-stage strategy would be an approximation of this.  In the end
you get this lovely self-consistent theoretical approach that unifies BMA and
predictive weighting.

* Caveat: Mike West didn’t agree with the appeal to exchangeability here.
But Dan Simpson agreed with me — in the end I believe de Finetti is an
if and only if, so the mixture form that is used has to imply exchangeability
of models.

On Sunday, February 7, 2016 at 11:35:37 AM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Sunday, February 7, 2016 at 5:16:14 AM UTC-5, Xulong Wang wrote:
> > Ben, does not mean that I have to use sampling() in Stan for a generalized linear mixed model?
> > I also found estimations of other parameters that I am mostly interested in, p and beta, are similar between optimizing() and sampling().
>
> Plain maximum likelihood doesn't have much justification for GLMMs because of the incidental parameter problem where the number of parameters to estimate increases as the number of levels of the grouping factors increases. For fixed levels, as the number of observations increases, maximizing the likelihood could be a consistent estimator, but otherwise only the invariance property of MLEs holds. That is why lme4::glmer and similar functions integrate out the group-specific unknowns.
>
> Ben

> On Feb 8, 2016, at 6:36 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
>> That would be great.  The whole “Bayesian model averaging” thing has been a useless time sink for decades.
>
> I wouldn’t go that far — I agree that it’s a mess in the social sciences, especially
> when models are hierarchical, but it has its use in applications with strong
> generative/causal models.  Although even in those applications where BMA
> is useful the predictive performance should still be good!
>
> The way I like to think about it is that _conditioned on the assumptions_ BMA
> is the mathematically self-consistent and conceptually elegant right answer.
> But in practice it’s almost impossible to build an analysis with the assumptions
> held constant and BMA becomes highly vulnerable to overfitting and we need
> some predictive diagnostics.
>
> Anyways, there’s a nice write up of Mike West’s approach in http://arxiv.org/abs/1601.07463.
> Basically if you assume that your individual models are exchangeable then
> de Finetti’s theorem holds and any model weighting has to take the form of
> a hierarchical model*.  The individual weights could be marginal likelihoods,
> in which case you recover BMA, or they could be sensitive to predictive
> structure and the whole process can be iterated with new measurements.
> Andrew’s two-stage strategy would be an approximation of this.  In the end
> you get this lovely self-consistent theoretical approach that unifies BMA and
> predictive weighting.
>
> * Caveat: Mike West didn’t agree with the appeal to exchangeability here.
> But Dan Simpson agreed with me — in the end I believe de Finetti is an
> if and only if, so the mixture form that is used has to imply exchangeability
> of models.
>

messages.body_plain:
First summary
1) variations of stacking make separate models and then weight the predictions
2) BMA is just plain Bayesian approach with model uncertainty
3) in usual mixture model, the mixture components affect each other
4) in Xian's mixture model there are additional restrictions and so far they've been able to get practical computation only for two component mixture

Note that the usual mixture model is more flexible. Consider that we
have data from t_4 and two candiate models N and t_20 (which is almost
same as N).
1) separate models will be almost identical and stacking will not be
   much different from either one
2) not much difference to 1 in this case
3) in a mixture N and t_20 can have different scales and the mixture
   can fit long tailed t_4 much better than either single model
4) ..?

So obviously in 1 and 2 we need to have models which behave
differently to get anything better than a single model.

Andrew:

> What we’re talking about _does_ appear to be stacking, and I have no
> idea why this is not a standard approach in Bayesian statistics.

I think like Mike:

> The way I like to think about it is that _conditioned on the
> assumptions_ BMA is the mathematically self-consistent and
> conceptually elegant right answer.

Naturally the problem is "conditioned on the assumptions", so that if
we make bad assumptions then something which is not self-consistent
and elegant may produce better results. But if we can find a way to
produce better results than BMA, why we don't use that same approach
for continuous parameters if it's so good? It seems that it's possible
to find examples where something else works better than BMA, but not
something which would better often enough.

> And why is it not in chapter 7 of BDA3?

Because there hasn't been convincing theory nor convincing
experiments. Maybe we can have it in the next edition?

I've been aware of some versions of stacking. I don't remember this
paper by Clarke, but can be also because it's not very convincing.
Although I advocate cross-validation I haven't used cross-validation
weighting expect for a few experiments because I haven't been aware of
theoretical justification similar to BMA. Clarke's paper provides some
experimental evidence but not good theoretical justification (and in
later paper he switch mean to median). There are also some papers
showing that point estimates of the parameters using cross-validation
are much noisier than by optimising the marginal likelihood. Which
raise the question why I'm advocating cross-validation for model
selection since parameter estimation is one kind of model selection,
too. In ... we show why we recommend cross-validation for model
selection only if there is a small number of models. It's possible
that when doing model averaging the noisiness is not as big problem
when doing model averaging.

BMA can be sensitive to priors if models have a large difference in
the number of parameters, in which case "pseudo BMA" (refering to term
pseudo Bayes factor) might be more stable, although I've seen also
case where uniform weighting performed better than cross-validation
weighting.

BMA can also difficult to compute (although often it's possible to
switch continuous model, like instead of spike-and-slab you can use
hierarchical shrinkage prior), and then pseudo BMA might be quick and
accurate enough approximation.

Now I have to go to sleep, but I'll read Mike's paper which Mike
recommended...

The function GeneralCptModel_CVODE() calls integrate_ode_cvode() to solve a system of equation describing a compartment model. It is a higher-order function, so I need to modify Stan's grammar to implement it, but I get stuck.

I modified six grammar files (ast.hpp, ast_def.cpp, generator.hpp, term_grammar.hpp, term_grammar_def.hpp, and var_decls_grammar_def.hpp), adding the GeneralCpt function everywhere where I found the cvode integrator, and doing what seemed to be appropriate modifications. When I try to build CmdStan (using make build), I get an error "symbol(s) not found for architecture x86_64".

I've double-checked each file, and everything looked fine. Replacing the edited files with the original grammar files, I found the error message changes only when substituting ast_def.cpp (same error, but longer message) or ast.hpp (fatal error: more than 20 errors, mostly because a ton of variables and structures have not been defined). I'm not sure how telling this is, but I suspect the error might lie in one of these two files.

I have attached the six modified grammar files.

Thank you for your help!

best,
charles

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayesian model averaging without reversible-jump MCMC on highly-dimensional models
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Bayesian model averaging without reversible-jump MCMC on highly-dimensional models
messages.body_plain:
This is all very interesting.  I want to work it out in a simple example and then maybe I can come back to you with more questions.  In particular, I agree that cross-validation optimization methods (including stacking) will not be optimal—and, given that stacking has been around for awhile and is _not_ so popular, it probably has problems—but asymptotically it should give the right answer, no?  Regarding Aki’s other point, yes, this is a point that I have raised too, i think in my paper with Shalizi:  when we do  Bayesian continuous-parameter models, we’re doing “Bayesian model averaging” and I have no problem with it (usually), so why is BMA so bad for some (discrete) models.  I think we can understand this based on some continuous-parameter models where the interpretation of one parameter changes when another parameter changes.  Anyway, we can discuss more, I think this is important, also I agree with Bob that it can make sense to think of the mixture model, even if only as a comparison point.
A

> On Feb 8, 2016, at 5:07 PM, Aki Vehtari <Aki.V...@aalto.fi> wrote:
>
> First summary
> 1) variations of stacking make separate models and then weight the predictions
> 2) BMA is just plain Bayesian approach with model uncertainty
> 3) in usual mixture model, the mixture components affect each other
> 4) in Xian's mixture model there are additional restrictions and so far they've been able to get practical computation only for two component mixture
>
> Note that the usual mixture model is more flexible. Consider that we
> have data from t_4 and two candiate models N and t_20 (which is almost
> same as N).
> 1) separate models will be almost identical and stacking will not be
>    much different from either one
> 2) not much difference to 1 in this case
> 3) in a mixture N and t_20 can have different scales and the mixture
>    can fit long tailed t_4 much better than either single model
> 4) ..?
>
> So obviously in 1 and 2 we need to have models which behave
> differently to get anything better than a single model.
>
> Andrew:
> > What we’re talking about _does_ appear to be stacking, and I have no
> > idea why this is not a standard approach in Bayesian statistics.
>
> I think like Mike:
> > The way I like to think about it is that _conditioned on the
> > assumptions_ BMA is the mathematically self-consistent and
> > conceptually elegant right answer.
>
> Naturally the problem is "conditioned on the assumptions", so that if
> we make bad assumptions then something which is not self-consistent
> and elegant may produce better results. But if we can find a way to
> produce better results than BMA, why we don't use that same approach
> for continuous parameters if it's so good? It seems that it's possible
> to find examples where something else works better than BMA, but not
> something which would better often enough.
>
> > And why is it not in chapter 7 of BDA3?
>
> Because there hasn't been convincing theory nor convincing
> experiments. Maybe we can have it in the next edition?
>
> I've been aware of some versions of stacking. I don't remember this
> paper by Clarke, but can be also because it's not very convincing.
> Although I advocate cross-validation I haven't used cross-validation
> weighting expect for a few experiments because I haven't been aware of
> theoretical justification similar to BMA. Clarke's paper provides some
> experimental evidence but not good theoretical justification (and in
> later paper he switch mean to median). There are also some papers
> showing that point estimates of the parameters using cross-validation
> are much noisier than by optimising the marginal likelihood. Which
> raise the question why I'm advocating cross-validation for model
> selection since parameter estimation is one kind of model selection,
> too. In ... we show why we recommend cross-validation for model
> selection only if there is a small number of models. It's possible
> that when doing model averaging the noisiness is not as big problem
> when doing model averaging.
>
> BMA can be sensitive to priors if models have a large difference in
> the number of parameters, in which case "pseudo BMA" (refering to term
> pseudo Bayes factor) might be more stable, although I've seen also
> case where uniform weighting performed better than cross-validation
> weighting.
>
> BMA can also difficult to compute (although often it's possible to
> switch continuous model, like instead of spike-and-slab you can use
> hierarchical shrinkage prior), and then pseudo BMA might be quick and
> accurate enough approximation.
>
> Now I have to go to sleep, but I'll read Mike's paper which Mike
> recommended...
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Metropolis proposal rejection due to numerical imprecision in dervied parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Metropolis proposal rejection due to numerical imprecision in dervied parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Just wondering if in this case it would possibly be better to declare p as simplex in the parameter block. Then declare what is now a parameter as transformed parameter and use Jacobians to transform correctly to the parameters to which priors should be applied to and that's it, no?

The upside of this is that the simplex automatically projects things to a 1 dimensional lower space such that you get the sum-to-one constraint for free. That should avoid sampling issues.

Best,
Sebastian

On Friday, February 5, 2016 at 7:18:06 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> You're right that it's not safe to ignore the errors
> due to possible bias.
>
> You can use priors that keep values away from zero.
> Sometimes you can reduce step size so that you can
> follow the extreme curvature near zero.
>
> The problem with max(0, alpha) is that if you go the
> zero route, the gradient w.r.t. alpha gets lost.
>
> I'd guess your problem arises from the exp() operations,
> which are very arithmetically unstable (prone to underflow).
>
> So you probably want to compute log(p[n]) rather than p[n].
> There are stable components for all those calculations, such
> as log_sum_exp and log1m_exp and log1p and log1m.
>
> Unfortunately, we don't have a log-scale or logit-scale
> multinomial implemented --- the best you'll be able to do
> is softmax for multinomial.  If the counts aren't too high
> and you want to reduce it to a categorical, we have a
> categorical_logit which is better behaved.  We really need to
> do that for multinomial, too.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Feb 5, 2016, at 8:39 AM, Björn Holzhauer <bjoernh...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Dear all,
> >
> >
> >
> > I have an issue with fitting a hierarchical model in Stan using NUTS and I think I understand, why it occurs. However, I wonder whether there are typical tricks to get around this type of issue.
> >
> >
> >
> > As background: this is a hierarchical model with a bivariate normal random effect. In each experimental unit the likelihood is multinomial (5 possible outcomes). The 5 probabilities are derived parameters that can be directly calculated (via relatively complex formulae) given a realization of the bivariate random effects for an experimental unit. Two of the probabilities are typically reasonably large and cause no issues, but the other 3 probabilities will often have values very close to zero.
> >
> >
> >
> > As far as I can figure out, Stan sometimes tries to assign values just barely under zero to the derived probabilities, which is of course outside of the support of the parameters. I assume this is an issue e.g. with numerical precision. I then get a warning like:
> >
> > "Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> >
> > validate transformed params: p[1] is -0.000181243, but must be greater than or equal to 0
> >
> > If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
> >
> > but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified."
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > I suspect that I cannot just ignore this warning, because the formulae cannot actually result in negative probabilities and the probability should simply be extremely close to zero. messages.body_plain:
There's a lot of variation due to warmup.  If something's
going this slowly and it's not because of a huge density
function (that is, there are lots of leapfrog steps per
iteration), then you want to think about reparameterizing
if at all possible to remove extreme curvature and correlations.

The K-variable parameterization of the simplex with softmax
is seriously non-identified, which can often be a problem
in sampling --- it produces a narrow ridge of high density,
as described in the problematic posteriors section.

One thing you can do is move to only dealing with (K-1)
parameters, but that leads to asymmetry in the predictors.
Either that, or you need strong priors to identify the
regression.

You can speed up a lot of your loops with vectorization, e.g.,

  for (d in 1:D) {
    // Transform hyper priors to have scale = hyper-hyper prior
    // Could potentially be
    hyper_0[d] <- hyper_0_raw[d] * hyper_hyper_0;
    hyper_sex[d] <- hyper_sex_raw[d] * hyper_hyper_sex;

can become

  hyper_0 <- hyper0_raw * hyper_hyper_0;
  hyper_sex <- hyper_sex_raw * hyper_hyper_sex;

and even more importantly,

  for (d in 1:D) {
    beta_0_raw[d] ~ normal(0, 1);

can become

  to_vector(beta_0_raw) ~ normal(0, 1);

if you declare the relevant vectors/matrices instead of arrays (see the manual
chapter on arrays vs. vectors --- you need vectors to do vector
operations).

- Bob

messages.subject: modeling a cyclic phase shift parameter
messages.subject_clean: modeling a cyclic phase shift parameter
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I have a (pretty much working) periodic time series model where I'm estimating a linear combination of a harmonic basis from some data.  Normalizing the period and phase units vs. the data, I'm using Stan to sample likelihood distributions of amplitude and phase for each harmonic; the periods are a fixed value divided by powers of 2.  At the moment I'm using prior knowledge about the phase (which ranges from 0 to 1 -- the 2pi factor is being accounted for) and using a Beta prior to keep the system about where I think it should be and push away from 0 or 1.  I'm getting a decent fit between the PPC and my data, and the chains are converging well.

Q: How do I relax this prior to be U(0,1) and tell the HMC random step to let it "wrap around" freely at the ends, or get a similar effect?

The effect of the phase is of course cyclic and the fractional part in (0,1) is all that matters, i.e. the mantissa.  I don't want to rely on useful prior knowledge about the phase, and I'd rather use a U(0,1) prior where the HMC random step is allowed to wrap around off either end, so that it can shift each harmonic in either direction from any initial guess, and explore the space without penalties near 0 or 1 because those will sometimes be the best answers.

It seems like this is something that HMC should be able to cope with trivially but I'm not sure how to express it, and I would guess someone has done this kind of a model before but didn't see such a trick in the forum or the stan reference manual.  Maybe by allowing an unconstrained phase to vary arbitrarily over the reals, give it a fairly flat N(.5, 3) prior or some such, and use only the mantissa of the result as a variable in the hierarchical model to judge convergence?  Is there any direct way to tell stan "real<lower=0,upper=1,wrap=true>"?  Maybe a different representation of the phase would be better?

Any suggestions on how to accomplish this would be appreciated.  Thanks in advance.

thanks,
Hamilton

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] modeling a cyclic phase shift parameter
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] modeling a cyclic phase shift parameter
messages.body_plain:
The problem is that in an amplitude/phase basis the phase is an element
of S^{1} which cannot be mapped into the real line and hence cannot be
run immediately in Stan.  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo itself can handle these
topologies just fine, we just don’t support them in Stan at the moment.

Although it’s difficult to implement new topologies like spheres and
torii and such into Stan generally, they’re straightforward to add in
a bespoke fashion if you’re up for coding your own implementation of
HMC.  See http://arxiv.org/abs/1301.6064 for details.

Alternatively, just switch to a sin+cos basis which can be fit directly in Stan.

On Feb 10, 2016, at 2:39 AM, Hamilton Link <ham...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi there,
>
> I have a (pretty much working) periodic time series model where I'm estimating a linear combination of a harmonic basis from some data.  Normalizing the period and phase units vs. the data, I'm using Stan to sample likelihood distributions of amplitude and phase for each harmonic; the periods are a fixed value divided by powers of 2.  At the moment I'm using prior knowledge about the phase (which ranges from 0 to 1 -- the 2pi factor is being accounted for) and using a Beta prior to keep the system about where I think it should be and push away from 0 or 1.  I'm getting a decent fit between the PPC and my data, and the chains are converging well.
>
> Q: How do I relax this prior to be U(0,1) and tell the HMC random step to let it "wrap around" freely at the ends, or get a similar effect?
>
> The effect of the phase is of course cyclic and the fractional part in (0,1) is all that matters, i.e. the mantissa.  I don't want to rely on useful prior knowledge about the phase, and I'd rather use a U(0,1) prior where the HMC random step is allowed to wrap around off either end, so that it can shift each harmonic in either direction from any initial guess, and explore the space without penalties near 0 or 1 because those will sometimes be the best answers.
>
> It seems like this is something that HMC should be able to cope with trivially but I'm not sure how to express it, and I would guess someone has done this kind of a model before but didn't see such a trick in the forum or the stan reference manual.  Maybe by allowing an unconstrained phase to vary arbitrarily over the reals, give it a fairly flat N(.5, 3) prior or some such, and use only the mantissa of the result as a variable in the hierarchical model to judge convergence?  Is there any direct way to tell stan "real<lower=0,upper=1,wrap=true>"?  Maybe a different representation of the phase would be better?
>
> Any suggestions on how to accomplish this would be appreciated.  Thanks in advance.
>
> thanks,
> Hamilton

On Sunday, January 31, 2016 at 2:35:18 PM UTC-8, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> The missing data handling is OK.
>
> The covariance matrices are very slow. Models are much faster (and more
> robust arithmetically) using Cholesky factors.  We don't have the (inverse) Wishart
> implemented for Cholesky factors because we use the LKJ prior on correlation
> matrices and scale it.  I think you'll find that more flexible in terms of prior
> (choose degree of concentration for correlation matrix around the unit vector and
> flexible scale modeling).  It'll also be a whole lot faster.
>
> You also want to vectorize the multi_normal calls.
>
>   for(i in 2:Ntch[5]) {
>         theta5[i] ~ multi_normal(rep_vector(0,ih_l[5]), Gamma5);
>   }
>
> is more efficient as
>
>   theta5[2:Ntch[5]] ~ multi_normal(rep_vector(0,ih_l[5]), Gamma5);
>
> because you only need to solve (invert and determinant) Gamma5 once.
>
> I find using Gamma5 and Gamma05 as variables very confusing!
>
> There are a lot of these --- it'll make a huge difference in speed.
>
> Also vectorize this:
>
>  for(i in 1:N) {
>    ...
>    y ~ multi_normal(u[i], Sigma);
>
> Also things like rep_vector(0,ih_l[5]) can be declared as transformed
> data --- it's a bit more efficient than creating and destroying it each
> time it's used (but with just data, it's not too bad).
>
> The loops like these can be made more efficient
>
>  for (i in 1:N) {
>    u[i,1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[i,1],1];
>
> as
>
>   u[, 1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[, 1], 1];
>
> but that's not going to work until I fix the includes for our next release.
> But you can do this:
>
>   u[1:N, 1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[1:N, 1], 1];
>
> Or, you can transpose the represntation of u and tchid and just do
>
>   u[1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[1], 1];
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>
>
> > On Jan 30, 2016, at 6:42 PM, Christopher Candelaria <chris.ca...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hello all,
> >
> > My question is about the efficiency of my code. I am not sure if I am leveraging Stan properly to take advantage of all its speed to estimate a value-added model, especially in the presence of missing data in the dependent variable vector.
> >
> > Here is a brief explanation of what I am doing:
> >
> > I have a few research projects that are using Stan to perform value-added estimation using the generalized persistence model that was developed by Louis Mariano, Dan McCaffrey, and J.R. Lockwood. The model was originally coded in WinBUGS, but I have translated it into Stan code. As I understand, very few people have attempted to estimate their model because it was prohibitively slow using WinBUGS. I started out using WinBUGS, but I could not estimate the model with a large data set. I have since transitioned to Stan and have had success.
> >
> > The model leverages the longitudinal nature of student test scores; however, in many cases, student test scores are missing. The model is layered so that one can account for the full history of teachers that a student has. Here is an example:

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to implement the pmf model. According to the paper <http://www.uvm.edu/~bbeckage/Teaching/DataAnalysis/Manuals/stan-resubmit-JSS1293.pdf>, there is a prior normal distribution over the latent factor of users and items like :

u ~ normal(0,(1/alpha_u) * I)

the alpha_u is a single value and the I is a unit matrix. So the product of them is matrix too. But stan just accept single value or vector. So how can I transform the variance to fit stan's requirement? I also wonder why a unit matrix is multiplied but not a 1*k vector. Thank you in advance!

messages.body_plain:
You can get the Stan code using

stancode <- rstan::get_stancode(mod$stanfit)
cat(stancode)

or by doing

launch_shinystan(mod)

and clicking on More and then Model Code.

However, the Stan code for stan_glm (and the other modeling functions) is long and complicated because it is flexible enough to be used for all the different model formulas, priors, other options, specified by the user. So it won't look like a simple Stan model for a glm, but I guess it could be helpful to you if you're interested in some of the tricks for numerical stability, speed, etc, that we've used. If you have any questions about it let us know!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Value-added model coding question (based on Mariano, McCaffrey, and Lockwood 2010)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Value-added model coding question (based on Mariano, McCaffrey, and Lockwood 2010)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Just a general comment -- when posting and asking about syntax errors, it helps to provide the full error message. It's a lot easier to help you interpret the message when the context is available.

More below.

On Wed, Feb 10, 2016 at 5:19 AM, Christopher Candelaria <chris.ca...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I have been trying to optimizing my code using all the suggestions given, but I am running into problems using the new R-style indexing.
>

> For example, I want to do the following:
>     theta1[2:Ntch[1]] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale1, L_Gamma1)*z_theta1[2:Ntch[1]];
>     theta2[2:Ntch[2]] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale2, L_Gamma2)*z_theta2[2:Ntch[2]];
>     theta3[2:Ntch[3]] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale3, L_Gamma3)*z_theta3[2:Ntch[3]];
>     theta4[2:Ntch[4]] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale4, L_Gamma4)*z_theta4[2:Ntch[4]];
>     theta5[2:Ntch[5]] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale5, L_Gamma5)*z_theta5[2:Ntch[5]];
>
> but I am getting the following compiling error:
>
> SYNTAX ERROR, MESSAGE(S) FROM PARSER:
>
> No matches for:
>
>   matrix * vector[]
>
>

The error message is telling you that Stan doesn't know how to multiply a matrix (matrix) by an array of vectors (vector[]).
- diag_pre_multiply(scale1, L_Gamma1) results in a matrix.
- z_theta1[2:Ntch[1]] results in an array of vectors. The size of the array is (Ntch[1] - 2 + 1).

We haven't vectorized our multiplication operator to broadcast the matrix on the left to multiply by each of the vectors in the array on the right to result in a array of vectors. Vectorizing all our operators in this way is on our todo list, but it'll be a while before you see it in Stan.

> Instead, I have written the code inefficiently as:
>
>     for(i in 2:Ntch[1]) {
>         theta1[i] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale1, L_Gamma1)*z_theta1[i];
>     }
>
>     for(i in 2:Ntch[2]) {
>         theta2[i] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale2, L_Gamma2)*z_theta2[i];
>     }
>
>     for(i in 2:Ntch[3]) {
>         theta3[i] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale3, L_Gamma3)*z_theta3[i];
>     }
>
>     for(i in 2:Ntch[4]) {
>         theta4[i] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale4, L_Gamma4)*z_theta4[i];
>     }
>
>     for(i in 2:Ntch[5]) {
>         theta5[i] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale5, L_Gamma5)*z_theta5[i];
>     }
>

You should cache the diag_pre_multiply(scale1, L_Gamma1) outside the for loop.

> Similar problem but with real+real[ ] being ill formed when I do the following:
>     u[1:N,1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[1:N,1],1];
>     u[1:N,2] <- mu[2] + theta1[tchid[1:N,1],2] + theta2[tchid[1:N,2],1];
>     u[1:N,3] <- mu[3] + theta1[tchid[1:N,1],3] + theta2[tchid[1:N,2],2] +
>                       theta3[tchid[1:N,3],1];
> ...etc.
>

Sorry -- not following.

> Finally, the last block of code that is causing issues is:
>
>     z_theta1[2:Ntch[1]] ~ normal(0,1); // implies theta1[2:Ntch[1]] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zeros, L);
>     z_theta2[2:Ntch[2]] ~ normal(0,1);
>     z_theta3[2:Ntch[3]] ~ normal(0,1);
>     z_theta4[2:Ntch[4]] ~ normal(0,1);
>     z_theta5[2:Ntch[5]] ~ normal(0,1);
>

You'll have to use a loop. We've vectorized the normal distribution to allow for arrays of reals, vectors, and row vectors, but we haven't recursively vectorized it so it will automatically recurse through arrays of those structures. If you're worried about computation time for those operations, no need. It won't affect the runtime in a noticeable way by looping here.

Daniel

>
> I have attached the revised version of my program. All the suggestions thus far have been extremely helpful. I assume I must use "for" loops? Perhaps I am missing something simple.
>
> Thanks!
>
> On Sunday, January 31, 2016 at 2:35:18 PM UTC-8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > The missing data handling is OK.
> >
> > The covariance matrices are very slow. Models are much faster (and more
> > robust arithmetically) using Cholesky factors.  We don't have the (inverse) Wishart
> > implemented for Cholesky factors because we use the LKJ prior on correlation
> > matrices and scale it.  I think you'll find that more flexible in terms of prior
> > (choose degree of concentration for correlation matrix around the unit vector and
> > flexible scale modeling).  It'll also be a whole lot faster.
> >
> > You also want to vectorize the multi_normal calls.
> >
> >   for(i in 2:Ntch[5]) {
> >         theta5[i] ~ multi_normal(rep_vector(0,ih_l[5]), Gamma5);
> >   }
> >
> > is more efficient as
> >
> >   theta5[2:Ntch[5]] ~ multi_normal(rep_vector(0,ih_l[5]), Gamma5);
> >
> > because you only need to solve (invert and determinant) Gamma5 once.
> >
> > I find using Gamma5 and Gamma05 as variables very confusing!
> >
> > There are a lot of these --- it'll make a huge difference in speed.
> >
> > Also vectorize this:
> >
> >  for(i in 1:N) {
> >    ...
> >    y ~ multi_normal(u[i], Sigma);
> >
> > Also things like rep_vector(0,ih_l[5]) can be declared as transformed
> > data --- it's a bit more efficient than creating and destroying it each
> > time it's used (but with just data, it's not too bad).
> >
> > The loops like these can be made more efficient
> >
> >  for (i in 1:N) {
> >    u[i,1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[i,1],1];
> >
> > as
> >
> >   u[, 1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[, 1], 1];
> >
> > but that's not going to work until I fix the includes for our next release.
> > But you can do this:
> >
> >   u[1:N, 1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[1:N, 1], 1];
> >
> > Or, you can transpose the represntation of u and tchid and just do
> >
> >   u[1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[1], 1];
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > > On Jan 30, 2016, at 6:42 PM, Christopher Candelaria <chris.ca...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hello all,
> > >
> > > My question is about the efficiency of my code. I am not sure if I am leveraging Stan properly to take advantage of all its speed to estimate a value-added model, especially in the presence of missing data in the dependent variable vector.
> > >
> > > Here is a brief explanation of what I am doing:
> > >
> > > I have a few research projects that are using Stan to perform value-added estimation using the generalized persistence model that was developed by Louis Mariano, Dan McCaffrey, and J.R. Lockwood. The model was originally coded in WinBUGS, but I have translated it into Stan code. As I understand, very few people have attempted to estimate their model because it was prohibitively slow using WinBUGS. I started out using WinBUGS, but I could not estimate the model with a large data set. I have since transitioned to Stan and have had success.
> > >
> > > The model leverages the longitudinal nature of student test scores; however, in many cases, student test scores are missing. The model is layered so that one can account for the full history of teachers that a student has. Here is an example:
> > >
> > > y_1stgrade = mu_1 + theta_11[grade1teacher] + error_1
> > > y_2ndgrade = mu_2 + theta_12[grade1teacher] + theta_22[grade2teacher] + error_2
> > > y_3rdgrade = mu_3 + theta_13[grade1teacher] + theta_23[grade2teacher] + theta33[grade3teacher] + error_3
> > >
> > > In this model, y is the test score vector for a given student, mu is a vector of year fixed effects, and the theta variables are random effects or the effects that teachers had on student test scores. What is unique about this model is that we can obtain the effect of the teacher in the year he or she teachers as well as the effect that he or she has when the students is in a future grade.
> > >
> > > Overall, the model above and my explanation is a gross simplification of everything the model can do; I just wanted to give a brief summary. The original paper can be found using the following doi: 10.3102/1076998609346967
> > >
> > > Back to my question...
> > >
> > > I would appreciate any general feedback about my code, but I think I found a reason why my model tends to run slowly; specially, I am not sure if I am handling missing test score data values efficiently. Specifically, I have been filling in missing test score data values with parameter values as necessary. Please see lines 153 to 167 for specific details. I borrowed some code from Ben Goodrich to do this, but I am not sure if there is a better way of handling missing values given that Stan has been updated regularly over the past year. I will also say that I am trying to estimate this model using a large, district data set.
> > >
> > > Any feedback would be greatly appreciated.
> > >
> > > Thanks,
> > >
> > > Chris
> > >
> > > P.S. I am also happy to share any other details that may be needed. FYI, I am using CmdStan given the complexity of the data.

You can also solve some of these problems by redeclaring

as a matrix (just make sure the dimensions are in the right order).

And if you have a matrix u on the left of ~, you can use

  to_vector(u) ~ ...

which will be more efficient than

> On Feb 10, 2016, at 10:05 AM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
>
> Hi Chris,
>
> Just a general comment -- when posting and asking about syntax errors, it helps to provide the full error message. It's a lot easier to help you interpret the message when the context is available.
>
> More below.
>
>
> On Wed, Feb 10, 2016 at 5:19 AM, Christopher Candelaria <chris.ca...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I have been trying to optimizing my code using all the suggestions given, but I am running into problems using the new R-style indexing.
>
> For example, I want to do the following:
>     theta1[2:Ntch[1]] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale1, L_Gamma1)*z_theta1[2:Ntch[1]];
>     theta2[2:Ntch[2]] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale2, L_Gamma2)*z_theta2[2:Ntch[2]];
>     theta3[2:Ntch[3]] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale3, L_Gamma3)*z_theta3[2:Ntch[3]];
>     theta4[2:Ntch[4]] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale4, L_Gamma4)*z_theta4[2:Ntch[4]];
>     theta5[2:Ntch[5]] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale5, L_Gamma5)*z_theta5[2:Ntch[5]];
>
> but I am getting the following compiling error:
>
> SYNTAX ERROR, MESSAGE(S) FROM PARSER:
>
> No matches for:
>
>
>   matrix * vector[]
>
>
>
> The error message is telling you that Stan doesn't know how to multiply a matrix (matrix) by an array of vectors (vector[]).
> - diag_pre_multiply(scale1, L_Gamma1) results in a matrix.
> - z_theta1[2:Ntch[1]] results in an array of vectors. The size of the array is (Ntch[1] - 2 + 1).
>
> We haven't vectorized our multiplication operator to broadcast the matrix on the left to multiply by each of the vectors in the array on the right to result in a array of vectors. Vectorizing all our operators in this way is on our todo list, but it'll be a while before you see it in Stan.
>
>
> Instead, I have written the code inefficiently as:
>
>
>     for(i in 2:Ntch[1]) {
>         theta1[i] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale1, L_Gamma1)*z_theta1[i];
>     }
>
>     for(i in 2:Ntch[2]) {
>         theta2[i] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale2, L_Gamma2)*z_theta2[i];
>     }
>
>     for(i in 2:Ntch[3]) {
>         theta3[i] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale3, L_Gamma3)*z_theta3[i];
>     }
>
>     for(i in 2:Ntch[4]) {
>         theta4[i] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale4, L_Gamma4)*z_theta4[i];
>     }
>
>     for(i in 2:Ntch[5]) {
>         theta5[i] <- diag_pre_multiply(scale5, L_Gamma5)*z_theta5[i];
>     }
>
>
> You should cache the diag_pre_multiply(scale1, L_Gamma1) outside the for loop.
>
>
> Similar problem but with real+real[ ] being ill formed when I do the following:
>     u[1:N,1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[1:N,1],1];
>     u[1:N,2] <- mu[2] + theta1[tchid[1:N,1],2] + theta2[tchid[1:N,2],1];
>     u[1:N,3] <- mu[3] + theta1[tchid[1:N,1],3] + theta2[tchid[1:N,2],2] +
>                       theta3[tchid[1:N,3],1];
> ...etc.
>
>
> Sorry -- not following.
>
>
> Finally, the last block of code that is causing issues is:
>
>     z_theta1[2:Ntch[1]] ~ normal(0,1); // implies theta1[2:Ntch[1]] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zeros, L);
>     z_theta2[2:Ntch[2]] ~ normal(0,1);
>     z_theta3[2:Ntch[3]] ~ normal(0,1);
>     z_theta4[2:Ntch[4]] ~ normal(0,1);
>     z_theta5[2:Ntch[5]] ~ normal(0,1);
>
>
> You'll have to use a loop. We've vectorized the normal distribution to allow for arrays of reals, vectors, and row vectors, but we haven't recursively vectorized it so it will automatically recurse through arrays of those structures. If you're worried about computation time for those operations, no need. It won't affect the runtime in a noticeable way by looping here.
>
>
> Daniel
>
>
> I have attached the revised version of my program. All the suggestions thus far have been extremely helpful. I assume I must use "for" loops? Perhaps I am missing something simple.
>
> Thanks!
>
> On Sunday, January 31, 2016 at 2:35:18 PM UTC-8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The missing data handling is OK.
>
> The covariance matrices are very slow. Models are much faster (and more
> robust arithmetically) using Cholesky factors.  We don't have the (inverse) Wishart
> implemented for Cholesky factors because we use the LKJ prior on correlation
> matrices and scale it.  I think you'll find that more flexible in terms of prior
> (choose degree of concentration for correlation matrix around the unit vector and
> flexible scale modeling).  It'll also be a whole lot faster.
>
> You also want to vectorize the multi_normal calls.
>
>   for(i in 2:Ntch[5]) {
>         theta5[i] ~ multi_normal(rep_vector(0,ih_l[5]), Gamma5);
>   }
>
> is more efficient as
>
>   theta5[2:Ntch[5]] ~ multi_normal(rep_vector(0,ih_l[5]), Gamma5);
>
> because you only need to solve (invert and determinant) Gamma5 once.
>
> I find using Gamma5 and Gamma05 as variables very confusing!
>
> There are a lot of these --- it'll make a huge difference in speed.
>
> Also vectorize this:
>
>  for(i in 1:N) {
>    ...
>    y ~ multi_normal(u[i], Sigma);
>
> Also things like rep_vector(0,ih_l[5]) can be declared as transformed
> data --- it's a bit more efficient than creating and destroying it each
> time it's used (but with just data, it's not too bad).
>
> The loops like these can be made more efficient
>
>  for (i in 1:N) {
>    u[i,1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[i,1],1];
>
> as
>
>   u[, 1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[, 1], 1];
>
> but that's not going to work until I fix the includes for our next release.
> But you can do this:
>
>   u[1:N, 1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[1:N, 1], 1];
>
> Or, you can transpose the represntation of u and tchid and just do
>
>   u[1] <- mu[1] + theta1[tchid[1], 1];
>
> - Bob

The model was originally coded in WinBUGS, but I have translated it into Stan code. As I understand, very few people have attempted to estimate their model because it was prohibitively slow using WinBUGS. I started out using WinBUGS, but I could not estimate the model with a large data set. I have since transitioned to Stan and have had success.
> >

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to deal with the variance if it is a matrix in pmf model?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How to deal with the variance if it is a matrix in pmf model?
messages.body_plain:
If u is an N-vector and alpha_u is scalar, you can do this:

  u ~ normal(0, 1 / alpha_u);

which is just a more efficient way of writing

  for (n in 1:N)
    u[n] ~ normal(0, 1 / alpha_u);

Although you can do this:

  u ~ multi_normal(0, diag_matrix(rep_vector(N, 1/alpha_u)));

but it works out to the same density but is not nearly
as efficient or easy to read.

- Bob

Please consult the manual regarding the tuning of the mass matrix,
in particular the “metric” argument.

See Sections 1.2.2, 2.2, and the last paragraph of 5 in

an immediate plan to implement this due to the fact that the improvements
are only moderate and introduce nasty I/O complications.

I meant reparameterizing the same likelihood, not moving to an

messages.body_plain:
[ From the perspective of a strictly applied statistics practitioner ]

If I follow you, we should have a compiler for some graphical model description language (let's call it SuperBUGS, for example) which might :
extract relevant information not directly representable in Stan terms (e. g. Markov blanket of discrete parameters),
write a Stan program encoding the Stan-representable information,
run this program
read the resultant sample
use the non-Stan-representable information to massage this output in a form closer to what is expected from a graphical-model perspective (i. e. the SuperBUGS representation).
Alternatively, one could write a program working directly in the SuperBUGS description (possibly creating a graph of stochastic nodes, as do current BUGS implementations), but using NUTS and other HMC samplers as they happen to fit part of the problem.

In both cases, we would have to subsume BUGS and Stan, in two directions :
competence (i. e. the class of models representable in SuperBUGS should have both Stan-representable models and BUGS-representable models as subsets),
performance (i. e. better execution times/CPU/RAM foothold) that should be at least as good as BUGS and Stan for their respective classes of representable models.
The first item is the most important.

In both cases, what the end-user would see would be :
the ease/difficulty of representing his/her model in SuperBUGS (i. e. preparation to step 1 above)
the time/computing resources necessary to go from 1 to 5.

Am I right in my reading ?

[ A question, by the way : do you have examples of Stan-expressible models that *cannot* be represented as graphical models (not necessarily directed acyclic graphs as in BUGS), however awkwardly ? ]

My two cents (and maybe some sense... )

--
Emmanuel Charpentier

I don’t think we want to internally encode any program as a graphical model. If I interpreted Andrew correctly, all he suggested is a wrapper for people to write in some form of syntax that looks like a graphical model, and internally it only outputs the log posterior density.

Dustin

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Discrete parameters...again!
messages.body_plain:
Right --- no way to do a superset of Stan with a graphical
model that'll let us do the BUGS-like computations we want.

I see three possible benefits for having a graphical modeling
language.

1.  Allow metaprogramming.  That is, write programs that build
up graphical models.  There's a natural structure of nodes
and links to manipulate.  I really have no idea how useful this
would be, so I'd love to see some real examples from, say,
PyMC or NIMBLE, both of which should allow this.

The other use for metaprogramming would be program transformation.
We have some hope of doing that now because we get an
intermediate abstract syntax tree for all the constructs in a Stan
program.

2.  Allow forward sampling.  Right now, we can't figure out what's
a prior and what's higher level because there's no graphical structure.
We'd like to be able to automatically simulate data sets.

3.  Allow easy Markov blanket computations so we can do
conditional sampling for discrete variables, which would allow us
to have missing data, variable selection (probably won't be able
to fit in any software), direct mixture model representations, etc.

The main reason we haven't done this is that the graphical
modeling language would be more restrictive.  For example, you
could write the expectations out for an HMM or a CRF directly using
the forward/backward algorithm in Stan for efficient fitting
and code it directly in Stan's language.

- Bob

messages.subject: Multilevel serial dilution assay
messages.subject_clean: Multilevel serial dilution assay
messages.body_plain:
I think someone inquired about the code for the serial dilution assay in the paper here <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/serial.pdf>. I have also been trying to implement it. I seem to have been able to code the model overall, but some issues remain. I did modify it a bit: I included 5 parameters instead of four (but have faced the same issues with a 4-parameter model) and I adjusted the priors for my assay. Also, the model does not take days into account (the paper had 3 levels: individual plate -> plates on same day -> days).

Two issues are beyond my math skills:
First, the model always runs into large numbers of divergent transitions even with adapt_delta = 0.95.
Second, (probably related) some of the R_hat's are terrible, especially for the correlation matrix Omega.

Third, should I be worried about all the warnings regarding positive-definite matrices and other related issues?

I also don't know if I am missing opportunities to vectorize (or otherwise speed up) the code...

I included 2 models, an initial one (which has the above issues) which simply calculates the curves, and a second one (ends in "unkn") which is meant to include multilevel interpolation of samples based on the curve. I was very interested in using the multilevel prediction across dilutions of unknown samples but the paper is vague. As I understand Stan, making the prediction multilevel requires putting it in the "model" block since it is a sampling statement (rather than just in the "generated quantities" for normal interpolation, which has worked fine in other models without any multilevel aspects). However, including unknowns completely messes up the curve parameters for that plate; I have included unknown data for one of the plates. The inclusion of unknowns also slows sampling substantially, the 3000 samples in the script generally take far longer than the 6000 for the model without unknowns.

I tried to comment the models as much as I could. I also included data and unknown data along with a script.

I am currently using Microsoft R Open 3.2.3 on Windows 7 (and 10) x64 along with the MKL libraries it provides. The script calls on the Checkpoint package to ensure that all package versions are stable.
Bayesian Analysis of Serial Dilution Assays - Columbia University <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/serial.pdf>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Discrete parameters...again!
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Discrete parameters...again!
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Emmanuel.  I’d like to think of Stan as the inference engine which can work with any objective function (which is considered as a log posterior density).  What you’re calling Superbugs would be a way to write graphical models and translate them into Stan for fitting and also be able to do things like fake-data simulation and posterior predictive checking.

In answer to your final question:  I’m not sure.  But I do think that in expressing a model it can be convenient to just add terms to the log-posterior.  Expressing in terms of a graphical model can at times be awkward, compared to simply adding penalty terms to the log-posterior.

messages.body_plain:
Ok, so I've run the above simplex model using the mean posterior predictions across 4000 samples.

The trouble is that, the predictions across the 7 models are very highly autocorrelated - upwards of 0.97. This degree of correlation in the predictors means that the regression model is very unstable (sensitive to inclusion/dropping certain variables, i.e. the predictions from each model).

The sum of this is that I end up with weights that are overly-biased towards the model which produces only marginally better predictions than its nearest competitor. For example, the correlation of each of the 7 model's predictions with the outcome is approximately: 0.81, 0.849, 0.82, 0.82, 0.847, 0.83 0.81. The weights the model suggests giving to each model are: 0 1 0 0 0 0 0. Note here that model 2 essentially gets all the weight even though its nearest competitor has a correlation of only 0.002 less with the outcome. I know that in my case, since all the models are very similar in terms of prediction, that essentially the weights I should want to find should be close to 1/7. It's just that I would like to do so in a less hand-wavy, more explicit and replicable way.

Basically the issue here is one of high degrees of autocorrelation amongst regressors. A way of dealing with it might be to use a penalty for weights, although what strength to give that penalty is unclear. Perhaps I could partition the dataset into training and test sets, and choose the weight which minimises the MSE?

Does anyone else have any other ideas?

Best,

Ben
