messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multinomial distribution & regression
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Multinomial distribution & regression
messages.body_plain:
To be fair, I actually think the use of multiple Poisson models instead of a multinomial is equivalent. In MLE terms, at least, and I’ve found a few articles with a Bayesian focus saying the same. The downside is that this kind of model causes a parameter explosion. I tried to reparameterise the multinomial to a Poisson log linear (https://gist.github.com/demodw/8c16d1eaa359aa36348d), following the recipe at http://data.princeton.edu/wws509/notes/c6.pdf (page 6-7). It seems like it has a hard time adjusting, or I messed up something. It has not gotten to first iteration after a few hours, and I keep getting the errors:

"Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
validate transformed params: hyper_0[1] is -nan, but must be greater than or equal to 0
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.”

Normally this would be fine. hyper_0 is, after all, constrained to be > 0. Usually I only see the error for the first few iterations.

The last element of K should be zero. At least, I force the last element of every beta coefficient to be zero. Is there a chance the hierarchical structure or prior distributions could be causing adaptation problems? Or could it be the distribution in each group? Group 1 usually have a few million counts, whereas group2-6 are relatively rare.

David

> On 10 Feb 2016, at 20:32, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> I meant reparameterizing the same likelihood, not moving to an
> approximation.  For instance, using K-1 in softmax.  If you
> do set one of the elements to 0 in a K-vector softmax, that
> will be identified.  I must have missed that in your model.
>

I know that this is the typical frequentist approach, since it’s difficult to get a multinomial regression to converge using a MLE. Or so I’ve been told, at least.
> >
> > I thought the multinomial softmax would be fully identified by setting one of the elements to 0. That’s what I got from reading https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinomial_logistic_regression#As_a_log-linear_model at least. I am getting quite a few errors hyper_0 is -nan in the start, but I guess that is due to the constraints on the scale parameters.
> >

> > > function (that is, there are lots of leapfrog steps per
> > > iteration), then you want to think about reparameterizing
> > > if at all possible to remove extreme curvature and correlations.
> > >
> > > The K-variable parameterization of the simplex with softmax
> > > is seriously non-identified, which can often be a problem
> > > in sampling --- it produces a narrow ridge of high density,
> > > as described in the problematic posteriors section.
> > >
> > > One thing you can do is move to only dealing with (K-1)
> > > parameters, but that leads to asymmetry in the predictors.
> > > Either that, or you need strong priors to identify the
> > > regression.
> > >
> > > You can speed up a lot of your loops with vectorization, e.g.,
> > >
> > > for (d in 1:D) {
> > >   // Transform hyper priors to have scale = hyper-hyper prior
> > >   // Could potentially be

> > >

> > >   beta_0_raw[d] ~ normal(0, 1);
> > >
> > > can become
> > >
> > > to_vector(beta_0_raw) ~ normal(0, 1);
> > >
> > > if you declare the relevant vectors/matrices instead of arrays (see the manual
> > > chapter on arrays vs. vectors --- you need vectors to do vector
> > > operations).
> > >
> > > - Bob

Hi all,

For a model I'm currently optimizing I get to the objective tolerance I need considerably faster using Newton than LBFGS/BFGS. This got me curious how Newton was actually getting the Hessian, and it seems from what I understand of the code it's some hybrid of autodiff and finite differences which is O(N^2) - is that correct? Also from the Stan math code it seems full autodiff for the Hessian would be O(N^3) in general, which is presumably why you're not using that by default?

Thanks!

David.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hessians
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Hessians
messages.body_plain:
Is this a very simple problem or might it be a tuning issue
with our L-BFGS?

Full autodiff for Hessians requires N passes, so
it's O(N*f(N)) where f(N) is the cost of the density eval,
which is usually just N, so it's usually O(N^2).  It gets
worse if there are operations like matrix factorizations
involved, where it usually goes up to O(N^2.5).

The reason we haven't used autodiff everywhere for Hessians
is lack of thorough testing, but we have everything at least basically
tested now, so we're going to be switching over to autodiff.

- Bob

Hi Chris,

The format used to read from the data file isn't quite native R. I believe technical details on what's allowed is in the CmdStan manual, but it's really not worth reading.

The quick fix is to change x to:
x <-
structure(c(1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 3, 1, 4, 1, 2, 2, 1),
.Dim = c(15, 1))

If you're using R to export the data, I'd suggest using rstan's stan_rdump() function. It handles edge cases better than just using dump() in R.

Daniel

messages.subject: Using loo::loo() when some data points have high Pareto k estimate
messages.subject_clean: Using loo::loo() when some data points have high Pareto k estimate
messages.body_plain:
Suppose that I run

    loo_obj <- loo::loo(log_lik_sample)

and find that data points i[1], ..., i[n] have Pareto k estimates >= 0.5. Following the advice in the documentation, I rerun explicit leave-one-out estimations, sampling from p(θ | y_{-i[j]}) to get improved elpd estimates and accompanying standard errors for data points i_1, ..., i_n.

How do I combine these results with the information in loo_obj to compute elpd_loo and its standard error? If I understand correctly, I can get a new elpd_loo estimate by taking loo_obj$pointwise[ , 'elpd_loo'], replacing the entries for i_1, ..., i_n, and summing the result. But how do I recompute se_elpd_loo?
messages.body_snippet:

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew,

Whilst each model does yield similar predictions, in terms of parameters of interest, they differ. In particular, I am looking at determinants of organisms' mean lifetimes, through mark-release-recapture studies.

Different assumptions can be made about how mortality varies with time, and dependent on the particular assumption made, this results in different predictions on mean lifetime. However, the crucial problem we have is that most studies are too short, or have too-low sample sizes, for us to differentiate between the different models in terms of their LOO-CV/WAIC; within error bounds of these criteria, all models perform relatively similarly.

As such, I want to take this epistemic uncertainty in model choice into account when making estimating mean lifetime, by using some sort of weighting, where the weights are determined by just how well each model predicts the data. Intuitively, since each of the models does a similarly-good job of predicting the data, we would like assign roughly equal weights to each model's estimates. It's just whether there is a more data-driven way to find these weights.

One particularly crude, and non-theory-derived way to do this would be to use something like:

weight of model i = 1 - (LOO-CV_i /(sum of LOO-CV across all models)

This would mean model i would be assigned a high weight if it has a good predictive accuracy, manifested through a low value of LOO-CV. Note: I only bring this up as a point for discussion, and am not actually suggesting that this is a sensible thing to do. I am only thinking that the above rule would get me approximately what I intuition suggests might be sensible.

Best,

Ben

Hi!

I am confused by the convention in stan-math for Jacobians. Assume I have a function f(x) which produces m=1...M outputs from n=1...N inputs x_n. Then I would expect the Jacobian matrix to be a M x N matrix with the usual definition:

df_m/dx_n = J_m,n

This is in line with what is written in the arXiv paper on page 13. However, the implementation in

math <https://github.com/stan-dev/math>/stan <https://github.com/stan-dev/math/tree/develop/stan>/math <https://github.com/stan-dev/math/tree/develop/stan/math>/rev <https://github.com/stan-dev/math/tree/develop/stan/math/rev>/mat <https://github.com/stan-dev/math/tree/develop/stan/math/rev/mat>/functor <https://github.com/stan-dev/math/tree/develop/stan/math/rev/mat/functor>/jacobian.hpp

returns the transpose of this matrix, i.e. I get a N x M matrix with elements J_n,m ... why is that? If so, then this is inconsistent with what is claimed to be the Jacobian on page 14.

Or did I read the code wrong? I am quite new to using stan-math, so please correct me here if I am wrong.

Thanks!

Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

at the moment i'm working on a model for growth prediction of trees for many species. So far it is working - but I think I need a little help with speed improvements for my model. I wrote the vectorized form where it was possible - the "MATT-Trick" is not really clear to me - and if I can use it here.
The input-data for the model are ~ 160.000 individuals within 217 species. The model takes really long to converge (Rhat <1.2) - like 7 days with 4 chains, 100.000 Iterations and 50.000 warmup Iterations - each chain running on a different core at a cluster. Is there a possibility of improvement of my code or something else I could check?

Thank you in advance!

messages.body_plain:
I'm sure that's my fault.  I can never keep these things
straight.

According to this:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_matrix_and_determinant

if f: R^N -> R^M, then the Jacobian should be M x N

But in

  math/rev/mat/functor/jacobian.hpp

you're right that the return is N x M.  I'm opening an issue:

https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/230

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is slow warmup indicative of 'necessity' or potentially wasteful?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Is slow warmup indicative of 'necessity' or potentially wasteful?
messages.body_plain:
I'm afraid we don't yet have a way to specify the mass matrix
for a run, but that's coming soon.  Then you will be able to warm
start everything.

You can look at the traceplot to see what's going on.  Sometimes
you need a different step size for the tails than the high mass
volume and Stan needs to adjust during warmup.

In addition to having reasonable priors, it helps immensely if
all the parameters are roughly unit scaled on the unconstrained
scale.  Stan transforms all constrained variables to be unconstrained
(see manual for transforms) and applies the Jacobian of the inverse
transforms automatically.  So you have to reason through what's going
on in the unconstrained space to really understand how Stan samples.

The closer you can get that to being unit normal on the margins
with no correlations, the easier time Stan will have sampling with
Euclidean HMC.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Some further speed improvement for Hierarchical Model possible?
messages.body_plain:
We also very strongly advise against those interval constrained
priors for both statistical and computational reasons.

You shouldn't need those 0.0001 lower bounds either.

You might want to make pred a local variable so it doesn't get saved
each iteration.

You have uniform distributions that don't match their constraints.
All parameters needs support (finite log density) on any values
that satisfy their constraints (that'd be sigma_sp, but I didn't
look for more).

It looks like you only have distribution on a_ind[i] if
(repind[i] == 1).  The rest of the a_ind will just be uniform over
(-4, 4).

And you definitely want the non-centered parameterization for all the
parameters that don't get normal(0, 1) priors (what we used to
call the "Matt trick").  See the manual for an explanation.  But the
basic idea is to replace

  u ~ normal(mu_u, sigma_u);

with

  u_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

  u <- mu_u + sigma_u * u_raw;

You can either do that literally with local variables or implicitly
wherever you use u.

- Bob

Hi John, There’s an init argument which enables you to specify the means in the original (possibly constrained) latent variable space; see CmdStan manual for more details. I don’t believe we currently support initialization in the transformed/unconstrained space(?). It should be the same as if MCMC initializations supports it.

If you know the transformations beforehand, which are given in the manual, you can of course apply the inverse of the functions to your desired transformed parameters, and use them as initializations on the original parameter space.

Dustin

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Multilevel serial dilution assay
messages.body_plain:
Hi…it’s been a few years since I worked on this. . . . I actually fit the model in Bugs, believe it or not!  One thing I remember for real data was that if you have some unknowns with zero concnentrations, the model can have problems because the lognormal model on the unknown concentrations won’t make sense.  In that case we needed to go with a mixture model.  Also, the model I fit did not have any correlation matrix.  I think that your problems are coming from letting all 5 betas vary like this. I’d suggest just keeping the betas constant, or maybe just varying one of them, not all 5.
A

> On Feb 10, 2016, at 5:45 PM, Joanthan Audet <jona...@hotmail.com> wrote:
>

> I think someone inquired about the code for the serial dilution assay in the paper here <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/serial.pdf>. I have also been trying to implement it. I seem to have been able to code the model overall, but some issues remain. I did modify it a bit: I included 5 parameters instead of four (but have faced the same issues with a 4-parameter model) and I adjusted the priors for my assay. Also, the model does not take days into account (the paper had 3 levels: individual plate -> plates on same day -> days).
>
> Two issues are beyond my math skills:
> First, the model always runs into large numbers of divergent transitions even with adapt_delta = 0.95.
> Second, (probably related) some of the R_hat's are terrible, especially for the correlation matrix Omega.
>
> Third, should I be worried about all the warnings regarding positive-definite matrices and other related issues?
>
> I also don't know if I am missing opportunities to vectorize (or otherwise speed up) the code...
>
> I included 2 models, an initial one (which has the above issues) which simply calculates the curves, and a second one (ends in "unkn") which is meant to include multilevel interpolation of samples based on the curve. I was very interested in using the multilevel prediction across dilutions of unknown samples but the paper is vague. As I understand Stan, making the prediction multilevel requires putting it in the "model" block since it is a sampling statement (rather than just in the "generated quantities" for normal interpolation, which has worked fine in other models without any multilevel aspects). However, including unknowns completely messes up the curve parameters for that plate; I have included unknown data for one of the plates. The inclusion of unknowns also slows sampling substantially, the 3000 samples in the script generally take far longer than the 6000 for the model without unknowns.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How long it may take to train the stan model?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How long it may take to train the stan model?
messages.body_plain:
For a start, I'd use a scale parameterization rather than
a sqrt(precision) one.  And include priors.

You want to vectorize those sampling statements (which
means converting the arrays of vectors to matrices --- indexing
with one index still provides a row vector).

You want to remove the unused definition of I.

And you want to move r_new to be defined in generated quantities
using normal_rng:

generated quantities {
  real<lower=0, upper=5> r_new[D_new]; //pridict rating
  for (d in 1:D_New)
    r_new[d] <- normal_rng(...);
}

But that won't quite work, because there's no guarantee the
result is in (0, 5).  You probably want to do this all on
the log-odds scale (logit link).

Then, when everything's fixed, try fitting simulated data
at a reasonable scale where you know the answer to make sure
you're getting the right answers.

- Bob

OK, I now realize I may have misunderstood section 2.6 of the paper. That multivariate normal is for each parameter across plates, not for each plate across parameters, i.e. the matrix sigma describes correlation of a single parameter across plates, correct?

On Saturday, 13 February 2016 00:30:56 UTC-6, Andrew Gelman wrote:

> Hi…it’s been a few years since I worked on this. . . . I actually fit the model in Bugs, believe it or not!  One thing I remember for real data was that if you have some unknowns with zero concnentrations, the model can have problems because the lognormal model on the unknown concentrations won’t make sense.  In that case we needed to go with a mixture model.  Also, the model I fit did not have any correlation matrix.  I think that your problems are coming from letting all 5 betas vary like this. I’d suggest just keeping the betas constant, or maybe just varying one of them, not all 5.
> A

I did modify it a bit: I included 5 parameters instead of four (but have faced the same issues with a 4-parameter model) and I adjusted the priors for my assay. Also, the model does not take days into account (the paper had 3 levels: individual plate -> plates on same day -> days).

You need to place constraints on the parameters in the declaration to deal with this, it's the <lower=min(OD), upper=...>, since you have three parameters and two constraints it's not too straightforward but should be doable.

When I pull out x I get:

log(x) = log(beta_3) + 1/beta_4 * (log(y-beta_1) - 1/beta_4 * log(beta_1+beta_2-y))

Based on your stated constraints: beta_1 < OD < beta_1 + beta_2, I think you need to change to something similar to:

real<upper=min(OD)> beta_1;
real<lower=OD-beta_1> beta_2;

Not checked for algebra/syntax but you get the idea.  It would be cool to see this model working well---I RA'd in an analytical chemistry lab for much of my undergrad and I kept thinking model-based calibration would be a great idea.  We did a lot of other quantitative stuff but never this.  Feel free to post more questions if there are other issues with it!

I wouldn't worry about modeling log_tau instead.  When you declare it as:

 vector<lower = 0>[5] tau;

Stan (hoping I get this right) internally uses log(tau) as a parameter (on the real line).

If the posterior really looks a lot like the prior I would wonder whether there's much information about it in the data, or if it's not well identified.  Since you can do these models plate-by-plate there ought to be... making the prior tighter is not going to solve this issue so I would avoid normal(.25,.1) and try to understand the model better.  If you can currently fit the model (even without unknowns) I would run that version and look at the pairs plots of other parameters with tau and see if some are highly or non-linearly correlated with it.

Also looks like the OD line (OD ~ normal(cOD, sigma_idiv);) and the parent cOD calculation makes a lot more sense now with the paper.

messages.body_plain:
> On Feb 14, 2016, at 10:07 AM, Zichao Li <ryla...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> @Bob, tons of thanks for your patience and answer. Your explanation is quite clear but I am just a little bit confused of something, as I am quite newbie to stan. Do you mean change the
> for (d in 1:D){
>         r[d] ~ normal(..., alpha);
>     }
> to
> for (d in 1:D){
>         r[d] ~ normal(..., alpha^2);
>     }
> by "use a scale parameterization rather than a sqrt(precision) one" and add a prior distribution over alpha?

Stan parameterizes the normal using standard deviation.
Most ath notation uses variance, which is std-dev^2.
BUGS uses precision, which is 1 / variance.

I just meant that if you were parameterizing in terms of alpha
and then using normal(..., 1 / alpha), then alpha is the sqrt
of the precision.   I suggested just making sigma a std
deviation and using normal(..., sigma) as in all the examples
in our manual.

BUGS tended use gamma priors for precision or inverse gammas
for variance because of conjugacy --- Stan doesn't require conjugacy
for efficiency.

> And is there any example of limiting the value in a certain range in the stan manual? Thank you so much.

If there is for anything other than a probability, it's
probably a mistake.  We're trying to discourage interval
bounds for anything other than physical/conceptual constraints.

- Bob

> Regarding tau, I did make it half-normal, its values in the posterior are all 0.05-0.5 so right now I think I put a normal(0.25, 0.1) prior on it. Would it be better to model log_tau instead?

> On Feb 13, 2016, at 7:38 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I wouldn't worry about modeling log_tau instead.  When you declare it as:
>
>  vector<lower = 0>[5] tau;
>
> Stan (hoping I get this right) internally uses log(tau) as a parameter (on the real line).

Right.  Each element of tau gets log transformed to be unconstrained
and Stan operates on the unconstrained space.  The log transform is only
used for user-specified inits;  otherwise, Stan operates on the unconstrained
space directly and uses  exp() to map back to the positive-only values (with
the Jacobian for sampling and VB but not optimization).

There's a chapter near the end of the manual that lists all the transforms.

- Bob

>
> > On Feb 14, 2016, at 10:07 AM, Zichao Li <ryla...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > @Bob, tons of thanks for your patience and answer. Your explanation is quite clear but I am just a little bit confused of something, as I am quite newbie to stan. Do you mean change the
> > for (d in 1:D){
> >         r[d] ~ normal(..., alpha);
> >     }
> > to
> > for (d in 1:D){
> >         r[d] ~ normal(..., alpha^2);
> >     }
> > by "use a scale parameterization rather than a sqrt(precision) one" and add a prior distribution over alpha?
>
> Stan parameterizes the normal using standard deviation.
> Most ath notation uses variance, which is std-dev^2.
> BUGS uses precision, which is 1 / variance.
>
> I just meant that if you were parameterizing in terms of alpha
> and then using normal(..., 1 / alpha), then alpha is the sqrt
> of the precision.   I suggested just making sigma a std
> deviation and using normal(..., sigma) as in all the examples
> in our manual.
>
> BUGS tended use gamma priors for precision or inverse gammas
> for variance because of conjugacy --- Stan doesn't require conjugacy
> for efficiency.
>
> > And is there any example of limiting the value in a certain range in the stan manual? Thank you so much.
>
> If there is for anything other than a probability, it's
> probably a mistake.  We're trying to discourage interval
> bounds for anything other than physical/conceptual constraints.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Parallel compilation in Stan?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Parallel compilation in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
It's down to the complexity of the template metaprogramming in C++. It's between the complexity of the Stan math library, Boost, and Eigen.

If you're really interested in finding out what's causing the C++ compiler to be incredibly slow, take a look at the generated C++ header file.

Also, try changing compiler optimization flags. I've seen a lot of variation in compile time (and run time) with the different levels.

Daniel

if you are installing rstan for the first time on that computer.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
The second parameter of the normal is a scale parameter
and the std-dev of a normal is the scale.  You don't want
to be squaring that variable --- it's not a variance parameter.

You probably do want to provide some kind of prior, but probably
not one that keeps it away from zero.

You want to figure out which normal is causing your problem and
ask whether 0 is consistent as an SD.  I'm not sure the hierarchical
priors are buying you  much for the factors.

Also, just a fair warning:  factor models are very hard to fit.

I'm appending a working example with some simulation code, and you see
that the autocorrelations in the fits are huge, so it'd require a lot
of samples to fit well.

- Bob

data {
  int<lower=0> I;
  int<lower=0> J;

  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=1, upper=I> ii[N];
  int<lower=1, upper=J> jj[N];
  real y[N];

  int<lower=0> K;
}
parameters {
  row_vector[K] alpha[I];
  vector[K] beta[J];
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
  sigma ~ normal(0, 1);
  for (i in 1:I) alpha[i] ~ normal(0, 1);
  for (j in 1:J) beta[j] ~ normal(0, 1);
  for (n in 1:N) y[n] ~ normal(alpha[ii[n]] * beta[jj[n]], sigma);
}

===========================

library(rstan);
I <- 200;
J <- 100;
K <- 3;
N <- 10000;

alpha <- matrix(rnorm(I * K), I, K);
beta <- matrix(rnorm(J * K), J, K);
sigma <- 0.75;
ii <- sample(1:I, N, replace=TRUE);
jj <- sample(1:J, N, replace=TRUE);
y <- rep(NA, N);
for (n in 1:N) {
  y[n] <- rnorm(1, t(alpha[ii[n],]) %*% beta[jj[n],], sigma);
}

fit <- stan("pmf.stan", data=c("I", "J", "K", "N", "ii", "jj", "y"),
            chains=1, iter=5000, refresh=50);

Jökull, if you're using g++ 4.2, then you're going to get much better performance with clang++ for compilation time. There isn't any blanket advice we can give you -- at this point, you'll have to figure out how the C++ interacts with the compiler you are using. messages.body_plain:
I'm not surprised that a 10K line program would take 90+
minutes to compile.  A 100 line program takes over a minute
with g++.

I think rather than generating ever-larger Stan programs,
you'd be better off generating some C++ and integrating that way.
Or pushing more work into functions and less into straight
generated code.

But if you can't share the code or concepts, we can't help
beyond generalities.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
OK, I did what Andrew did and made an estimator for each plate, I did try to make some parameters multilevel but that makes for atrocious sampling and does not help with prediction. I think I figured out how unknown estimation is done in the paper, I was going to write "see above" but it appears my email failed me (which explains why no one reacted to it...). The advantage is that there is no need to deal with the beta1 < OD < beta1 + beta2 constraint. I added some generated quantities to keep track of the variation in coefficients between the plates and named the coefficients for their function.

I only have one question left:

Is there some vectorisation or optimization that I am missing, or something that can be reparameterized better? Every now and then (on the exact same data) I get a complete chain of divergent transitions (and the other 3 chains are quite fine) and the model takes 25 minutes (on my computer) to generate 4000 draws (including 1500 warmup). Using shinystan, I could not relate divergent transitions to any specific parameter. The chains also look a bit correlated.

On Saturday, 13 February 2016 18:38:51 UTC-6, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:

> On Saturday, February 13, 2016 at 5:45:37 PM UTC-5, Jonathan Audet wrote:
> >
> > The model without the unknown, while still having sampling issues, actually retrodicts the curves quite well already.
> >
> > I am including a corrected script, I noticed some missing functions in the original one. Also, a version of the curve-only model with the cholesky decomposition.
>
> That's great! Thanks for sharing the improved code.
>
> >
> > Regarding tau, I did make it half-normal, its values in the posterior are all 0.05-0.5 so right now I think I put a normal(0.25, 0.1) prior on it. Would it be better to model log_tau instead?
>
> I wouldn't worry about modeling log_tau instead.  When you declare it as:
>
>  vector<lower = 0>[5] tau;
>
> Stan (hoping I get this right) internally uses log(tau) as a parameter (on the real line).
>
> If the posterior really looks a lot like the prior I would wonder whether there's much information about it in the data, or if it's not well identified.  Since you can do these models plate-by-plate there ought to be... making the prior tighter is not going to solve this issue so I would avoid normal(.25,.1) and try to understand the model better.  If you can currently fit the model (even without unknowns) I would run that version and look at the pairs plots of other parameters with tau and see if some are highly or non-linearly correlated with it.
>
> Also looks like the OD line (OD ~ normal(cOD, sigma_idiv);) and the parent cOD calculation makes a lot more sense now with the paper.
>
> Krzysztof
>
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > Sent from  Mail <https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?LinkId=550986> for Windows 10
> >
> >
> >
> > From: Krzysztof Sakrejda
> > Sent: February 13, 2016 3:29 PM
> > To: Stan users mailing list
> > Subject: [stan-users] Re: Multilevel serial dilution assay
> >
> >
> > On Saturday, February 13, 2016 at 2:04:08 PM UTC-5, Jonathan Audet wrote:
> > > I will try out your suggestions today.
> > >
> > > Regarding the unknown calculations, I have to admit I don't quite follow the reasoning of section 3.2 of the paper. In the context of least-squares fit, I would just isolate x instead of y and work from there. This is what I did here. But that method is only valid if "y" is between the bottom and top, each of which moves with the state of the sampler.
> > >
> >
> > You need to place constraints on the parameters in the declaration to deal with this, it's the <lower=min(OD), upper=...>, since you have three parameters and two constraints it's not too straightforward but should be doable.
> >
> > When I pull out x I get:
> >
> > log(x) = log(beta_3) + 1/beta_4 * (log(y-beta_1) - 1/beta_4 * log(beta_1+beta_2-y))
> >
> > Based on your stated constraints: beta_1 < OD < beta_1 + beta_2, I think you need to change to something similar to:
> >
> > real<upper=min(OD)> beta_1;
> > real<lower=OD-beta_1> beta_2;
> >
> > Not checked for algebra/syntax but you get the idea.  It would be cool to see this model working well---I RA'd in an analytical chemistry lab for much of my undergrad and I kept thinking model-based calibration would be a great idea.  We did a lot of other quantitative stuff but never this.  Feel free to post more questions if there are other issues with it!
> >
> > Krzysztof
> >
> >
> >
> > > On Saturday, 13 February 2016 08:40:31 UTC-6, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
> > > > I looked through the model and here are the issues I noticed:
> > > >
> > > > - Use lkj_corr_cholesky instead of lkj_corr (section 51.2 in the 2.9 manual).
> > > > - It would help to figure out the appropriate scale for tau, and perhaps at least while you are figuring out the model make it half-normal.
> > > > - This:
> > > >
> > > > //Use the current parameters to calculate the interpolated concentration of each unknown value.
> > > > //The OD (Y value) must be higher than the bottom asymptote (beta[1]) and lower than the top asymptote (beta[1] + beta[2]) or RStan throws an error at the end (for RStan > 2.6).
> > > > //So any value outside the asymptotes gets the "marker value" of -50. Additional R-side commands deal with this afterwards.
> > > > for(i in 1:N_unkn){
> > > >   vector[5] beta;
> > > >   beta <- exp(logBeta[pID_unkn[i]]);
> > > >   if(Unknown[i] > beta[1] && Unknown[i] < (beta[1] + beta[2])){
> > > >     indiv_theta[i] <- log10((beta[3] / pow(pow((beta[1] - (beta[1] + beta[2])) / (beta[1] - Unknown[i]), 1 / beta[5]) - 1, -1 / beta[4])) * Dilution[i]);
> > > >   } else {
> > > >     indiv_theta[i] <- -50;
> > > >   }
> > > >
> > > > This should be (?) generating a warning about using a non-linear transform on the LHS of a sampling statement, ultimately associated with the line:
> > > >
> > > >    indiv_theta[i] ~ normal(theta[uID[i]], sigma_unkn);
> > > >
> > > > So that's not quite the model you think it is.  I don't quite see how this version matches up with with the article so I won't try to make more detailed comments on it but it looks like you could simplify this a fair bit---I don't think the '-50' flag value should be necessary in this model.
> > > >
> > > > Krzysztof
> > > >
> > > > On Wednesday, February 10, 2016 at 5:45:35 PM UTC-5, Jonathan Audet wrote:
> > > > > I think someone inquired about the code for the serial dilution assay in the paper  here <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/serial.pdf>. I have also been trying to implement it. I seem to have been able to code the model overall, but some issues remain. I did modify it a bit: I included 5 parameters instead of four (but have faced the same issues with a 4-parameter model) and I adjusted the priors for my assay. Also, the model does not take days into account (the paper had 3 levels: individual plate -> plates on same day -> days).
> > > > >
> > > > > Two issues are beyond my math skills:
> > > > > First, the model always runs into large numbers of divergent transitions even with adapt_delta = 0.95.
> > > > > Second, (probably related) some of the R_hat's are terrible, especially for the correlation matrix Omega.

> > > > > I included 2 models, an initial one (which has the above issues) which simply calculates the curves, and a second one (ends in "unkn") which is meant to include multilevel interpolation of samples based on the curve. As I understand Stan, making the prediction multilevel requires putting it in the "model" block since it is a sampling statement (rather than just in the "generated quantities" for normal interpolation, which has worked fine in other models without any multilevel aspects). However, including unknowns completely messes up the curve parameters for that plate; I have included unknown data for one of the plates. The inclusion of unknowns also slows sampling substantially, the 3000 samples in the script generally take far longer than the 6000 for the model without unknowns.

On Monday, February 15, 2016 at 8:31:37 PM UTC-5, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
> I just got done reading the vignette "Estimating Regularized Linear Models with rstanarm," and I'm having a hard time making sense of its description / derivation of the R2 prior. Is there a paper that goes into this prior in more detail?

No, there isn't. I would say that the less you think about it, the easier it is to understand. What do you think the prior location (mode by default if K > 2) of the R^2 is? The answer to that question pins down the single hyperparameter to the joint prior on the coefficients. Marginally, each coefficient has a symmetric prior centered at zero with fairly heavy tails (although how heavy depends on the hyperparameter).

Ben

messages.subject_clean: Question on cutpoint prior for stan_polr
messages.body_plain:
I'm reading through the vignette "Estimating Ordinal Regression Models with rstanarm," and in the discussion of the cutpoint prior I'm getting confused as to what we are conditioning on when using the distribution for y^*.

It says that we specify a Dirichlet prior on \pi, where

  \pi_j = Pr(y = j | \bar{x})

I understand this to mean the conditional probability that y = j when x is set to its mean in the data set.

Later on it says that the j-th cutpoint is given by F^{-1}(p), where

  p = SUM(i: 1 <= i <= j: \pi_j))

and F is the cumulative probability distribution for y^*. Which distribution?

1. The distribution p(y^* | R)?
2. The distribution p(y^* | R, x = \bar{x})?

The definition of \pi implies that (2) is the distribution used to define the cutpoints... but then the vignette states that the scale parameter is \sigma_{y^*}, which implies that (1) is the defining distribution.

My model is somehow of the form:

totalRevenue (y) ~    X1  + X2  + X3 + (X2|country)+(X2|group)

X1, X2, and X3 continous. I’ve tried to re-scale (centred and divided by sigma) them before running model as I was getting messages that they were in different scales.

    R^2(X, beta, \tilde{y}),

    ER2(beta) = E[R^2 | X, beta, \sigma_{\eps}],
where the expectation is over \tilde{y}, and X and \sigma_{\eps} are taken as fixed?

Or do you mean something else entirely?

Hi Ana,

Sorry you're running into these issues. Some comments and questions below:

On Monday, February 15, 2016 at 10:17:48 PM UTC-5, AM Madrigal wrote:
> Hello all,
>
> I’m trying to run a model using rstan arm, but I am having some problems and unsure where can I find more advise.

You found the right place!

>
> Questions /comments.

> I tried changing the algorithm to “meanfield” and “fullrank” to test models but output seems quite random and it sometimes comes out with errors, sometimes it just goes quiet with no feedback and doesn’t create model, sometimes it gives some answers, mainly with warnings of not coverging and when it doesn’t complain I am unsure how to check convergence as there is no Rhat statistic…So have kept it again to the MCMC, which takes long so I don’t get immediate feedback , but at least when it doesn’t collapse, I seem to be able to assess convergence or use the shinystan (which is really good!! Congrats!)…

When you say it "goes quiet with no feedback and doesn't create the model" do you mean nothing at all happens when you run the code? When it errors, are the messages about "numeric overflow"? Those do seem to happen occasionally with the variational algorithms. If it does converge it should say "MEDIAN ELBO CONVERGED", although that's not the same sort of convergence as for MCMC, which is why there is no Rhat statistic. That said, there has been some discussion of developing something similar to Rhat, but we haven't gotten there yet.

> I tried centering the response (so I have positive and negatives) and use a gaussian and I do get some results converging after some time, however, the ppcheck shows that the normal doesn’t really fit the response which is quite skewed.

Have you tried a log transformation of the positive response in combination with a gaussian likelihood?

> I tried a family=Gamma, which seems conceptually a better option for my response. It doesn’t converge.
> I tried adjusting the link to see if that helped, but it drops the “link= “ parameter fromt he function… I followed the usual glm specification of the family-link, but it doesn’t work, do you know how do I specify different links (e.g. Identity/ inverse / log)

The link parameter should work the way you describe. How do you know it's ignoring it? I just tried out a few stan_glmer models with family = Gamma(link = "inverse") and family = Gamma(link = "log") and they seem to be ok.

> I have tried adapt_delta to higher values like 0.98 / 0.99, and still not convergence

By not convergence do you mean you're getting warnings about divergences? Or bad looking trace plots / large Rhat values?

> There was a comment in one of the feedbacks about increasing the value for tree depth, but I haven’t find exactly how I pass that to the stan_glmer () .. I tried: "control = list(max_treedepth = 20)”, but it seems to ignore / drop it. Any ideas in how to make that go through?

control = list(max_treedepth = 20) is the right way to do it. I just double checked and I think it's working properly. If you specify control = list(max_treedepth = 20) and then run a model, what it does it say if you then look at model$stanfit@stan_args[[1]]$control, which will pull out the internal control arguments used?

> I’ve tried adding some priors to the coefficients , but maybe I need some more appropriate / vaguer ones, as when I add, the process goes into limbo. So for the moment leaving that out.
> in the priors: when writing BUGs-type code, one usually specify one distribution for each of the parameters... in here it all seems to be collapsed by the "priors" option. I probably don't need to add different priors for each coefficient and I'm guessing priors for variances are ok to leave as "default"

In rstanarm, the location and scale arguments for the different priors (e.g. normal, student_t, etc) can be vectors if you want to provide different values for the different coefficients. If they're just scalars then the values are replicated to the appropriate length.

> Basic question: when specifying the priors in rstanarm, does it follow usual R convention where the scale is the standard deviation? or does it refer to "precisions" (1/sigma2).

Yes, scale is the standard deviation.

Also, which version of rstanarm are you using? There is a new version on CRAN that we haven't announced yet because the binaries might still be building, but I think for now at least the RStudio CRAN mirror it should be available. So I would definitely update to the most recent version if you haven't already.

Best,

Jonah

messages.subject_clean: Question on cutpoint prior for stan_polr
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, February 15, 2016 at 9:55:40 PM UTC-5, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
> I'm reading through the vignette "Estimating Ordinal Regression Models with rstanarm," and in the discussion of the cutpoint prior I'm getting confused as to what we are conditioning on when using the distribution for y^*.
>
> It says that we specify a Dirichlet prior on \pi, where
>
>   \pi_j = Pr(y = j | \bar{x})
>
> I understand this to mean the conditional probability that y = j when x is set to its mean in the data set.

Correct.

> Later on it says that the j-th cutpoint is given by F^{-1}(p), where
>
>   p = SUM(i: 1 <= i <= j: \pi_j))
>
> and F is the cumulative probability distribution for y^*. Which distribution?

This depends on whether you are estimating an ordered logit model, an ordered probit model, etc. In the case of an ordered logit model, F() is the scaled logistic CDF.

This is one of the few cases where the relevant code is actually pretty readable. It is the make_cutpoints() function at

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstanarm/blob/master/exec/polr.stan

>
> 1. The distribution p(y^* | R)?
> 2. The distribution p(y^* | R, x = \bar{x})?
>
> The definition of \pi implies that (2) is the distribution used to define the cutpoints... but then the vignette states that the scale parameter is \sigma_{y^*}, which implies that (1) is the defining distribution.

You can choose the Dirichlet prior on the simplex vector whose typical element is \pi_j without conditioning on the R matrix. This prior also determines the distribution of the cumulative sum of these probabilities, and then you can use the scaled inverse CDF to figure out what set of cutpoints is consistent with those cumulative probabilities.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: R2 prior in stan_lm
messages.subject_clean: R2 prior in stan_lm
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, February 15, 2016 at 10:22:12 PM UTC-5, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
> R^2 is defined for a particular design matrix X, coefficient vector beta, and response vector y... so it's unclear to me what is meant by a prior for R^2.

That is the usual way of looking at the R^2 in a OLS context, yes. However, the R^2 is invariant to a rotation of the design matrix X, so we can utilize its QR decomposition to go from

y_hat = X * beta = (QR) * beta = Q * (R * beta) = Q * theta

where theta = R * beta. So, you can think of this as a regression of y on Q and then beta = R^{-1} * theta is a generated quantity.

Okay, so what is the prior distribution on theta, the vector of coefficients for Q? Since Q'Q = I, theta_k can be conceptualized as the correlation between y and the k-th column of Q multiplied by the standard deviation of y, divided by the standard deviation of the k-th column of Q which is the square root of N - 1.

That pushes back the question to what is your prior on the correlations between y and the columns of Q? Here we make the assumption that this vector of correlations has a spherical distribution, which can be represented as \sqrt{R^2} * u, where u is uniformally distributed on the surface of a hypersphere. Since u'u = 1, the sum-of-squared correlations is R^2, which is the proportion of variance in the outcome attributable to the predictors in a linear model.

And that brings us to the question, what is your prior on R^2? The LKJ paper implies that if you have a correlation matrix among both the predictors and the outcome, the distribution of the R^2 is beta with shape parameters K / 2 and eta. So, in principle, a user would need to choose eta to reflect their subjective beliefs about the R^2. However, the R2() function that is called by stan_lm() reverses this around and asks what do you think the prior mode / mean / median / log-expectation of the R^2 is? Given the answer to that question, it can solve for the implied value of eta.

All together, the primitive parameters are R^2, u, and sigma_y (the marginal standard deviation of Y). Since sigma_y is a scale parameter and not of much interest, it is given a Jeffreys' prior, which is uniform on the log scale. Given these three things (and the fixed R), we can calculate beta and sigma (the conditional standard deviation of Y) as generated or intermediate quantities, where sigma = sigma_y * sqrt(1 - R^2).

So, in summary, this is really just a way of eliciting an informative prior on the R^2 that happens to imply a pretty reasonable set of joint prior beliefs about beta (it's centered at the origin, has fat tails, is round at the mode, etc.). Consequently, relative to OLS the posterior medians will usually be shrunk toward zero a bit, which is usually a good thing for out-of-sample predictions.

> Do you mean
>
> 1. The marginal prior for
>     R^2(X, beta, \tilde{y}),
> where
>     \tilde{y} ~ Normal(X * beta, \sigma_{\eps})
> and X and \sigma_{\eps} are taken as fixed?

You can choose the prior location of the R^2 given what you know about X, but it is not conditioning on beta or y or sigma. Rather, beta and sigma are functions of the R^2.

> 2. The prior for
>     ER2(beta) = E[R^2 | X, beta, \sigma_{\eps}],
> where the expectation is over \tilde{y}, and X and \sigma_{\eps} are taken as fixed?

If you specify what = "mean", then you are saying "Here is what I think the prior mean of R^2 is given X", but again it does not condition on beta or sigma. But the default is what = "mode", so it is asking what is the most likely value of R^2 given X.

> Or do you mean something else entirely?

I think the key point is that beta and sigma are generated / intermediate quantities that are both functions of the primitive R^2. So, the prior for R^2 does not explicitly condition on beta or sigma in the mathematical sense. Nevertheless, saying "I think the most likely value for R^2 is 0.75" conveys some information about beta and sigma.

As with any stan_ function in rstanarm, you can get a sense for the prior distribution(s) by specifying prior_PD = TRUE, in which case it will run the model but not condition on the data so that you just get draws from the prior. In the case of stan_lm, the Jeffreys' prior on sigma_y is improper, so it just sets sigma_y = 1 when prior_PD = TRUE. So, the resulting distribution of beta is implicitly assuming a standardized outcome but it should be centered on zero with some extreme positive and negative values.

Ben

> 2: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems
>
> What does it mean to have "X divergent transitions"? Is that over all chains? If so, having one over 8000 length chains doesn't seem dangerous (?)

It is 1 out of 4000 (the warmup is ignored), but it is still not too dangerous. For an explanation, see

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstanarm/vignettes/rstanarm.html#divergent-transitions

and / or

https://github.com/stan-dev/cmdstan/releases/download/v2.9.0/cmdstan-guide-2.9.0.pdf

and search for the text n_divergent.

> What is the right use of the pairs() plot in this context(?) I tried directly using it as pairs(stan_glmermodel) and it returns errors, so assuming this is not the way.

That is the right way. What were the errors?

> Quick question in terms of goodness of fit and comparing models with different explanatory variables. I know there is no BIC / AIC measures to compare if a model with  / without a variable is "better" than other... do you have any ideas for that?

Our preferred measure is LOOIC (Leave-One-Out Information Criterion) which is conceptually similar to the AIC (but both are different than the BIC) but is better because the LOOIC allows for there to be prior information and posterior distributions that are not multivariate normal. Each of these information criteria is intended to estimate the expected log posterior density (ELPD) for a new observation. The compare() function can be used to compare different models (that have the same outcome, the same number of observations, and the same likelihood) on the ELPD criterion. The compare() function is used several times in the rstanarm vignettes and is based on this paper

http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.04544

Ben

> >
> Thanks! Ran the log-normal combination and looks much more promising. Took about an hour and seem to be converging. It came with some warnings...
>
> Warning messages:
> 1: There were 1 divergent transitions after warmup. Increasing adapt_delta above 0.98 may help.
> 2: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems
>
> What does it mean to have "X divergent transitions"? Is that over all chains? If so, having one over 8000 length chains doesn't seem dangerous (?)

It has to due with the numerical error from approximating integrals. I wouldn't be too concerned by one in 8000 iterations, but if you get a decent number of them then that's a problem. Also, in most cases you can use a much smaller number of iterations. 8000 seems like a lot for this kind of model. Of course if it really does converge then having that many draws isn't actually a problem, just often unnecessary.

>
> Quick question in terms of goodness of fit and comparing models with different explanatory variables. I know there is no BIC / AIC measures to compare if a model with  / without a variable is "better" than other... do you have any ideas for that?

For model fit I would start by taking a look at the posterior predictive checks. For comparing models, you can use the loo function in rstanarm, which uses the loo package to do a Bayesian approximation to leave one out cross validation <http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.04544>. You can compare models on their estimated out of sample predictive accuracy. This has some similarities to AIC/BIC but it integrates over uncertainty in the parameters instead of using point estimates. There are a bunch of details on the help page for the loo function in rstanarm, as well as the loo and compare functions in the loo package. I would check those out.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

messages.subject: rstanarm 2.9.0-3 released on CRAN (major bug fixed)
messages.subject_clean: rstanarm 2.9.0-3 released on CRAN (major bug fixed)
messages.body_plain:
A new version of rstanarm is now on CRAN and its binaries have mostly been mirrored out. If you are not familiar with rstanarm, see

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/HUwIufOT97E/bLp-2_bwAAAJ

This is the second official release of rstanarm and fixes a major bug that was found with lme4-style models that estimate group-specific coefficients, such as y ~ x + (1 + x | group). The correct model was being estimated but the group-specific coefficients were often mislabeled, so they might be mixed up with group-specific intercepts in the summary output. Also, ranef() would extract mis-labeled estimates and the posterior predictions may well be wrong. In short, if you used a previous version of rstanarm from CRAN or GitHub to estimate a model with group-specific coefficients, you should download the new version and reestimate that model.

Various other smaller bugs have been fixed as is mentioned in

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstanarm/NEWS

Also, there is a new vignette on pooling in hierarchical models that is available from browseVignettes(package = "rstanarm") or from

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstanarm/index.html

So, we would recommend that everyone update to the new version of rstanarm by executing

update.packages("rstanarm")

or, if you have not installed rstanarm before,

install.packages("rstanarm")

Due to some changes in other packages, this version of rstanarm requires R version 3.2.0 (which was released in April 2015) or later. In particular, it imports from the most recent version of nlme, which is a recommended package that comes with R. Hence, the old version of nlme might be installed in a different directory than rstanarm and you might not have write permissions to the directory that nlme is in. If so, ask your system administrator to update nlme or install nlme to a personal directory that appears first on .libPaths().

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Ben,

I have also noticed the kind of stability issue you pointed out where I tried it on something that's very similar to what you have.

Instead of using the optimizer to find the weights, for me, going down the route of matrix algebra min variance seems to provide much more stable results.

Essentially, if we have a covariance matrix Sigma, it had been shown that the linear weight for min variance combination is inv(Sigma) * 1 / (1' * inv(Sigma) * 1). This is popular in finance, but I have also come across it from belief aggregation literature, e.g. PDF:http://faculty.washington.edu/ezivot/econ424/portfolioTheoryMatrix.pdf

Stan code to do this:
  vector compute_min_var_weights (matrix Sigma, int J) {
    matrix[J, J]  Sigma_inv;
    vector[J]     vec_1;
    row_vector[J] vec_1_t;

    vec_1   <- rep_vector(1, J);
    vec_1_t <- rep_row_vector(1, J);
    Sigma_inv <- inverse(Sigma);

    return (Sigma_inv * vec_1)/(vec_1_t * Sigma_inv * vec_1);
  }

I have looked at the following approach:
- 1: (from Andrew): First fit the 7 models separately.  Use these to get point predictions for each data point.
- 2: fit the historical error (actual - forecast) as a multi-normal (0, Sigma)
- 3: compute weights with above function.

Vs optimization, for my problem at least, this way seems to be more stable weights (mean of weights not going out of whack across a different seeds).

There is something tricky in step 2 with the covar/correlation estimation. I think it had been discussed elsewhere on the list, if your data size is not big and you use a LJK prior, the posterior of your correlation matrix can "under-estimate" the level of positive correlation and thus affects the min var computation. I have tried a few ways to get around this issue, but haven't given it much thought. Is there a "best practice" on how to fit a MV whose correlation (prior) is highly correlated?

Andy

messages.subject: Improve efficiency for categorical factor analysis model?
messages.subject_clean: Improve efficiency for categorical factor analysis model?
messages.body_plain:
Hello Stan Users,

I am estimating a series of factor analysis models with 2 correlated factors and 10 binary indicators (this is also a multidimensional item response theory model, and the same model I posted about here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!profile/stan-users/APn2wQeiMptC_Yne81AHqJKGZpKvOCjNm5qA6auUhF-ZnAA5oFRpb5oAlUvOl-DdCvvf6sMcUmxb/stan-users/85Uatb7W6Ro/8Ecd1BLhAQAJ>).

Previously I scaled the latent factors N(0,1) and estimated the covariance between them, but because of the previous thread about sign indeterminacy, I now scale the latent factors by setting one factor loading =1 for each factor and estimating the variance and covariance for both factors. This has solved the sign indeterminacy issue, but the reparameterized model is performing more poorly in terms of effective sample size and Rhat.

I've run this on 500 simulated data sets. With 2 chains and 10,000 iterations each (half warmup), in 11 of the 500 replications, Rhat is above 1.1 and n_eff is less than 50 for 1 or more parameters (I count this as a "failed" replication). In the remaining 489 replications, average n_eff seems much too low to me (tabled below).
> ---------------------------------------------------------
>  parmType   Mean Est   Avg n_eff   Min n_eff   Max n_eff
> ---------- ---------- ----------- ----------- -----------
>    cov       0.301       4808        2020        6637
>   lambda      1.11       318.7       70.22       627.1
>     nu      0.003462     7005        987.1       10000
> sigma[1,1]   2.126       203.7       50.09       355.3
> sigma[1,2]   0.6166      444.2       63.29       1181
> sigma[2,1]   0.6166      444.2       63.29       1181
> sigma[2,2]   2.135       204.6       58.46       357.7
> ---------------------------------------------------------
I have tried to optimize by expressing the covariance matrix as a cholesky factor and vectorizing when possible. My understanding is that the "matt trick" doesn't apply here, because I'm only estimating the covariance matrix (means are set to zero for the latent factors).

I'm attaching an example program and data set. Are there suggestions to improve this model?

In this condition and example data set, each indicator has p=.5 probability of endorsement. Ultimately, I am interested in using this model when the probability of endorsement is low for some items and using priors to stabilize the parameter estimates. In theory, this should be a big improvement over ML, however at the moment I am having trouble getting good performance for this baseline condition. The low probability conditions are, of course, much worse.

I used the following code in R to read in the example data and fit the model:
dat<-read.table("data1.dat", header=FALSE)
N<-500
K<-10
F<-2
cfa.data<-list(N=N,K=K,F=F,y=dat)
Nchains<-2
Niter<-10000

#compile model
model=rstan::stan_model(file='cfa2factor-chol2.stan')
#evaluate model
out=rstan::sampling(object = model
                    , data=cfa.data
                    , chains=Nchains
                    , iter=Niter
                    , warmup=Niter/2
                    , refresh=Niter/10
                    , seed=1)

messages.subject: Re: RStanARM: posterior_predictive probabilities for binomial GLMM
messages.subject_clean: RStanARM: posterior_predictive probabilities for binomial GLMM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

Can you update to the just-released update of rstanarm on CRAN (version 2.9.0-3)? We added a Note section to the documentation for posterior_predict that explains how N is handled for binomial models and changed some things internally related to this.

If you don't specify newdata when calling posterior_predict the Ns are the Ns from the original data. If you do specify newdata then you should be required to specify your own Ns and get an error otherwise (the error wasn't being thrown in the first version of rstanarm). In your case, since the LHS of your formula is cbind(K, N-K) you could include in newdata a variable K=0 and a variable N that has the number of trials you want to use. If there are multiple observations in newdata N can be different for each of them. The predicted counts can then easily be divided by the number of trials if you want probabilities.

Relatedly, we don't recommend trying to directly use the posterior distribution of the inverse-logit transformed linear predictor (i.e., the predicted probabilities), but rather to always sample from the posterior predictive distribution of the outcome. If you want you can then get probabilities by division, as mentioned above.

Also, in case it's helpful, one of the examples in the How to Use the rstanarm Package vignette has been updated in the new version of the package and now shows how to correctly specify the number of trials to use for prediction after binomial models.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

> On Feb 16, 2016, at 3:12 AM, andy...@cubist-asia.com wrote:
>
> ...

> There is something tricky in step 2 with the covar/correlation estimation. I think it had been discussed elsewhere on the list, if your data size is not big and you use a LJK prior, the posterior of your correlation matrix can "under-estimate" the level of positive correlation and thus affects the min var computation.

It works just like any other prior.  The larger the parameter (1 is uniform),
the more the prior concentrates around the unit correlation matrix and the more
it pulls the posterior to be a unit.  You also have the issue of the posterior
mean not being the same as the posterior mode, which might make it look like
an underestimate compared to a point estimate.

You can get an intuitive idea of how this works by using simulated data
where you know the answer and seeing what the fits look like.

> I have tried a few ways to get around this issue, but haven't given it much thought. Is there a "best practice" on how to fit a MV whose correlation (prior) is highly correlated?

Other than using the Cholesky factors for stability and some
regularization with LKJ, I don't think we have any other recommendations.
At least not written out.

- Bob

Hi Ana, rstanarm uses lme4's parser to parse the model formula (just the estimation algorithms differ) so you should be able to do anything that's possible to express using the lme4 syntax. I think something along the lines of what you're talking about can be done using ":" instead of "*" but I would double check the lme4 documentation to make sure it corresponds to what you're looking for. As an example, I think including something like

(1|x1) + (1|x1:x2)

in a model formula would give you intercepts varying by level of x1 as well as by level of x1 within x2.

Jonah

And just to clarify, because I think I see the confusion now, it's still true that the model was being estimated correctly in the previous version. But the labelling mistake was occurring immediately after estimation when renaming the parameters (changing their names from those used in the underlying Stan code to the more substantive names returned to the user). So it was happening after estimation but before returning the fitted model object. That is, the fitted model object had the right estimates in it, they were just labeled incorrectly. The post-estimation functions were working properly, but they assumed the labels were correct.

Anyway, I'm glad we got that sorted out. Thanks for your patience!

Jonah

I think I am starting to figure out what the main issue is with this model. Normally, the curve parameters are dependent on the standard, i.e. P(Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope | x_std, OD_std), and the unknown concentrations are dependent on the curve parameters, i.e. P(theta | Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope, OD_unkn). In the current model, since everything is calculated at once we have P(Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope, theta | x_std, OD_std, OD_unkn) which implies that the curve parameters are also optimized as a function of the unknowns, this makes no logical or physical sense. Also, since there are 72 wells of unknowns (18 samples, 2 dilutions each, in duplicate) and 24 wells of standard per plate, the unknown overwhelm the standards.

As I said earlier, one solution is to use inverse calculation in the generated quantities block. However that has two problems: 1) Artificial limits have to be placed on some parameters (so that Bottom < OD < Bottom + Span), even though OD readings above the top of the curve are possible due to measurement and enzymatic noise (this is an ELISA <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ELISA> assay); 2) In biological assays, in my experience, interpolated values do not quite scale across dilutions, i.e. simply multiplying to reverse the dilution can yield surprisingly different values, that is the strength (in theory) of the approach used in the paper, it can weigh different dilutions depending on the precision they yield.

Is there a way to make the curve parameters independent of the unknowns' OD while keeping the multilevel unknown estimation? That issue did not seem to be a problem in the paper.

> OK, I did what Andrew did and made an estimator for each plate, I did try to make some parameters multilevel but that makes for atrocious sampling and does not help with prediction. I think I figured out how unknown estimation is done in the paper, I was going to write "see above" but it appears my email failed me (which explains why no one reacted to it...). The advantage is that there is no need to deal with the beta1 < OD < beta1 + beta2 constraint. I added some generated quantities to keep track of the variation in coefficients between the plates and named the coefficients for their function.
>
> I only have one question left:
>
> Is there some vectorisation or optimization that I am missing, or something that can be reparameterized better? Every now and then (on the exact same data) I get a complete chain of divergent transitions (and the other 3 chains are quite fine) and the model takes 25 minutes (on my computer) to generate 4000 draws (including 1500 warmup). Using shinystan, I could not relate divergent transitions to any specific parameter. The chains also look a bit correlated.

> On Feb 15, 2016, at 5:23 PM, Jonathan Audet <jona...@hotmail.com> wrote:

I think I figured out how unknown estimation is done in the paper, I was going to write "see above" but it appears my email failed me (which explains why no one reacted to it...). The advantage is that there is no need to deal with the beta1 < OD < beta1 + beta2 constraint. I added some generated quantities to keep track of the variation in coefficients between the plates and named the coefficients for their function.
>
> I only have one question left:
>
> Is there some vectorisation or optimization that I am missing, or something that can be reparameterized better?

Yes to efficiency, but it'll be some work because we don't have ^ vectorized,
so you have to work on pieces with temp variables.  The goal is to reduce number
of repeated operations and do vector operations all at once.

for(i in 1:N){
  cOD[i] <- Bottoms[pID[i]] + (Spans[pID[i]] / (1 + (Inflecs[pID[i]] / x_i[i]) ^ Slopes[pID[i]]) ^ Asyms[pID[i]]);
  sigma_indiv[i] <- ((cOD[i] / 2) ^ (2 * alpha)) * sigma;
}

you can vectorize and remove redundant operations using:

  {
    real alpha_alpha;
    alpha_alpha <- 0.5 * alpha;
    sigma_indiv  <- 0.5 * cOD;
    for (n in 1:N) cOD[i] <- cOD[i] ^ alpha_alpha;
  }

multiplication is faster than division, so 0.5 * x is better than x/2.

As to parameterization and arithmeitc, you want to stay away from exp()
if you can, and work on the log scale until it's absolutely necessary (hopefully
never) to go back to the linear scale.  So you may want to work
in terms of log_cOD, for example, which you can define in a single line:

  log_cOD <- log(sigma) + (0.5 * alpha) * (log_half + log(cOD));

Then if you really absolutely need to work on the exponentiated scale, use

  cOD <- exp(log_cOD);

You may still overflow, but it's the best you can do for stability.

Also, you'd have to define log_half as log(0.5) in the transformed data.

Are OD and cOD constrained to be positive?  If so, normal may not be
the most appropriate density.  I see a lot of other lognormals there
(e.g., log_Inflecs ~ normal(...)).

I don't know what scale all the variables are on, but it helps immensely
to get everything as close to unit-scale as possible.

Rather than calculating means and std devs for variables like Bottoms,
it can make sense to create a hierarchical model --- it sometimes fits
much better if your hard-wired prior isn't great.  So you should check
that your posterior for Bottoms really is normal(0.05, 0.1).

It can sometimes help to compress repeated calculations.  For instance,
if there aren't too many pID[i] values, you could precalculate most
of the cOD term.

Also, hard constraints like upper=4 can be problematic if there's
not some physical constraint --- so you should check that the estimates
in the posterior for Spans doesn't get near 4 (if it does, you truncate
the part above 4 and force the posterior means to be lower compared
to if the variable wasn't truncated).

There are all kinds of little things you can do here, too:

  x_init <- exp(log_x_init);
...
 for(i in 1:N_unkn){
    real x_i_unkn;
    x_i_unkn <- ser_dilutions[i] * x_init[uID[i]];

If you take log_ser_dilutions as a transformed data variable, then you
can define

  x_i_unkn <- exp(log_x_init[i] + log_ser_dilutions[i]);

and you've replaced a multiply with an addition, which is faster
during evaluation and during differentiation.

You don't need to save all the variables like x_init, either.  It
can save time during sampling to calculate those after the fact,
but it can be error prone to do that.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Question on cutpoint prior for stan_polr
messages.subject_clean: Question on cutpoint prior for stan_polr
messages.body_plain:
I took a look at polr.stan, and it seems inconsistent with the claim that

  \pi_j = Pr(y = j | x = \bar{x})

The above equation is true for the cut-points computed in make_cutpoints() only if

1. \bar{x} = 0, so that E[y^*] = 0, and
2. scale = 1.

On Monday, February 15, 2016 at 10:05:20 PM UTC-7, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Monday, February 15, 2016 at 9:55:40 PM UTC-5, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
> > I'm reading through the vignette "Estimating Ordinal Regression Models with rstanarm," and in the discussion of the cutpoint prior I'm getting confused as to what we are conditioning on when using the distribution for y^*.
> >
> > It says that we specify a Dirichlet prior on \pi, where
> >
> >   \pi_j = Pr(y = j | \bar{x})
> >
> > I understand this to mean the conditional probability that y = j when x is set to its mean in the data set.
>
> Correct.
>
> > Later on it says that the j-th cutpoint is given by F^{-1}(p), where
> >
> >   p = SUM(i: 1 <= i <= j: \pi_j))
> >
> > and F is the cumulative probability distribution for y^*. Which distribution?
>
> This depends on whether you are estimating an ordered logit model, an ordered probit model, etc. In the case of an ordered logit model, F() is the scaled logistic CDF.
>
> This is one of the few cases where the relevant code is actually pretty readable. It is the make_cutpoints() function at
>
> https://github.com/stan-dev/rstanarm/blob/master/exec/polr.stan
> >
> > 1. The distribution p(y^* | R)?
> > 2. The distribution p(y^* | R, x = \bar{x})?
> >
> > The definition of \pi implies that (2) is the distribution used to define the cutpoints... but then the vignette states that the scale parameter is \sigma_{y^*}, which implies that (1) is the defining distribution.
>
> You can choose the Dirichlet prior on the simplex vector whose typical element is \pi_j without conditioning on the R matrix. This prior also determines the distribution of the cumulative sum of these probabilities, and then you can use the scaled inverse CDF to figure out what set of cutpoints is consistent with those cumulative probabilities.
>
> Ben
>

messages.subject: Re: R2 prior in stan_lm
messages.subject_clean: R2 prior in stan_lm
messages.body_plain:
There is an inconsistency between your definition of theta and the vignette's definition of theta:

1. Your definition: theta = R * beta, or equivalently, theta = Q' * y_hat
2. Vignette's definition: theta = Q' * y

y and y_hat are not the same thing. Which definition is correct?

"theta_k can be conceptualized as the correlation between y and the k-th column of Q multiplied by..."

Here you seem to be using theta = Q' * y, instead of your earlier definition of theta = Q' * y_hat.

"You can choose the prior location of the R^2 given what you know about X, but it is not conditioning on beta or y or sigma. Rather, beta and sigma are functions of the R^2."

Borrowing some terminology from Interaction Design, you're talking about the implementation model, whereas I'm talking about the conceptual model. The conceptual definition of R^2 is in terms of X, beta, and y:

  R^2 = 1 - SS_r / SS_t
  SS_r = SUM(i:: (y_i - yhat_i)^2)
  SS_t = SUM(i:: (y_i - ybar)^2)
  ybar = empirical mean of y_i

or, an alternative and slightly different definition uses expected values according to the model:

  SS_r = E[SUM(i:: (y_i - yhat_i)^2)] = n * sigma_{eps}^2
  SS_t = E[SUM(i:: (y_i - ybar)^2)] = n * sigma_{eps}^2 + n * V_{i=1}^n yhat_i
  yhat_i = X_i * beta

I'm guessing that underlying the derivation of the R2 prior is one of these two conceptual definitions for R^2.

On Monday, February 15, 2016 at 10:46:22 PM UTC-7, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Monday, February 15, 2016 at 10:22:12 PM UTC-5, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
> > R^2 is defined for a particular design matrix X, coefficient vector beta, and response vector y... so it's unclear to me what is meant by a prior for R^2.
>
> That is the usual way of looking at the R^2 in a OLS context, yes. However, the R^2 is invariant to a rotation of the design matrix X, so we can utilize its QR decomposition to go from
>
> y_hat = X * beta = (QR) * beta = Q * (R * beta) = Q * theta
>
> where theta = R * beta. So, you can think of this as a regression of y on Q and then beta = R^{-1} * theta is a generated quantity.
>
> Okay, so what is the prior distribution on theta, the vector of coefficients for Q? Since Q'Q = I, theta_k can be conceptualized as the correlation between y and the k-th column of Q multiplied by the standard deviation of y, divided by the standard deviation of the k-th column of Q which is the square root of N - 1.
>
> That pushes back the question to what is your prior on the correlations between y and the columns of Q? Here we make the assumption that this vector of correlations has a spherical distribution, which can be represented as \sqrt{R^2} * u, where u is uniformally distributed on the surface of a hypersphere. Since u'u = 1, the sum-of-squared correlations is R^2, which is the proportion of variance in the outcome attributable to the predictors in a linear model.
>
> And that brings us to the question, what is your prior on R^2? The LKJ paper implies that if you have a correlation matrix among both the predictors and the outcome, the distribution of the R^2 is beta with shape parameters K / 2 and eta. So, in principle, a user would need to choose eta to reflect their subjective beliefs about the R^2. However, the R2() function that is called by stan_lm() reverses this around and asks what do you think the prior mode / mean / median / log-expectation of the R^2 is? Given the answer to that question, it can solve for the implied value of eta.
>
> All together, the primitive parameters are R^2, u, and sigma_y (the marginal standard deviation of Y). Since sigma_y is a scale parameter and not of much interest, it is given a Jeffreys' prior, which is uniform on the log scale. Given these three things (and the fixed R), we can calculate beta and sigma (the conditional standard deviation of Y) as generated or intermediate quantities, where sigma = sigma_y * sqrt(1 - R^2).
>
> So, in summary, this is really just a way of eliciting an informative prior on the R^2 that happens to imply a pretty reasonable set of joint prior beliefs about beta (it's centered at the origin, has fat tails, is round at the mode, etc.). Consequently, relative to OLS the posterior medians will usually be shrunk toward zero a bit, which is usually a good thing for out-of-sample predictions.
>
> > Do you mean
> >
> > 1. The marginal prior for
> >     R^2(X, beta, \tilde{y}),
> > where
> >     \tilde{y} ~ Normal(X * beta, \sigma_{\eps})
> > and X and \sigma_{\eps} are taken as fixed?
>
> You can choose the prior location of the R^2 given what you know about X, but it is not conditioning on beta or y or sigma. Rather, beta and sigma are functions of the R^2.
>
> > 2. The prior for
> >     ER2(beta) = E[R^2 | X, beta, \sigma_{\eps}],
> > where the expectation is over \tilde{y}, and X and \sigma_{\eps} are taken as fixed?
>
> If you specify what = "mean", then you are saying "Here is what I think the prior mean of R^2 is given X", but again it does not condition on beta or sigma. But the default is what = "mode", so it is asking what is the most likely value of R^2 given X.
>
> > Or do you mean something else entirely?
>
> I think the key point is that beta and sigma are generated / intermediate quantities that are both functions of the primitive R^2. So, the prior for R^2 does not explicitly condition on beta or sigma in the mathematical sense. Nevertheless, saying "I think the most likely value for R^2 is 0.75" conveys some information about beta and sigma.
>
> As with any stan_ function in rstanarm, you can get a sense for the prior distribution(s) by specifying prior_PD = TRUE, in which case it will run the model but not condition on the data so that you just get draws from the prior. In the case of stan_lm, the Jeffreys' prior on sigma_y is improper, so it just sets sigma_y = 1 when prior_PD = TRUE. So, the resulting distribution of beta is implicitly assuming a standardized outcome but it should be centered on zero with some extreme positive and negative values.
>
> Ben
>

If you prefer, I could have said it with an error term rather than with the y_hat

y = X * beta + epsilon = (QR) * beta + epsilon = Q * (R * beta) + epsilon = Q * theta + epsilon

where theta = R * beta. But this is all prior to observing the y vector. We can ask ourselves "What are our prior beliefs about theta = (Q'Q)^{-1} Q'y = Q'y? For fixed R, whatever those prior beliefs about theta are they imply some prior beliefs about beta = R^{-1} theta. Specifically, if theta has a spherical prior distribution, then beta has an elliptical prior distribution. And the stochastic representation of a spherical distribution implies

theta = sigma_y * sqrt(N - 1) * sqrt(R^2) * u

where u is uniform on the surface of a hypersphere. So, you need some prior distribution for sigma_y and some prior distribution for R^2, which can be interpreted as the proportion of variance in y attributable to Q (or X) in a linear model.

> "You can choose the prior location of the R^2 given what you know about X, but it is not conditioning on beta or y or sigma. Rather, beta and sigma are functions of the R^2."
>
> Borrowing some terminology from Interaction Design, you're talking about the implementation model, whereas I'm talking about the conceptual model. The conceptual definition of R^2 is in terms of X, beta, and y:
>

>   SS_r = SUM(i:: (y_i - yhat_i)^2)
>   SS_t = SUM(i:: (y_i - ybar)^2)
