>   SS_t = E[SUM(i:: (y_i - ybar)^2)] = n * sigma_{eps}^2 + n * V_{i=1}^n yhat_i
>   yhat_i = X_i * beta
>
> I'm guessing that underlying the derivation of the R2 prior is one of these two conceptual definitions for R^2.

Yes, in any textbook on regression from a frequentist perspective, you see those definitions for R^2. But in that setup, the R^2 is not a parameter in the model, it is a statistic that is calculated afterward as a function of the data and the estimates of beta. What I am saying is that in lm.stan, the R^2 is a primitive parameter and the posterior distribution of beta = R^{-1} theta is a function of the R^2 (via theta) and the data (which define the R matrix in QR = X). So, in my view, it does not make sense to conceptually define the R^2 in terms of an estimate of beta because beta is defined in the lm.stan code in terms of the primitive parameter R^2. But conceptually, the R^2 can still be interpreted as the proportion of variance in the outcome attributable to the predictors for the purpose of expressing your prior beliefs about its location. In other words, since sigma is an intermediate quantity that is defined as sigma_y * sqrt(1 - R^2), the model implies that the variance of the outcome is

(sigma_y)^2 * (R^2 + (1 - R^2)) = (sigma_y)^2

where sigma_y is also a primitive unknown that is estimated but is not especially interesting. So, you can ascribe some proportion of that to the predictors and the complementary proportion to the errors.

To conceptualize the R^2 as a primitive parameter, it helps to envision a random correlation matrix among both the predictors and the outcome. Let L be the Cholesky factor of that correlation matrix. The so-called onion method for constructing L implies that the bottom-right element of L is sqrt(1 - R^2) and the elements in the last row of L to the left of the diagonal can be written as sqrt(R^2) * u, so that the sum-of-squares along the last row of L is 1. If your beliefs about that correlation matrix are described by the LKJ distribution with shape parameter eta, then your beliefs about R^2 are a beta distribution with first shape parameter K / 2 and second shape parameter eta. That is why some prior information about R^2 is solicited in order to pin down the second shape parameter, eta.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Multilevel serial dilution assay
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Multilevel serial dilution assay
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, February 16, 2016 at 6:52:42 PM UTC-5, Jonathan Audet wrote:
> I think I am starting to figure out what the main issue is with this model. Normally, the curve parameters are dependent on the standard, i.e. P(Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope | x_std, OD_std), and the unknown concentrations are dependent on the curve parameters, i.e. P(theta | Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope, OD_unkn). In the current model, since everything is calculated at once we have P(Bottom, Span, Inflec, Asym, Slope, theta | x_std, OD_std, OD_unkn) which implies that the curve parameters are also optimized as a function of the unknowns, this makes no logical or physical sense.

I disagree that it makes no logical or physical sense.  The "unknowns" are run repeatedly so they have a known dilution and a known reading.  The fact the dilution level is known _should_ contribute because the reading should go down with the dilution in a sensible way, following the estimated curve.  I get that in practice this model is not working out as written but I wouldn't blame it on logical/physical inconsistency.  In BUGS people avoid this kind of problem using a function called (I think...) "cut", but Stan does not do that.  It's possible that dealing with this issue takes this project from "applying a model described in a paper" to "extending the paper" and if you don't want to do that using generated quantities is the right way  to go.

> Also, since there are 72 wells of unknowns (18 samples, 2 dilutions each, in duplicate) and 24 wells of standard per plate, the unknown overwhelm the standards.

Yes, I think the most likely issue is that a level of noise is not being taken into account---e.g.-the variation inherent in the enzyme that leads wells to develop at different speeds.

> As I said earlier, one solution is to use inverse calculation in the generated quantities block. However that has two problems: 1) Artificial limits have to be placed on some parameters (so that Bottom < OD < Bottom + Span), even though OD readings above the top of the curve are possible due to measurement and enzymatic noise (this is an ELISA <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ELISA> assay);

These limits are not so much artificial as physical if you include the appropriate noise.  The true OD for a very low concentration sample can't be lower than the true instrument output with a negative control, but those things are all measured and recorded as averages.  The best data to go into a model like this would be a series of measurements (not averaged) or the sufficient statistics (mean measurement, measurement noise) and the equations for the curve would only be written for the "true" values not the measured values.  I think this is all possible in Stan just maybe more work that you want to put in at the moment.

> 2) In biological assays, in my experience, interpolated values do not quite scale across dilutions, i.e. simply multiplying to reverse the dilution can yield surprisingly different values, that is the strength (in theory) of the approach used in the paper, it can weigh different dilutions depending on the precision they yield.

That's the aspect of the model I find most interesting as well but it might take more work on the model itself to get the benefits---especially since you mentioned divergent iterations in the previous post.  It's a good signal that part of the parameter space is difficult for the sampler to deal with.

> Is there a way to make the curve parameters independent of the unknowns' OD while keeping the multilevel unknown estimation? That issue did not seem to be a problem in the paper.

This is what the "cut" function does in BUGS, there is no parallel in Stan.

Sorry I can't be more helpful, I don't have time to dig in at the moment.

Krzysztof

messages.body_plain:
I'm working on a project comparing estimates of survival and detection for mark-recapture from Stan to two maximum likelihood methods. Specifically, I'd like to simulate survival and detection typical for mark juvenile Chinook salmon in the Snake River that migrate past eight hydropower projects which serve as detection points. These fish are listed under the endangered species act and mark-recapture models have become an integral part of management and recovery (at the cost of several million dollars a year). My simulation numbers are derived from this report <http://www.nwfsc.noaa.gov/assets/26/8380_05132015_110147_Spring-Survival-2014.pdf>.  For the simulation fish are only marked once at the beginning of the migration. They do not lose marks and we're going to assume independence of each fish, independence of survival and detection at any one project, and independence among projects.

I'm attempting to adapt the code on page 133 of the Stan manual to this situation. But with 128 potential detection histories, that is a lot of code to write! I spent a couple of tedious hours copy and pasting, but I'm still not done yet. I'm also thinking that there's got to be a better way. There is a natural recursive structure to the likelihood for each capture history. So I'm thinking it should be possible to write a function in R to automatically write the code for me for any number of recapture events. I've gotten a start on some code, but I'm getting a little stuck on how to write out the model piece of the code. I've attached my R script that writes out everything through the transformed parameters stage and I've got a place holder for a double for loop that I think can be used to write each increment_log_prob step. I'm hoping for a little help from this community on how to proceed, or maybe for somebody to tell me that I'm thinking about this the wrong way and that there's a better way.

Here is an excerpt from the stan code that show the recursive structure to modelling each detection history. I work the capture history from left to right. We always start with a one. You can see the base 2 structure. I'm sure there's got to be a clever way of stepping through a nested for loop to reproduce this for any number of detection histories, but it's eluded me so far. Any ideas?

model {

  increment_log_prob(history[1] * ( #10000000
                     log(chi[1])));
##################################################
  increment_log_prob(history[2] * ( #11000000
                     log(phi[1]) + log(p[2]) +
                     log(chi[2])));
##################################################
  increment_log_prob(history[3] * ( #10100000
                     log(phi[1]) + log1m(p[2]) +
                     log(phi[2]) + log(p[3]) +
                     log(chi[3])));

  increment_log_prob(history[4] * ( #11100000
                     log(phi[1]) + log(p[2]) +
                     log(phi[2]) + log(p[3]) +
                     log(chi[3])));
##################################################
  increment_log_prob(history[5] * ( #10010000
                     log(phi[1]) + log1m(p[2]) +
                     log(phi[2]) + log1m(p[3]) +
                     log(phi[3]) + log(p[4]) +
                     log(chi[4])));

  increment_log_prob(history[6] * ( #11010000
                     log(phi[1]) + log(p[2]) +
                     log(phi[2]) + log1m(p[3]) +
                     log(phi[3]) + log(p[4]) +
                     log(chi[4])));

  increment_log_prob(history[7] * ( #10110000
                     log(phi[1]) + log1m(p[2]) +
                     log(phi[2]) + log(p[3]) +
                     log(phi[3]) + log(p[4]) +
                     log(chi[4])));

  increment_log_prob(history[8] * ( #11110000
                     log(phi[1]) + log(p[2]) +
                     log(phi[2]) + log(p[3]) +
                     log(phi[3]) + log(p[4]) +
                     log(chi[4])));
##################################################

If so, any way I can return to my original levels to identify which is which?

This is because one of the factors is an "ordered factor" in which case by default R uses whatever the contr.poly() function does when creating dummy variables, which have never understood nor seen in any research context. There are two and a half ways around this:
Make the variable an unordered factor with g <- factor(g, ordered = FALSE) before running the model
Call the following before running the model
options(contrasts = c(unordered = 'contr.treatment',
                        ordered = 'contr.treatment'))
which makes it subsequently operationalize dummy variables with "treatment" contrasts (which is the convention in the social sciences and elsewhere; basically the dummy variables are 1 if the observation falls in a category and 0 otherwise)
Put the code from (2) into a file called .Rprofile (note the leading period) in your home directory in which case it will be executed each time you start R
Ben

messages.subject_clean: Question on cutpoint prior for stan_polr
messages.body_plain:
Yes, I know that there is a scale parameter passed to make_cutpoints; that is what I was referring to when I said that the condition

  \pi_j = Pr(y = j | x = \bar{x})

holds only if scale = 1, that is, only if the scale parameter passed in to make_cutpoints() equals 1. The reason it only holds when scale = 1 is because the error scale itself is 1, as described in the vignette, and as an examination of the pw_polr() and CDF_polr() functions confirms.

But the scale parameter passed in to make_cutpoints() does NOT equal 1 -- the Stan model uses 1/sqrt(1 - R^2), a value that is equal to 1 only if R = 0, and is otherwise strictly greater than 1.

> >

The CJS model with arbitrary numbers of capture times
is here:

https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/misc/ecology/mark-recapture/cjs-K.stan

It relies on precomputing first and last capture time and
then looping through the middle.

An even better way to do this would be to write up a bunch
of these pieces using functions.  I had thought I or someone
else had done that at some point, but I can't find it.

Was that the kind of model you were looking for?  If not, there
are also a bunch of CJS models in Hiroki Itô's translation of
some of the examples from Kéry and Schaub's book:

https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/example-models/BPA

If not, if you can specify the functions you need in math
notation without trying to generate Stan code, we can probably
figure out how to do it either with a loop or recursively.

For instance, if you're not working at the individual level, you can
code up the histories as input data and key off that in the code.

- Bob

On Thursday, February 18, 2016 at 8:57:43 AM UTC-5, Ron wrote:
> I've tried supplying initial values for exp_subclinical and/or exp_infective_pool, with the same error.
>
> Is my problem purely one of getting sensible initial values? And if so, on which transformed parameter(s)?
>
> Or is there something wrong with what I am trying to do?

Good initial values are only rarely necessary. And you can't supply initial values on transformed parameters because they are just derived from the initial values of the parameters. I would put a
print("log-posterior = ", get_lp());
before and after every statement in the model block involving ~ or increment_log_prob() to see where it starts to underflow. These Poisson models can be prone to numerical problems and it is usually best to use the
~ poisson_log(alpha);
parameterization described in section 40.6 of the Stan User manual, which allows you to keep everything in log-units.

Ben

On Thursday, February 18, 2016 at 12:13:13 PM UTC-5, Dalton Hance wrote:
> I was hoping to see not much more of a penalty for bumping up to seven capture events after marking (128 capture histories), but I'm looking at about 30 minutes or so for 50000 iterations with 17500 individuals. Maybe I have unrealistic hopes, but I'd like to cut that down.

The real issue is not that your hopes are unrealistic but that your number of iterations is too large. For the vast majority of well-written Stan models, the effective sample sample size is going to be at least 10% of the nominal post-warmup sample size. And you do not need an effective sample size of 2500 to estimate a mean sufficiently well. Just using the default values of 2000 iterations (of which half are discarded as warmup) with 4 chains should get you an effective sample size of a few hundred. And if you had a few hundred independent draws from the posterior, you would be fine in terms of estimating the posterior means. There are some exceptions to all this, but you shouldn't start by assuming your research project is one of the exceptions.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question about Wiener Diffusion Model Distribution in rstan_2.7.0-2
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Question about Wiener Diffusion Model Distribution in rstan_2.7.0-2
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

I have a related comment.
There are three potential typos in the STAN manual (2.9.0) in the
PDF for 'Wiener Diffusion Model Distributions’, but I’m not sure if these
bugs 2&3 proliferated into the code.

1. y is defined as 'y \in (0, \tau)’ but it should be 'y \in (\tau, \infty)’
otherwise the term \sqrt{y - \tau} is undefined.

Two others based on reference paper (Blurton et at. 2012)

2. the exponent of the denominator (y - \tau) should be 3/2 instead of 3
See attached PDF plots for
alphaB=3.25;tauB=0.25;betaB=0.4;deltaB=0.65; N = 150;

3. the numerator in standard normal distribution function \phi reads
‘(2k + \beta) \alpha’ instead of '2k + \alpha \beta’.
The difference between these two results in very minor changes.

Best Regards, Maciej

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multinomial distribution & regression
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Multinomial distribution & regression
messages.body_plain:
I made some tweaks and whatnot and managed to at least get it running. Now the problem is, it’s not converging! Normally, I would just throw more iterations at the model, but this does not seem like a good solution in this case. There is some indications that something else is going on. Something I don’t quite understand. I read an excellent post by Michael Betancourt at https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/hjYWqJZfSgw (I don’t know why I had not found that post until now, it was so useful! it should really be exposed more), and I’ve been using the suggestions from there to diagnose the model.

The simplified model is can be seen at https://gist.github.com/demodw/98424b08f42bcd8e09dc. Just to re-iterate, this is a hierarchical multinomial regression model over D experiments, and in each experiment there are the same K outcomes. K=6 is set as the reference category, and fixed to be zero. There is a  hyper prior on outcomes 1 and 2, and another on outcomes 3, 4, and 5.

I decreased the size of my data set a lot, and removed all of the covariates (age, age^2 and sex) to make diagnostics simpler. This R code will generate data that’s fit as input, and in the same size range:

NROW <- 100
K <- 6
NChapters <- 3
Count <- matrix(nrow=NROW, ncol=K)
Count[,1] <- round(runif(100, 20, 2000))
Count[,2] <- round(runif(100, 20, 2000))
Count[,3] <- round(runif(100, 20, 300))
Count[,4] <- round(runif(100, 20, 300))
Count[,5] <- round(runif(100, 20, 300))
Count[,6] <- round(runif(100, 1*10^6, 4*10^6))

# Quite a lot of outcomes from group 3, 4, or 5 are zero.
Count[,3][sample(100, 30, replace=F)] <- 0
Count[,4][sample(100, 30, replace=F)] <- 0
Count[,5][sample(100, 30, replace=F)] <- 0

Di <- seq(1:NROW)
DUnique <- NROW
N <- NROW

D <- NROW
ICD_Chapter <- round(runif(NROW, 1, NChapters))
ICD_B <- round(runif(NROW, 1, NROW))
ICD_A <- round(runif(NROW, 1, NROW))

ICD_combination_index_length <- 10
ICD_combination_index <- round(runif(NROW, 1, ICD_combination_index_length))

stan_rdump(c("NROW", "K", "NChapters", "Count", "Di", "DUnique", "N", "D", "ICD_Chapter", "ICD_B", "ICD_A", "ICD_combination_index", "ICD_combination_index_length"), file='dummy.R')

Test 1. Default settings.
Rhat for beta_0_raw’s are between 1.1-3154. Neff between 2 and 28. Clearly not converged. Trace plots show that chain get stuck and don’t mix at all, see http://imgur.com/Mz916tr. 3 divergences. Seemingly a lot of iterations hit tree depth.

Test 2. Increased acceptance probability to 0.9
Same story. A bit mixing on some parameters, but overall no mixing at all. 9 divergences. Does not hit tree depth.

Test 3. Decrease step size to 0.1.
Rhat’s between 1.06-15333. Some chains are trying to explore values, instead of just sticking with the same values for all iterations, but most just stuck. See http://imgur.com/a3wpmI1. 8 divergences. Does not hit tree depth.

Test 4. Decrease step size to 0.01.
R-hat between 1.09-641. Same problem, chains are not exploring any values. Does not hit tree depth.

Test 5. Decrease step size to 0.01 and increase delta to 0.95
No difference, same result.

Test 6. Decrease step size to 0.01 and increase delta to 0.95, 2000 warmup steps, 2000 samples.
No difference.

Same 6 tests, using a Student-t prior with df=3, center=0, scale=10. Same results. High R-hat values, no mixing.

Adding hyper-hyper priors onto the hyper priors does not change the situation either.

The odd thing is, if I remove the priors on the scale, all chains mix beautifully and all R-hat values are <1.0001 and zero divergences. Why would putting a prior on the scale suddenly change this? Could there be identifiability issues in the posterior? The prior on the scale of the coefficients should be “weakly informative”, according to posts I’ve read on this forum. The density of the converged beta0_raw’s has most of their mass around -6 to -8. This is probably due to the reference category always having a rather large count. I don’t see why a student-t with 3 df and a rather large hyper prior on the scale should not be able to explore this area.

Could anyone offer some insight into what might be wrong?

Cheers,
David

messages.body_plain:
On Friday, February 19, 2016 at 11:21:37 AM UTC-5, Eric Innocents EBOULET wrote:
> Hi Users'stan.
>
> I'm writing hierarchical model to models response and response time defining in Rstan_Code.pdf. To do this, I'm writing model in ModelTimeResponse.stan.
> I you  think my model is OK, is it possible to explain why I obtain an errorr.

The screenshot is an informational message rather than an error. It says that there were 5 out of thousands of iterations where a correlation matrix in your model evaluated to

| 1 -1 |
|-1  1 |

which is not positive definite. This has to do with the transformation from the unconstrained space to the constrained space of a correlation, which utilizes the hyperbolic tangent transformation. If the parameter goes below about -9 in the unconstrained space, then tanh(-9) = 1 as far as the computer knows.

In any event, if this only happens a few times out of thousands of iterations, then you do not need to worry about it. Moreover, you do not need to worry about positive definiteness warnings when the correlation matrix or covariance matrix in question is declared in the parameters block because those matrices are positive definite by construction, even though they may be singular numerically. The informational message is there out of an abundance of caution for people who are constructing their own correlation or covariance matrices in the transformed parameters block and may have made a mistake in the implementation so that the resulting matrix is not positive definite by construction.

Ben

You can make all that a bit faster.

If you convert your data types from arrays to vectors, you
can replace this

  for(i in 1:N) {
    age_C1[i] <- age[i]*C1[i];

with

  age_C1 <- age .* C1;

This is more to prevent errors (e.g., bounds checks built in,
no indexes to fiddle) than for efficiency.

The big win will be expressing the linear predictor as
a vectorized operation.  First, glm and everything else needs
to be defined as a vector rather than array.  Then you can
replace

 for ( i in 1:N ) {
    vary[i] <- vary_subject_index[subject_index[i]];
    glm[i] <- vary[i] + Intercept
    + beta_age * age[i]
    + beta_Fsex2 * Fsex2[i]
    + beta_C1*C1[i]
    + beta_C2*C2[i]
    + beta_ageC1*age_C1[i]
    + beta_agec2*age_C2[i]
    + beta_C1C2*C1_C2[i]
    + beta_ageC1C2*age_C1_C2[i];
  }

with

  glm <- Intercept
       + vary_subject_index[subject_index]
       + beta_age * age
       + beta_Fsex2 * Fsex2
       + beta_C1 * C1
       + beta_C2 * C2
       + beta_ageC1 * age_C1
       + beta_agec2 *age_C2
       + beta_C1C2 * C1_C2
       + beta_ageC1C2 * age_C1_C2;

You could even just put this all right inside normal, but defining
the variable and assigning isn't that expensive (cheap copy).

That still has a bunch of multiply-by-zero you don't need in
the Fsex2 case, which is a boolean indicator, but there's not
a great way to speed that up without writing a function that either
inserts aconstant 0 if Fsex2[n] is 0 and inserts beta_Fsex2 otherwise.
No useless multiplications by 1 or 0 that way.

  vector fill_if(int[] include, real beta) {
    vector[num_elements(vector)] v;
    real z;
    z <- 0;
    for (i in 1:num_elements(vector))
      if (include[i])
        v[i] <- beta;
      else
        v[i] <- z;
    }
  }

and then replace

         + beta_Fsex2 * Fsex2

with

         + fill_if(Fsex2, beta_Fsex2)

It's goofy to define the zero and reuse it, but it's a bit more
efficient with memory than using v[i] <- 0, which creates a new
autodiff variable for each instance.

Finally, you want to use a non-centered parameterization and
replace this:

  for ( j in 1:N_subject_index )
    vary_subject_index[j] ~ normal( 0 , sigma_subject_index );

by making vary_subject_index a vector and using

  vary_subject_index_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

and then replacing the line above

  + vary_subject_index[subject_index]

with

  + sigma_subject_index * var_subject_index_raw[subject_index]

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This probably is a terrible idea, but I was wondering, is there any precedent for using Gaussian/other-Copulas to specify hierarchical priors?

The particular example I am considering is probably a model I wouldn't necessarily code in Stan, since the parameters are discrete. (Obviously this could be done by marginalising parameters, but it might be quite messy). However, I wanted to see whether the community 'Bayes-brain' had seen something like this before.

I have two parameters X1 and X2, which are both discrete, and I want to assign very different negative binomial marginal priors to each. However, I would like there to be a rather complex dependence between these parameters. One way of specifying this dependence would be to use a Copula. This would allow me the flexibility to set the marginal priors independently, whilst allowing for an arbitrary dependence between the priors.

I know this can be done nicely for likelihoods, but I was wondering whether anyone had seen anything like this for priors? I suspect that it may suffice to use simpler options for examples where there is a lot of data. However in a few cases I am considering there are relatively few data points, and I would want to incorporate this complex dependency structure that is quite well known a priori.

Best,

Ben

Hi Seth,

On Feb 20, 2016, at 6:20 AM, Seth Flaxman <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:

> If I do:
>
> y ~ normal(mu, sigma) T[0,ymax];
>
> Can I do the equivalent with normal_log (I have a mixture model so can't use the above syntax), e.g.:
>
> lp <- normal_log(y,mu,sigma) T[0,ymax];

No. See "Truncated and Censored Data" and the subsection on "Truncated Distributions" (pg 280).

You have to subtract the normalizing term:
lp <- normal_log(y,mu,sigma) - log(normal_cdf(ymax, mu, sigma) - 0.5);

(What is lo declared as? You might want to use increment_log_prob() directly).

>
> And if this isn't supported at the moment, is there a hack or reparameterization for just a positively constrained normal distribution?
>
> parameters {
>    real<lower=0> y;
> }
> model {
>    // ...
>    lp <- normal_log(y,mu,sigma) T[0,];
> }

If y is a scalar parameter with constraints, then there's no need to add T[lower, upper] (if the bounds match). Stan will behave as though you e provided the truncation.

If you need to use it in a mixture model with different constraints, you may need to include the normalizing constants on your own.

>

Theoretically my data covers a really large range (time from 0 to 365 days, space from 0 to 20 km) but I'm only interested in a short-range model so I truncate my observations to 7 days and 2 km.

Providing the full Stan model would be useful.

messages.subject: Re: Question on cutpoint prior for stan_polr
messages.subject_clean: Question on cutpoint prior for stan_polr
messages.body_plain:
On Friday, February 19, 2016 at 4:29:05 PM UTC-7, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> On Wednesday, February 17, 2016 at 11:08:05 PM UTC-5, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
> > The reason it only holds when scale = 1 is because the error scale itself is 1
>
> Hi Kevin, can you clarify what you mean by this? Indeed the error scale (sigma_epsilon) is fixed at 1 since it isn't identified. But I'm not sure why if the unit-scaled cut-points are subsequently scaled by something other than 1 it invalidates the claim about the definition of pi. Thanks,

Let's step through the math. Since x is centered, the condition x = \bar{x} become x = 0, and P(y = k | x = \bar{x}) becomes P(y = k | x = 0). Then

    P(y = k | x = 0)
    = P(cutpoint[k-1] <= y^* <= cutpoint[k] | x = 0)
    = P(cutpoint[k-1] <= epsilon <= cutpoint[k])    # epsilon is the error term
    = F(cutpoint[k]) - F(cutpoint[k-1])                    # F is the CDF for the error distribution

If we define cutpoint[j] for all j to be F^{-1}(sum(\pi[1:j])), then we can continue as follows:

    = F(F^{-1}(sum(\pi[1:k]))) - F(F^{-1}(sum(\pi[1:(k-1)]))
    = sum(\pi[1:k]) - sum(\pi[1:(k-1)])
    = \pi[k]

If, however, we define cutpoint[j] = scale * F^{-1}(sum(\pi[1:j])) for scale != 1, then the equality no longer holds: F(scale * F^{-1}(z)) != z in general when scale != 1.

messages.subject: Regression-coefficient priors that depend on X
messages.subject_clean: Regression-coefficient priors that depend on X
messages.body_plain:
The R2 prior, like Zellner's g prior, depends on the matrix of covariates X. This feature of both priors troubles me, for these reasons:

1. It's not clear to me why one's prior on the regression coefficients should depend on the observed values of the input variables. The problem is clearest when your input variables are all control variables and the regression coefficients can be interpreted causally -- in that case, the input variables are whatever you chose them to be for your experimental design, and clearly contain no information at all about the regression coefficients. The same objection holds for purely observational data when you have a sufficiently complete set of input variables that there is little chance of important confounding variables; the x values occurring in the data tell you nothing about the causal relationship between the input variables and outcome variable.

2. Are such priors even consistent with Bayes' Rule? Assuming independent priors on beta and sigma, and iid observations, we have

    p(beta | y, X)
    is proportional to
    p(beta) * p(y, X | beta)
    = p(beta) * p(X | beta) * p(y | X, beta)
    = p(beta) * PRODUCT(i: 1 <= i <= n: p(X_i | beta)) * p(y | X, beta)

We effectively have an X-dependent prior on beta only if the distribution for X_i depends on beta, in which case we get an (effective) prior of the form

    pi(beta | X)  is proportional to  p(beta) * PRODUCT(i: 1 <= i <= n: p(X_i | beta))

Does either of the R2 prior or Zellner's g-prior fit this form?

3. One possible way around the problem of (2) above is to make the prior for beta depend, not on X itself, but on other parameters that determine the distribution for the vector of input variables. That is, we have

    x_i ~ Distribution_x(psi)
    beta ~ Distribution_b(psi)
    y_i ~ Normal(x_i' * beta, sigma)

The Zellner prior could be viewed as an empirical Bayes approximation to such a model, if

  a) For any covariance matrix Sigma there is some vector psi such that Distribution_x(psi) has Sigma as its covariance matrix;

  b) Distribution_b(psi) depends on psi only via the covariance matrix Sigma corresponding to Distribution_x(psi); and

  c)  (1/n) * X' * X is used as a point estimate of Sigma^{-1}.

Of course, that leads us to the deficiencies of empirical Bayes -- it's only an approximation to the full Bayesian answer, and it's not obvious how much the approximation alters the results.

Can the R2 prior also be viewed in this manner?

They're exactly the same.  Because of the form of the
normal log density, if you do this:

  for (n in 2:N) {
    delta <- mu[n] - mu[n - 1];
    delta ~ normal(0, sigma_mu);
  }

you get exactly the same density as if you do this:

  for (n in 2:N)
    mu[n] ~ normal(mu[n - 1], sigma_mu);

The latter's just the typical way of writing a time series.

It's modeling the difference from the previous value either way.

>

I'm not surprised that's what happens.  Just look at what happens
to the density as delta_sd -> 0 and all the mu approach the same value.
So it's not just Stan, it's that your model's not really well
identified for the data you have.  Stan's very good at identifying these
pathologies in models and data.

With very little data, your prior's going to keep delta_sd very low.
What happens if you relax that prior?

Basically, I'd try to simulate data according to the model and see if
you can recover it.  But with no predictors or anything else to grab
onto, there may just not be enough info to keep delta_sd from degenerating.

messages.body_plain:
"The R2 prior does not depend on the values in X; only the number of columns of X.  In addition, beta is not a parameter in those models; rather it is a generated quantity."

There is a one-to-one, onto mapping between (beta, sigma_eps) and (r^2, u, omega); thus any prior over one defines a prior over the other, via the usual change-of-variables formula. I can choose to consider either (beta, sigma_eps) or (r^2, u, omega) as my model parameters, and since we are talking about a linear regression model, it is most natural to think in terms of (beta, sigma_eps) as the parameters.

Furthermore, when considering the relationship between y_i and X_i, it is the vector of regression coefficients beta that is of interest, whether I choose to consider beta a primitive parameter or a derived parameter. All of the concerns I expressed apply regardless of whether you choose to treat beta as a primitive parameter or as a derived parameter.  And since

    beta = R^{-1} * u * sigma_y * sqrt(r^2 * (n-1))

where R is a function of X, we have a prior on beta that is a function of X.

On Sunday, February 21, 2016 at 9:28:50 PM UTC-5, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
> BTW, I hope I'm not coming across as too critical with all these questions. I will likely be training other people in using rstanarm, and I want to make sure that I understand it very well myself before doing so.

It's all good. Everything should be questioned, particularly with rstanarm because it is new and because a lot of the users of it will not be questioning the default priors.

With an experiment or some other situation where you have informative priors about the regression coefficients, stan_glm with family = gaussian may be more appropriate. The stan_lm function is more intended for the situation where your beliefs about the regression coefficients are centered at zero with fat tails. One way to look at it is to imagine the correlation matrix among the K predictors and the outcome before you observe the values of either. If you have an LKJ(eta) prior on that correlation matrix, then you have a Beta(eta, K/2) prior on conditional variance of Y | X when all variables are standardized. Conversely, you have a Beta(K/2, eta) prior on the R^2 and need to then choose eta. Equivalently, you could say

R^2 = 1 - (sigma_epsilon)^2 / (sigma_Y)^2

but I don't like to write it that way because it makes it look like sigma_epsilon is primitive and the R^2 is derived, when actually the code does the reverse:

sigma_epsilon = sigma_Y * sqrt(1 - R^2)

But either way is perfectly good for thinking about the prior location of R^2 under a Beta(K/2, eta) distribution, which implies a particular value of eta. Also, for the reasons you mentioned, about the concerns with empirical Bayesianism, sigma_Y is a primitive to be estimated rather than conditioned on.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the tip on using stan_glm for a wider selection of priors; I hadn't even thought of using it for just plain old linear regression.

"The stan_lm function is more intended for the situation where your beliefs about the regression coefficients are centered at zero with fat tails."

Fat tails? I'm not seeing that. The equation

    R * beta = sigma_y * sqrt(r^2 * (n-1))

implies that the regression coefficients are bounded, doesn't it?

On Sunday, February 21, 2016 at 7:49:01 PM UTC-7, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> With an experiment or some other situation where you have informative priors about the regression coefficients, stan_glm with family = gaussian may be more appropriate. The stan_lm function is more intended for the situation where your beliefs about the regression coefficients are centered at zero with fat tails. One way to look at it is to imagine the correlation matrix among the K predictors and the outcome before you observe the values of either. If you have an LKJ(eta) prior on that correlation matrix, then you have a Beta(eta, K/2) prior on conditional variance of Y | X when all variables are standardized. Conversely, you have a Beta(K/2, eta) prior on the R^2 and need to then choose eta. Equivalently, you could say
>
> R^2 = 1 - (sigma_epsilon)^2 / (sigma_Y)^2
>
> but I don't like to write it that way because it makes it look like sigma_epsilon is primitive and the R^2 is derived, when actually the code does the reverse:
>
> sigma_epsilon = sigma_Y * sqrt(1 - R^2)
>
> But either way is perfectly good for thinking about the prior location of R^2 under a Beta(K/2, eta) distribution, which implies a particular value of eta. Also, for the reasons you mentioned, about the concerns with empirical Bayesianism, sigma_Y is a primitive to be estimated rather than conditioned on.
>
> Ben
>

messages.subject_clean: Regression-coefficient priors that depend on X
messages.body_plain:
On Sunday, February 21, 2016 at 8:52:32 PM UTC-5, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
> "The R2 prior does not depend on the values in X; only the number of columns of X.  In addition, beta is not a parameter in those models; rather it is a generated quantity."
>
> There is a one-to-one, onto mapping between (beta, sigma_eps) and (r^2, u, omega); thus any prior over one defines a prior over the other, via the usual change-of-variables formula. I can choose to consider either (beta, sigma_eps) or (r^2, u, omega) as my model parameters, and since we are talking about a linear regression model, it is most natural to think in terms of (beta, sigma_eps) as the parameters.
>
> Furthermore, when considering the relationship between y_i and X_i, it is the vector of regression coefficients beta that is of interest, whether I choose to consider beta a primitive parameter or a derived parameter. All of the concerns I expressed apply regardless of whether you choose to treat beta as a primitive parameter or as a derived parameter.  And since
>
>     beta = R^{-1} * u * sigma_y * sqrt(r^2 * (n-1))
>
> where R is a function of X, we have a prior on beta that is a function of X.

You can have a distribution of prior beliefs about beta that is implied by your prior beliefs about the parameters in the parameters block, but that doesn't affect what Bayes rule implies for those parameters:

f(alpha, u, sigma_y, r^2 | y, X = QR, eta) \propto f(alpha) * f(u) * f(r^2 | K / 2, eta) * f(sigma_y) * f(y | Q, u, r^2, sigma_y)

The beta distribution for r^2 with shape parameters K / 2 and eta does not vary according to the values in X, only its number of columns, K. In stan_glm(), the default priors do depend on the standard deviations of the columns of X (which I don't mind so much) and the standard deviation of y (which I would like to get rid of but it is difficult to come up with a reasonable alternative).

There has to be some joint prior distribution for the alternative primitive parameters beta and sigma_epsilon that implies the new generated quantities alpha, u, sigma_y, and r^2 have the same distribution as in the posterior distribution above. However, that doesn't mean the two distributions are equally easy to sample from in Stan. We do reparameterizations in rstanarm and Stan generally all the time, usually for computational benefits at the cost of readability of the .stan files. But once you have the posterior distribution of the quantities of interest, the interpretation of them is the same.

In this case, it also makes it easier for the user. It is hard to get people to thoughtfully specify multivariate distributions, and it is hard to get people to specify anything other than location and sometimes scale parameters. With stan_lm, all that is needed is some prior information about the location of r^2, and it can infer eta.

Ben

The problem is going to arise when you try to generate a RNG
that will overflow the integer sizes (the max allowable value is
roughly 2^31).  You can modify the code to catch cases where
the parameters give some chance of overflowing and just return -1
there in the generated quantities block.  I'll make a note of
that in the manual, but it's going to be buried so deep nobody's
likely to see it:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1709#issuecomment-187382422

You didn't send enough of your program (ideally send ***all*** of
it) for us to diagnose what the root cause is.  But the answer is
probably that you want more reasonable priors and/or inits.  Or
you want to guard against the problem with a conditional in the
generated quantities.

If you're generating int variates on the scale of 2^31, you
probably have bigger problems.  At that point, normal approximations
are pretty darn good.

- Bob

related to this questions, I was wondering whether I should also divide the log_lik for each subject by the number of observations for that subject if I want to use psis-loo to compare models? I have 29 subjects and they each have between 190 and 200 observations on a psychological learning task- which means that if I compute for each subject the log likelihood as the sum of the log_lik across all observations, the ones with more trials will have a higher log_lik.

When I put these log_lik into psisloo (matlab), most ks are >1. If I however divide the log_lik first by the number of observations per subject, then no ks are larger than 0.02, but some are negative (~-0.1). Does this mean that I can compare models based on the psis-loo?

Many thanks
Jacquie

On Friday, December 18, 2015 at 6:27:16 PM UTC, Aki Vehtari wrote:
>
> On Friday, December 18, 2015 at 6:35:31 PM UTC+2, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> > Hi!
> >
> > Apologies for going stray slightly, but this happens so often: Suppose I want to do k-fold-cv on the basis of subjects as in the example described by Lei - in his case I understood that each subject has exactly 100 trials. However, I am often facing the situation that subjects can have vastly different number of observations. Is a leave-subjects-out approach then meaningful or should on average each subject have the same number of observations?
>
> Leave-subjects-out approach is meaningful in this case. If you want each subject have same weight in the predictive performance estimate than you can divide log_lik for each subject by the number observations for that subject.
>
> Aki
>
> >
> > These regular data-sets happen so rarely in my applications...
> >
> > Thanks (Aki)!
> >
> > Sebastian
> >
> > On Friday, December 18, 2015 at 4:21:30 PM UTC+1, Aki Vehtari wrote:
> > >
> > >
> > > On Friday, December 18, 2015 at 4:22:59 PM UTC+2, Lei Zhang wrote:
> > > > Hi Stan,
> > > >
> > > > I've been modeling a 2-armed bandit task with a basic reinforcement learning model in a trial-by-trial fashion. For instance, I have 129 subjects who performed the same task for 100 trials, and run overall 4000 samples in Stan. I've implemented 'loglik' in the generated quantities section, who gave me a 4000 by 129 log-likelihood matrix. For such a trial-by-trial model, we normally do not consider the log-likelihood per subject per trial, but rather, we sum the loglik for all trials and get the loglik only per subject, because each trial is not full independent according the model, i.e. the expected value on the current trial is updated from the last trial.
> > >
> > > It is sensible to consider the leave-one-subject-out performance as you describe. I often make such performance estimates and they can give different results than leave-one-observation-out.
> > >
> > > >
> > > > When passing two model fits to the LOO() function, I obtained a huge proportion of subjects whose k-hat are larger than 0.5 and even 1.0 (see below). Please note that, each pointwise k-hat represents a subject, rather than a single data point. For even more complex models, we have more subjects whose k-hat are greater than 1.
> > > >
> > > > (1) I wonder if I am doing this correctly? Is the model comparison based on PSIS-LOO still reliable?
> > >
> > > Based on a quick look, it seems your code is correct. Large khats tell that PSIS-LOO is not reliable. PSIS (and TIS, IS, and WAIC) work when leave-one-out distribution is close to the full posterior. It is more likely that when you are leaving 100 observations out that the distribution changes too much for the importance sampling able to work well. Figures 5 and 6 in our paper Pareto Smoothed Importance Sampling http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.02646 shows how the performance of PSIS (and IS and TIS) gets worse when the number dimensions (in your case the number of left out observations) increase.
> > >
> > >
> > > > (2) I also read from the paper (Vehtari et al, 2015) that I would consider computing k-fold CV instead, however as this is not implemented in the {LOO} package, I have no clear idea how I could do it for our trial-by-trial model. Am I suppose run a k(-trial)-fold CV per subject, or run a k(-subject)-fold CV for all the subjects? Any suggestions about how to calculate a k-fold CV for such a reinforcement learning model?
> > >
> > > I recommend k-fold-CV where data is divided based on subjects (e.g. with k=10, leave 12-13 subjects out in each fold). Vehtari et al (2015) has an example code. If you are able to compute separate log_lik for each subject (summing 100 trials) as in your current code, then you can do the same also for the test data in k-fold-CV. We could add some helper functions to make the data divisions to training and test sets (I have them in Matlab, but need to port to R and Python, too).
> > >
> > > > (3) or alternatively, how about using WAIC?
> > >
> > > If PSIS-LOO fails then WAIC fails, too. Currently our WAIC code just doesn't warn you about that. Adding warnings to our WAIC code is on TODO list.
> > >
> > > Aki
> > >
> > > >
> > > > You may want to check the attached stan model file. Any input/suggestion is welcome.
> > > >
> > > > > loo_RL
> > > > Computed from 4000 by 129 log-likelihood matrix
> > > >
> > > >          Estimate    SE
> > > > elpd_loo  -6920.1 150.0
> > > > p_loo       172.6  13.0
> > > > looic     13840.2 299.9
> > > > Warning messages:
> > > > 1: 110 (85.3%) Pareto k estimates between 0.5 and 1
> > > > 2: 19 (14.7%) Pareto k estimates greater than 1
> > > >
> > > > > loo_RLnc
> > > > Computed from 4000 by 129 log-likelihood matrix
> > > >
> > > >          Estimate    SE
> > > > elpd_loo  -6562.5 166.6
> > > > p_loo       230.7   8.9
> > > > looic     13125.1 333.2
> > > > Warning messages:
> > > > 1: 74 (57.4%) Pareto k estimates between 0.5 and 1
> > > > 2: 55 (42.6%) Pareto k estimates greater than 1
> > > >
> > > > > compare(loo_RL, loo_RLnc)
> > > > elpd_diff        se   weight1   weight2
> > > >     357.6      42.3       0.0       1.0

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm running a rather large model (around 2K parameters) with 5,000 posterior samples for each parameter. I've been running the model on a remote cluster, saving the sampling output from PySTAN using the sample_file argument:

model.sampling(..., sample_file='chains')

to save a CSV of the posteriors from each chain. I then load the chains into Python on my personal computer to plot coefficients, examine convergence, and do all of the necessary backend work.

The problem is that the sample_file output adds extra rows (like #Sample generated by Stan, #stan_version_major) at the top, and halfway through where the burn-in iterations cease there is a row break for #adaptation terminated, etc. Normally, I can open the posteriors in Excel and delete the extra rows, along with the adaptation samples, so that my posteriors can be read into Python or R. However, for my current files (2K columns, 10K rows) this is impossible. The file size is nearly 2 GB (above the internal limit for 32-bit Excel), and other programs without file size limits like LibreOffice put a limit on the number of columns. The result being that I cannot find a spreadsheet program capable of opening the sample_files to delete the extra rows and adaptation steps.

I've looked, but I've found no option in the PySTAN API that allows sample_files to ignore writing the details and, ideally, burn-in steps. Is this possible, or planned?

Also, the logical solution would be to get 64-bit Excel, which does not have a file size limit, and open the chains. But Microsoft does not (or will not) make a 64-bit version of Office for Mac. The newest 2016 Office for Mac is still 32-bit. So this seems like an issue that is not easily solvable at the moment.

Any advice for how to get around this issue?

Nate

messages.body_plain:
Stan is really not ideal for factor models at scale.
It's possible, but it won't scale well with number of dimensions
and data points and it's very hard to get it to converge (and
indexes won't be identified in different chains).  The efficient
algorithms to do what you're trying to do tend to work one
rank (singular vectors/value) at a time, fit that, then work
on the residuals.  I don't know if it'd be possible to build some
kind of direct model in Stan that would be much more efficient.

At K=30, I think you're going to have problems with speed and
convergence.

- Bob

really curious why you'd ever load one of these files into Excel.)

If you set the comment character in Excel, it should delete the
extra rows for you.  It's just an ordinary CSV file with "#" as
the line comment.

You should be able to set PyStan so it doesn't save warmup (don't
let Andrew hear you say "burnin" :-)).  If not, please create an
issue on stan-dev/pystan.

The formats are going to get cleaned up and the options for
running Stan unified across interfaces in Stan 3.   But that's
still a long way off.

- Bob

Check out the section in the regression chapter of the manual
on multivariate priors to see how to do this robustly and
efficiently in terms of Cholesky factors of correlation matrices
plus scales.

You may want to read our other prior advice, because we strongly
recommend against uniform priors on an interval.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] PSIS-LOO for trial-by-trial modeling
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] PSIS-LOO for trial-by-trial modeling
messages.body_plain:
Hi, you don’t want to be dividing by number of observations.  There are more general questions of what to do if you care more about some observations than others.  In theory one could define a weighted LOO or WAIC that counts some observations more than others.  I have not seen this but I could easily imagine settings where it would make sense, as a sort of poststratification.

Regarding k:  You don’t want to divide by number of observations.  So if k is greater than 1, this does indicate high variance.
A

> On Feb 23, 2016, at 6:44 AM, jacquie...@gmail.com wrote:
>

> Hi all,
>
> related to this questions, I was wondering whether I should also divide the log_lik for each subject by the number of observations for that subject if I want to use psis-loo to compare models? I have 29 subjects and they each have between 190 and 200 observations on a psychological learning task- which means that if I compute for each subject the log likelihood as the sum of the log_lik across all observations, the ones with more trials will have a higher log_lik.
>
> When I put these log_lik into psisloo (matlab), most ks are >1. If I however divide the log_lik first by the number of observations per subject, then no ks are larger than 0.02, but some are negative (~-0.1). Does this mean that I can compare models based on the psis-loo?
>
> Many thanks
> Jacquie
>

> >

> > > Hi!
> > >
> > > Apologies for going stray slightly, but this happens so often: Suppose I want to do k-fold-cv on the basis of subjects as in the example described by Lei - in his case I understood that each subject has exactly 100 trials. However, I am often facing the situation that subjects can have vastly different number of observations. Is a leave-subjects-out approach then meaningful or should on average each subject have the same number of observations?
> >
> > Leave-subjects-out approach is meaningful in this case. If you want each subject have same weight in the predictive performance estimate than you can divide log_lik for each subject by the number observations for that subject.

For instance, I have 129 subjects who performed the same task for 100 trials, and run overall 4000 samples in Stan. I've implemented 'loglik' in the generated quantities section, who gave me a 4000 by 129 log-likelihood matrix. For such a trial-by-trial model, we normally do not consider the log-likelihood per subject per trial, but rather, we sum the loglik for all trials and get the loglik only per subject, because each trial is not full independent according the model, i.e. the expected value on the current trial is updated from the last trial.
> > > >
> > > > It is sensible to consider the leave-one-subject-out performance as you describe. I often make such performance estimates and they can give different results than leave-one-observation-out.

> > > > >

PSIS (and TIS, IS, and WAIC) work when leave-one-out distribution is close to the full posterior. It is more likely that when you are leaving 100 observations out that the distribution changes too much for the importance sampling able to work well. Figures 5 and 6 in our paper Pareto Smoothed Importance Sampling http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.02646 shows how the performance of PSIS (and IS and TIS) gets worse when the number dimensions (in your case the number of left out observations) increase.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > > (2) I also read from the paper (Vehtari et al, 2015) that I would consider computing k-fold CV instead, however as this is not implemented in the {LOO} package, I have no clear idea how I could do it for our trial-by-trial model. > > > > I recommend k-fold-CV where data is divided based on subjects (e.g. with k=10, leave 12-13 subjects out in each fold). Vehtari et al (2015) has an example code. > > > >
> > > > > (3) or alternatively, how about using WAIC?
> > > >
> > > > If PSIS-LOO fails then WAIC fails, too. Currently our WAIC code just doesn't warn you about that. Adding warnings to our WAIC code is on TODO list.
> > > >
> > > > Aki
> > > >
> > > > >

> > > > > Warning messages:

> > > > >

> > > > >     357.6      42.3       0.0       1.0

> > > > >

messages.body_plain:
Weighting categories equally is not uncommon in search and
natural language classifier evaluations, which are a kind
of model comparison.  It's known as  macro-averaging:

http://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/evaluation-of-text-classification-1.html

It ignores the population distribution and treats each category
equally, so has exactly the opposite effect to what Andrew was
suggesting with poststratification.   Macro-averaging inflates
the importance of each item from a small category tremendously.

You also often get training data that has undergone stratified
sampling, with an equal number of items for each category even
though that doesn't represent the actual distribution of items.

- Bob

Ben saves the comments here first before overwriting chains*.csv.

messages.body_plain:
Bob:
Your suggestion is not opposite to poststratification, it’s a special case of poststratification where you adjust to a distribution in which all categories are weighted equally.
A

> On Feb 23, 2016, at 7:34 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> Weighting categories equally is not uncommon in search and
> natural language classifier evaluations, which are a kind
> of model comparison.  It's known as  macro-averaging:
>
> http://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/evaluation-of-text-classification-1.html
>
> It ignores the population distribution and treats each category
> equally, so has exactly the opposite effect to what Andrew was
> suggesting with poststratification.   Macro-averaging inflates
> the importance of each item from a small category tremendously.
>
> You also often get training data that has undergone stratified
> sampling, with an equal number of items for each category even
> though that doesn't represent the actual distribution of items.
>
> - Bob
>
>> On Feb 23, 2016, at 5:52 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>
>> Hi, you don’t want to be dividing by number of observations.  There are more general questions of what to do if you care more about some observations than others.  In theory one could define a weighted LOO or WAIC that counts some observations more than others.  I have not seen this but I could easily imagine settings where it would make sense, as a sort of poststratification.
>>
>> Regarding k:  You don’t want to divide by number of observations.  So if k is greater than 1, this does indicate high variance.
>> A
>>
>>
>>> On Feb 23, 2016, at 6:44 AM, jacquie...@gmail.com wrote:
>>>
>>> Hi all,
>>>
>>> related to this questions, I was wondering whether I should also divide the log_lik for each subject by the number of observations for that subject if I want to use psis-loo to compare models? I have 29 subjects and they each have between 190 and 200 observations on a psychological learning task- which means that if I compute for each subject the log likelihood as the sum of the log_lik across all observations, the ones with more trials will have a higher log_lik.
>>>
>>> When I put these log_lik into psisloo (matlab), most ks are >1. If I however divide the log_lik first by the number of observations per subject, then no ks are larger than 0.02, but some are negative (~-0.1). Does this mean that I can compare models based on the psis-loo?
>>>
>>> Many thanks
>>> Jacquie
>>>
>>> On Friday, December 18, 2015 at 6:27:16 PM UTC, Aki Vehtari wrote:
>>>
>>> On Friday, December 18, 2015 at 6:35:31 PM UTC+2, Sebastian Weber wrote:
>>> Hi!
>>>
>>> Apologies for going stray slightly, but this happens so often: Suppose I want to do k-fold-cv on the basis of subjects as in the example described by Lei - in his case I understood that each subject has exactly 100 trials. However, I am often facing the situation that subjects can have vastly different number of observations. Is a leave-subjects-out approach then meaningful or should on average each subject have the same number of observations?
>>>
>>> Leave-subjects-out approach is meaningful in this case. If you want each subject have same weight in the predictive performance estimate than you can divide log_lik for each subject by the number observations for that subject.
>>>
>>> Aki
>>>
>>>
>>> These regular data-sets happen so rarely in my applications...
>>>
>>> Thanks (Aki)!
>>>
>>> Sebastian
>>>
>>> On Friday, December 18, 2015 at 4:21:30 PM UTC+1, Aki Vehtari wrote:
>>>
>>>
>>> On Friday, December 18, 2015 at 4:22:59 PM UTC+2, Lei Zhang wrote:
>>> Hi Stan,
>>>
>>> I've been modeling a 2-armed bandit task with a basic reinforcement learning model in a trial-by-trial fashion. For instance, I have 129 subjects who performed the same task for 100 trials, and run overall 4000 samples in Stan. I've implemented 'loglik' in the generated quantities section, who gave me a 4000 by 129 log-likelihood matrix. For such a trial-by-trial model, we normally do not consider the log-likelihood per subject per trial, but rather, we sum the loglik for all trials and get the loglik only per subject, because each trial is not full independent according the model, i.e. the expected value on the current trial is updated from the last trial.
>>>
>>> It is sensible to consider the leave-one-subject-out performance as you describe. I often make such performance estimates and they can give different results than leave-one-observation-out.
>>>
>>>
>>> When passing two model fits to the LOO() function, I obtained a huge proportion of subjects whose k-hat are larger than 0.5 and even 1.0 (see below). Please note that, each pointwise k-hat represents a subject, rather than a single data point. For even more complex models, we have more subjects whose k-hat are greater than 1.
>>>
>>> (1) I wonder if I am doing this correctly? Is the model comparison based on PSIS-LOO still reliable?
>>>
>>> Based on a quick look, it seems your code is correct. Large khats tell that PSIS-LOO is not reliable. PSIS (and TIS, IS, and WAIC) work when leave-one-out distribution is close to the full posterior. It is more likely that when you are leaving 100 observations out that the distribution changes too much for the importance sampling able to work well. Figures 5 and 6 in our paper Pareto Smoothed Importance Sampling http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.02646 shows how the performance of PSIS (and IS and TIS) gets worse when the number dimensions (in your case the number of left out observations) increase.
>>>
>>>
>>> (2) I also read from the paper (Vehtari et al, 2015) that I would consider computing k-fold CV instead, however as this is not implemented in the {LOO} package, I have no clear idea how I could do it for our trial-by-trial model. Am I suppose run a k(-trial)-fold CV per subject, or run a k(-subject)-fold CV for all the subjects? Any suggestions about how to calculate a k-fold CV for such a reinforcement learning model?
>>>
>>> I recommend k-fold-CV where data is divided based on subjects (e.g. with k=10, leave 12-13 subjects out in each fold). Vehtari et al (2015) has an example code. If you are able to compute separate log_lik for each subject (summing 100 trials) as in your current code, then you can do the same also for the test data in k-fold-CV. We could add some helper functions to make the data divisions to training and test sets (I have them in Matlab, but need to port to R and Python, too).
>>>
>>> (3) or alternatively, how about using WAIC?
>>>
>>> If PSIS-LOO fails then WAIC fails, too. Currently our WAIC code just doesn't warn you about that. Adding warnings to our WAIC code is on TODO list.
>>>
>>> Aki
>>>
>>>
>>> You may want to check the attached stan model file. Any input/suggestion is welcome.
>>>
>>>> loo_RL
>>> Computed from 4000 by 129 log-likelihood matrix
>>>
>>>         Estimate    SE
>>> elpd_loo  -6920.1 150.0
>>> p_loo       172.6  13.0
>>> looic     13840.2 299.9
>>> Warning messages:
>>> 1: 110 (85.3%) Pareto k estimates between 0.5 and 1
>>> 2: 19 (14.7%) Pareto k estimates greater than 1
>>>
>>>> loo_RLnc
>>> Computed from 4000 by 129 log-likelihood matrix
>>>
>>>         Estimate    SE
>>> elpd_loo  -6562.5 166.6
>>> p_loo       230.7   8.9
>>> looic     13125.1 333.2
>>> Warning messages:
>>> 1: 74 (57.4%) Pareto k estimates between 0.5 and 1
>>> 2: 55 (42.6%) Pareto k estimates greater than 1
>>>
>>>> compare(loo_RL, loo_RLnc)
>>> elpd_diff        se   weight1   weight2
>>>    357.6      42.3       0.0       1.0
>>>
>>>
>>> Thanks in advance!
>>>
>>> Lei
>>>
>>>
>>>

Absolutely.  But the effect is the opposite of the usual
poststratifications I've seen, the point of which has been
to take some kind of biased data sample and adjust it for

random sample from the population of interest, and then you
poststratify to something that weights each category equally and
doesn't represent any population of interest (except maybe to
consumers of classifier evaluations involving macro averaging).

messages.subject: priors for hierarchical modeling of over-dispersion parameter phi for neg_binomial_2
messages.subject_clean: priors for hierarchical modeling of over-dispersion parameter phi for neg_binomial_2
messages.body_plain:
Thanks everyone for chiming in!

About Andrews advocacy for scale free models:
I try to follow this recommendation when possible.
However, for the data I am working with I need
to use the negative binomial distribution, and here
the over dispersion parameter can take larger values
that are maybe not best modeled with normal(0,1) or
chauchy(0,1) as priors

About my attempts to find suitable priors for hierarchical
modeling of the overdispersion parameter (i.e. the phi of
neg_binomial_2):
I chose to model the hierarchical prior phi with the gamma
distribution, because it has to be larger than zero.
I could also have tried the chauchy, but it appeared more
natural for me to choose the gamma for a _hierarchical_ prior
whose mean I expect to be larger than zero.

Modeling the gamma directly with shape and inverse scale
parameters alpha and beta did not work well. Instead I used
priors for the mean and sd of the gamma distribution
and transformed them to alpha and beta.

Using the cauchy as a prior for the mean of the gamma works
well. Finding a good prior for the sd of the gamma seems
harder. I get the same posteriors for the variance of the
gamma independent if I use a cauchy or uniform prior, but
n_eff is generally low (around 50-80 effective samples from 3
chains with 400 samples each). The low n_eff seems mainly
to be caused by relatively high auto-correlation of the sd
of the gamma distribution (see attachments). I'd welcome
any suggestion to reduce this auto-correlation (of course
i can always run the chain longer).

here are the relevant snippets of how i am currently modeling
hierarchical priors for phi:

parameters {
  ...
  // overdispersion of negative binomial
  real<lower=0, upper=pi()/2> phi_mu_unif;
  real<lower=0, upper=pi()/2> phi_sigma_unif;
  real<lower=0> phi[M]; // M = number of groups
  }

transformed parameters {
 ...
  phi_mu <- 5 * tan(phi_mu_unif);
  phi_sigma <- 2.5 * tan(phi_sigma_unif);
}

model {
  ...
  phi ~ gamma(phi_mu^2/phi_sigma^2, phi_mu/phi_sigma^2);
  // could also calculate alpha and beta in the transformed parameters block ...
  ...
}

Some more observations:
It looks as if I can stick to the default adapt_delta when using
uniform priors for the variance of the gamma, whereas I have
to increase adapt_delta when using cauchy priors in order to avoid
divergent iterations (I only tried .95, which worked)

I find the re-parameterization of the cauchy described in the manual
very useful.This seems especially useful for the prior scale tau of
the hierarchical regression model. Maybe it would be useful for
other users to include a version of the model on page 75 of the
manual (version 2.9.0) into the manual that also uses a
re-parameterization for the prior scale tau.

Cheers - Guido

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Ragged R-hat and n_eff
messages.body_plain:
I'm thinking one edge case is a low jump distance
random-walk Metropolis --- we'll get huge autocorrelations,
huge numbers of draws, and may not even cover the posterior.
So the question is how much does it get downweighted?
Weighing by chain, one bad apple destroys the bunch.

The other edge case is perfect Monte Carlo.  Then we'll
get all the different chains of HMC from different initializations
and with different adaptations in between these extremes, which
is the real use case we care about.

I also think the rule needs to do the right thing with thinning,
but I think that comes for free.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Saving Shinystan sessions?
messages.subject_clean: Saving Shinystan sessions?
messages.body_plain:
Hi John,

I don't have a great answer, but I might have a somewhat helpful suggestion.

First, when you call launch_shinystan it doesn't actually send anything to the cloud. Everything is happening locally on your machine and the web browser is just used to display the content. What's slow is that when you call launch_shinystan it has to do a bunch of computations before it can show you anything. Usually that doesn't take long but for very large models it can take quite some time unfortunately, as you've noticed.

When you say you have a large model, do you mean it has a lot of parameters? That's usually the culprit when it takes so long.  If it does have a lot of parameters, do you need to look at all of them in shinystan or are you mostly interested in looking at a subset of them? If the latter, then there's a new function called drop_parameters that will be introduced in the next version of the shinystan package that might help. It's already available in the version of shinystan on the develop branch on github, which you can install using

devtools::install_github("stan-dev/shinystan", ref = "develop")

Then you could do something like this:

sso <- as.shinystan(fit) # still could take a very long time to initially create the shinystan object
sso <- drop_parameters(sso, pars = c("alpha", "theta")) # but use the names of some parameters in your model
launch_shinystan(sso) # should be faster than launch_shinystan(fit)

If any of the parameters in pars are non-scalar (e.g. vectors, matrices, etc.) then all of their elements will be dropped.

Creating sso will still take a long time, but then if you drop a bunch of parameters that you don't need to look at the slimmer sso should launch faster. And you can save the smaller sso so you don't need to repeat the process of creating the original sso if you want to launch shinystan again at some later time.

Unfortunately there's not really a better option at the moment, although I'm planning on eventually modifying the as.shinystan function so it can drop parameters internally if the user specifies some parameters to remove. That would be faster than having to create sso using all parameters and then dropping them.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

messages.subject: Summarizing chains individually?
messages.subject_clean: Summarizing chains individually?
messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone,

I'm in the process of converting several latent profile/mixture models to stan by means of marginalizing out the discrete parameters, using simplexes to weight the likelihoods, etc.

Some observations:
1) In JAGS, I often hit the label-switching problem *between* chains, but rarely within (probably due to the conditional sampling method rather than surfing a probability surface for solutions).
2) In Stan, I hit a within-chain label-switching problem. I can solve this by setting constraints (whether it's ordered simplexes or ordered means).

With JAGS, I could visually compare the chains in trace plots and tell obviously that labels were switching, then summarize chains that labeled the same.

With Stan, I can plot each chain's trace separately, but is there an 'easy' way of summarizing a subset of the chains?
That is, if I run a model with 4 chains, is there a way of running summary() on only one of those chains?
I ask because in one model, 2 chains converge to the "correct" mixture and 2 chains definitely do not, and I would like to summarize each chain separately.

A hacky solution is to use coda: coda::summary(As.mcmc.list(stan.out)[[1]])

Is there a more elegant solution using rstan's tools?

A few other tips that might not be applicable in this case but might be useful for future reference:

1) If your model has a lot of parameters/transformed parameters, then if some are not of direct interest you can specify pars when calling stan() in rstan which will only save the parameters in pars and give you a smaller stanfit object and in turn a smaller shinystan object. Some transformed parameters may also be able to be declared and defined in the model block, in which case they won't be saved but you can still use them in the model.

2) launch_shinystan will always be faster if the input is a shinystan object rather than a stanfit object. This is because it first converts the stanfit object to a shinystan object. So if you might end up calling launch_shinystan more than once it's a good idea to first create a shinystan object and use that. For small models the difference is negligible but for large models it can make a big difference.

Jonah

On Wed, Feb 24, 2016 at 2:32 PM, Jonah Sol Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:

> A few other tips that might not be applicable in this case but might be useful for future reference:
>
> 1) If your model has a lot of parameters/transformed parameters, then if some are not of direct interest you can specify pars when calling stan() in rstan which will only save the parameters in pars and give you a smaller stanfit object and in turn a smaller shinystan object. Some transformed parameters may also be able to be declared and defined in the model block, in which case they won't be saved but you can still use them in the model.
>
> 2) launch_shinystan will always be faster if the input is a shinystan object rather than a stanfit object. This is because it first converts the stanfit object to a shinystan object. So if you might end up calling launch_shinystan more than once it's a good idea to first create a shinystan object and use that. For small models the difference is negligible but for large models it can make a big difference.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Using a vector as a lower bound of another vector
messages.body_plain:
No, you basically have to do the transforms yourself.

data {
  int N;
  vector[N] L;  // lower bounds

parameters {
  vector[N] my_vec_raw;

transformed parameters {
  vector[N] my_vec;
  my_vec <- L + exp(my_vec_raw);

model {
  increment_log_prob(sum(my_vec_raw));  // Jacobian

I should at least put this in the manual until I can implement
vectors of lower bounds.  I made the lower bound data here, but
it could also be a parameter itself.  As long as the parameter
L isn't computed in terms of my_vec_raw, then the Jacobian above
is sufficient for the transform (L, my_vec_raw) -> (L, my_vec).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Summarizing chains individually?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Summarizing chains individually?
messages.body_plain:
It's better for Stan to identify the model if you can.

If you can't, you could just go directly to computing inferences
for quantities of interest, which very often won't depend
on the labels.  Unfortunately, this can potentially mask
non-convergences that would be detected otherwise.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
In some models, it won't matter which label is which.

In this model, the parameter of interest does depend on labels.

The issue in this particular model, actually, is that different chains are converging on different solutions.

Using PPC, both solutions actually do appear to be good fits.

The true values are as follows:
K = 2, mu[1] = 0, mu[2] = 5, sd[1] = 1, sd[2] = 3, alpha[1] = .66, alpha[2] = .33 (where alpha is the mixing proportion).
One solution is very close to the true parameters.

The other solution is basically mu[1] and mu[2] = 0, sd[1] = 1, sd[2] = 6.
Both of the map decently well onto the observed density. N(0,1) takes care of the heavier density near 0, and N(0,6)'s upper tail essentially covers the second cluster's density.

I'm not sure how to change the model to converge on only the correct solution.
I could probably make the prior of sd[2] smaller.

Edit:
I'll add that I've had similar experiences using other cluster modeling packages.
In a similar dataset, Mclust found the correct solution, but flexmix found a solution akin to the second I mentioned, where the means are equal, but the second group's distribution is much, much wider.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Meta-mixture models?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Meta-mixture models?
messages.body_plain:
This doesn't help with mixing, but it's more efficient
computationally to use a single prior with a beta
prior than a simplex[2] with a Dirichlet prior (the
second component of the simplex is just one minus the
first).

And rather than this:

>    vector[2] mu_2s; //unsorted mu, to be sorted later
>
>     vector<lower=0>[1] sigma_1;
>     vector<lower=0>[2] sigma_2;
> }
> transformed parameters{
>     ordered[2] mu_2;
>     mu_2 <- sort_asc(mu_2s);

you can jut declare mu_2 directly as an ordered[2] parameter.
That actually should help some with mixing because otherwise,
the mu_2s aren't identified (only the sorted ones are).

And to address the last other email, if you have mass around
two different local modes in the posterior, you technically
want to integrate over both for inference.

In general, mixtures are very hard, and often people just
go with a fit around a single local mode (typical in LDA
models, for example) because the entire posterior's known
to be intractable.  There are some approaches, but I don't know
of any system that really solves the problem in a satisfying
way.  Maybe others will have suggestions.

- Bob

I also just realized that my likelihood was incorrect (it was weighting pk *way* too much; log(pk) should only weight the model likelihoods once, not N times).

I think by fixing it, it stabilized the chains and allowed them to converge properly.

Moreover, when the true model is not a mixture, p(k=1|D) > p(k=2|D), and when the true model is a mixture, it flips. Perfect!
It also accurately recovered the means, sds, and membership probabilities when K=2.

The point is to converge to the true data generating process, under the assumption that one of the models you’re mixing over is the truth. But I agree, I feel that’s an overemphasized assumption which can’t be checked so we may as well use a prior that you suggested in practice.

Dustin

messages.body_plain:
Generally, I am for complex models for the same reasons you express. The world is complex, and thus for the best predictive model one should model it with the complexity it warrants.

However, for 1) testing particular hypotheses 2) pitting two competing theoretical models against each other and 3) for fairly niche questions, I do indeed need to compare whether a simpler model is explanatory "enough".

Eventually, I am going to be converting a fairly complex bayesian model to Stan that assesses the probability and extent of DIF in various CFA and IRT models assuming latent groups are present.
The model requires the techniques used in the opening post, which is why I'm trying to get my feet wet in this particular example before converting the more complex model to Stan.
In that model, we do not want to marginalize over items' probabilities of exhibiting DIF to predict anything; we actually want the probability of items exhibiting DIF, because that guides our decision about the scale itself.
For that, we need to pit models against one another to make a decision.

> > > > >     }
> > > > >     alpha_2 ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1.0,2));
> > > > >

> > > > >

> > > > >     }
> > > > > }

> > > > > # Label switching problem; cycles between labels

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Meta-mixture models?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Meta-mixture models?
messages.body_plain:
Yeah, I'm incorporating PPCs too.

The meta-mixture's purpose is two-fold.
1) To serve as a baseline toy example for a more complex DIF IRT model with latent groups.
2) To serve as an alternative to AIC/BIC/*IC for selecting a sufficient number of mixture components. I.e., instead of using *ICs to check for the 'optimal' number of latent components, determine the optimal number via probability.

So far, it worked for 2) fairly well, but I'll have to run simulations to determine how well it performs.
I'll be extending it for 1) soon.

Thanks for the help everyone.
