messages.body_plain:
> On Feb 24, 2016, at 8:46 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Oh, thanks!
>
> I didn't know Stan could sample ordered vectors directly.
>
> And for inference and prediction, yes, one should integrate over all modes.
> I'm comfortable with that, since it's straightforwardly telling you there are a few probable solutions to the model.
>
> However, knowing the "true" model, I'm trying to see how to recover the "true" model.

That won't always work (though I'm glad to see it did here after
some debugging).

Let's say I actually know the model p(y, theta) and use it to
generate a simulated data set y' given parameters theta'.
It's still possible that the posterior p(theta | y') is
multimodal and/or to has a posterior mean other than theta'.
The only thing we can hope is that the model's calibrated and
captures the true value of theta in the 50% (or 95% or whatever)
interval 50% (95%) of the time.  Of course, defining something
like a 50% interval is tricky when the model's multimodal.  But
it shouldn't matter how you define it for the calibration.

- Bob

P.S.  What you're doing is exactly what we always recommend---start
with a simple model and simulate data and make sure the model is
well calibrated in recovering the parameters.  The reason we
recommend it is exactly as you reported---it lets you debug your
code and model pathologies.  Thanks for sharing.

messages.subject: normal prior in rstanarm with scale = NULL
messages.subject_clean: normal prior in rstanarm with scale = NULL
messages.body_plain:
A question and a comment on normal priors in rstanarm.

1. rstanarm::normal() has a default scale = NULL. The documentation does not say what scale = NULL means, except in the specific case when it is used as the prior_intercept argument of stan_lm. In this case the stan_lm documentation says that scale is chosen to be "the marginal standard deviation of the outcome, divided by the square root of the sample size." Is that true in general?

2. The above-mentioned default scale for rstanarm::normal() is incompatible with Bayes' Rule. The problem is NOT the dependence on the sigma_Y parameter -- it is the division by sqrt(N). A legitimate prior cannot depend on the number of data points you will be observing. This default scale has you getting more and more certain of the intercept as the number of data points to be observed increases.

messages.subject: Stan for complex survey designs?
messages.subject_clean: Stan for complex survey designs?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all!

I've been doing some work with complex survey designs, specifically, using Thomas Lumley's survey package for R to run differences-in-differences analyses using the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS). The NHIS uses weighting, nested stratification, and clusters. With the R survey package I can simply set these parameters into the svydesign function and all the pesky math is done for me. This is great, because my grasp on the equations underlying statistics with complex survey designs is very limited.

I would love to be able to take a Bayesian approach to my research questions using Stan. In particular, I have been trying to figure out how I would run logistic regressions that take weights, strata, and clusters into account. It would have to involve an interaction term to capture the differences-in-differences effect.

Has anyone tried using Stan with complex survey designs like these? Is there a way to do this that isn't prohibitively complicated?

Thank you very much.

Peter

messages.subject: Re: normal prior in rstanarm with scale = NULL
messages.subject_clean: normal prior in rstanarm with scale = NULL
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, February 25, 2016 at 10:41:12 AM UTC-5, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
> A question and a comment on normal priors in rstanarm.
>
> 1. rstanarm::normal() has a default scale = NULL. The documentation does not say what scale = NULL means, except in the specific case when it is used as the prior_intercept argument of stan_lm. In this case the stan_lm documentation says that scale is chosen to be "the marginal standard deviation of the outcome, divided by the square root of the sample size." Is that true in general?

For models with continuous outcomes, yes. For coefficients, there is an adjustment to the prior scale based on the scales of the predictors. For other families, such as binomial, it does a 1.6 scaling of the logit priors if the model is probit but not for other link functions. I think the behavior comes from

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/priors11.pdf

> 2. The above-mentioned default scale for rstanarm::normal() is incompatible with Bayes' Rule. The problem is NOT the dependence on the sigma_Y parameter -- it is the division by sqrt(N). A legitimate prior cannot depend on the number of data points you will be observing. This default scale has you getting more and more certain of the intercept as the number of data points to be observed increases.

I agree that in most cases, it does not make sense to consider N to be fixed.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, February 25, 2016 at 10:41:12 AM UTC-5, Kevin Van Horn wrote:

> A question and a comment on normal priors in rstanarm.
>
> 1. rstanarm::normal() has a default scale = NULL. The documentation does not say what scale = NULL means, except in the specific case when it is used as the prior_intercept argument of stan_lm.

If you go help("priors", package = "rstanarm") then it does say the default scale is NULL because it depends on the family of prior used and whether the prior is for the intercept or for the other coefficients. For the normal prior this is the Student t family, which is described in a section in the same help page:

> If scale is not specified it will default to 10 for the intercept and 2.5 for the other coefficients, unless the probit link function is used, in which case these defaults are scaled by a factor of dnorm(0)/dlogis(0), which is roughly 1.6.

I don't believe we do any scaling by 1/sqrt(N) for stan_glm or stan_glmer. Regarding the particular case of stan_lm, Ben would know best.

messages.subject: GPs on a sphere (again): simpler than we thought?
messages.subject_clean: GPs on a sphere (again): simpler than we thought?
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

A while back, the list discussed the application of Gaussian Process modelling to a spherical topology (https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/z2hj0Zb1I6A/gFHK-BDhBpQJ) at which time it seemed that it was unsupported. I'm possibly (likely) being naive here, but after mulling it over I think that conclusion might be false. That is, Michael Betancourt's response was that placing and exploring a probability mass on a sphere is tricky, but so far as I understand it, that's not what we'd be doing in the case of a GP.

The probability mass explored by all GPs will necessarily be a multivariate Gaussian, and where the spherical bit comes in would be in the computation of the covariance matrix. In my prior thinking, I was erroneously thinking that having spherical data defined by lat/long put me in the "multivariate inputs" case (page 161 of manual version 2.9.0). I now realize that while the spherical data is indeed defined by two variables, what is important for any given pair of points is merely their great circle distance, thus reducing to the univariate case after all. (Note I also talked of including time as a variable, which would put things back in the multivariate inputs world again, time & space, but still just using great circle distance for the space dimension)

So, am I wrong here? Happy to be corrected, but excited to try this if I'm right!

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] GPs on a sphere (again): simpler than we thought?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] GPs on a sphere (again): simpler than we thought?
messages.body_plain:
Sort of.  Yes there is a distinguished distance function on the sphere (geodesic distance with respect to the unique flat metric on the sphere and the  Levi-Cevita connection), but that doesn't mean that you can just throw it into a squared exponential kernel.   You
still have to choose a kernel that is consistent with functions on the sphere and deal with any potential nonidentifiabilities.

For a sine kernel I think this might be okay, but just remember that you'll only be able to make inferences relative to your data, not absolute on the sphere.  Ultimately the GP uses the data to anchor the coordinates and remove many of the problems, but only when making statements relative to those points.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Stan for complex survey designs?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Stan for complex survey designs?
messages.body_plain:
Hello Stanners, I attach 2 papers that, together, offer a very general approach for incorporating information from the sampling design distribution (to account for an informative sampling design) using the first order sampling weights.  The first paper illustrates the formulation and use of the pseudo posterior.  The second paper provides the frequentist consistency properties of the pseudo posterior.  To Jonah's point, the approach incorporates the first order sampling weights in a plug-in fashion, so it is not fully bayesian.

our observed sample may be viewed to come from two successive processes; 1. the (unknown) population generating distribution; 2. the (known) sampling design distribution.   The observed sample, y, is - therefore - not able to "comment" on the sampling design distribution.   One may view a fully Bayesian approach as co-modeling the first order sampling weights - in direct association with y or through a shared parameter approach.   A challenge here is that the distribution for weights, w, conditioned on y in the observed sample is not the same as that for the population.  So one must impute quantities from the non-sampled units.  Secondly, the first order weights don't convey the dependence structure among the sampled units (e.g., in a sampling without replacement design).   One would need higher order inclusion probabilities.

using the plug-in approach also doesn't capture the dependence structure, but pfefferman and sverchkov show that the conditional *expectation* of the (first order) weights given the response under the distribution for the observed / sampled units is equal to that under the distribution for the population.   the implication is that one may - under an inefficient sampling design - smooth the weights for the observed sample by regressing them on the response and then using those smoothed weights to form the pseudo posterior distribution described in the attached papers.

The use of the pseudo posterior approach has the virtue that it can be used for any population generating model without changing the parameterization.  This is especially useful where the sampling design is viewed as a nuisance or where the analyst may not know the sampling design to parameterize it in the model.   Additionally, using the pseudo posterior allows one to retain the geometry of the MCMC sampler.

Terrance Savitsky.

messages.subject: Conceptual question on time-series posterior prediction
messages.subject_clean: Conceptual question on time-series posterior prediction
messages.body_plain:
Just a conceptual question on a thought I've been toying with, and wanted to check if it sounded insane.

I have some models that I'm using I am using to generate forecasts for T+1, T+2, ... , T + S. When fitting the model, I use a bunch of covariates X that are constructs of my lagged dependent value. Because it's a forecasting model and I'm using lagged dependent values, I'm wary of using known Xs to construct my posterior predictions. I construct (forward-looking) posterior predictions, which give me uncertainty in my parameters, my future Xs (which are constructs now of the lagged simulated dependent variable), and my outcome given parameters and future Xs.

The question is how insane it would be to use loo to generate prediction intervals by weighting different models according to the forecast horizon? That is, in the fitting process, generate forward-looking posterior predictions (and log likelihood contributions) for T + 1, T + 2 and so on. Then, when I'm calculating a forecast interval for some T + s, I'd weight each model using loo::compare, calculating loo using the likelihood contributions at T+s.

What sort of things should I be aware of in this sort of setup?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Conceptual question on time-series posterior prediction
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Conceptual question on time-series posterior prediction
messages.body_plain:
For this to work you basically have to assume stationarity of the time
series so that you can think of the windows of length S as identically
distributed measurements that admit LOO-like calculations.  Of course
they also won’t be independent anymore, which will make the validity
of LOO-like calculations more subtle.

On Feb 26, 2016, at 8:34 PM, James Savage <jav...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Just a conceptual question on a thought I've been toying with, and wanted to check if it sounded insane.
>
> I have some models that I'm using I am using to generate forecasts for T+1, T+2, ... , T + S. When fitting the model, I use a bunch of covariates X that are constructs of my lagged dependent value. Because it's a forecasting model and I'm using lagged dependent values, I'm wary of using known Xs to construct my posterior predictions. I construct (forward-looking) posterior predictions, which give me uncertainty in my parameters, my future Xs (which are constructs now of the lagged simulated dependent variable), and my outcome given parameters and future Xs.
>
> The question is how insane it would be to use loo to generate prediction intervals by weighting different models according to the forecast horizon? That is, in the fitting process, generate forward-looking posterior predictions (and log likelihood contributions) for T + 1, T + 2 and so on. Then, when I'm calculating a forecast interval for some T + s, I'd weight each model using loo::compare, calculating loo using the likelihood contributions at T+s.
>
> What sort of things should I be aware of in this sort of setup?
>

messages.subject: log_prob-methods
messages.subject_clean: log_prob-methods
messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,

I'm currently trying to implement an HMC experiment outside of stan but would like to use stan to evaluate the log-probability and its gradient.  I found the log_prob-methods section in the rstan manual and would like some clarification on the following excerpt from the 'Details' section before I proceed:

> However, when using the log density function for a model exposed to R, we need to be careful. For example, if we are interested in finding the mode of parameters on the constrained space, we then do not need the adjustment. For this reason, there is an argument named adjust_transform for functions log_prob and grad_log_prob.

 At the end of the day, I would like the log-probability evaluated on the constrained parameters.  After some tooling around, I settled on first getting the unconstrained transformed parameters and then plugging them into log_prob with 'adjust_transform = FALSE'.  Here is an example with a simple exponential distribution model:

test_model <- stan_model('log_prob_test.stan')
test             <- sampling(test_model, data=list(y=1), iter=1, chains=1)
un               <- unconstrain_pars(test, pars=list(lambda=2))
log_prob(test, upars=un,adjust_transform=FALSE)

It gave me what I wanted for the simple model, but are there any issues I should know about in general?  I will be using these log-probabilities as part of the accept/reject step, so I intuit that the log-Jacobians should not be included.

Next, I want to evaluate the gradient.  After playing around I'm under the impression that

grad_log_prob(test,upars=un,adjust_transform=TRUE)

will give me the gradient of the log-probability plus log Jacobian.  It seems correct to take the unconstrained transformation into account in this way.  But am I wrong to use the transform when evaluating the gradient but not for the log-probability?  Keep in mind I will be using these values within HMC.

Thanks in advance,
Andrew

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] log_prob-methods
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] log_prob-methods
messages.body_plain:
If you want to do HMC (or random-walk Metropolis) in the unconstrained space,
then you need the Jacobians in the gradients and in the Metropolis
accept/reject step.

But, the log densities drop constant terms (additive terms in the log density
only involving constants and data as declared in the data block).

If you really need the log density on the constrained parameters without
the Jacobian, then you have to evaluate that with propto=false in the C++
template to avoid dropping constant terms.  I'm not sure how to do this
through RStan;  internally, Stan doesn't care about the constant terms.

- Bob

> On Feb 27, 2016, at 2:42 AM, Andrew James Holbrook <ahol...@uci.edu> wrote:
>
> Thanks, that was very helpful.  And for clarification, including the Jacobians corresponds to 'adjust_transform = TRUE'?

Yes.  If you take a positive-constrained parameter, you
should be able to see the effect (the log Jacobian is just
the parameter value, so that should be how much the difference
is with a single positive-constrained parameter).

- Bob

>
> Thanks,
> Andrew
>
> On Fri, Feb 26, 2016 at 11:07 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> If you want to do HMC (or random-walk Metropolis) in the unconstrained space,
> then you need the Jacobians in the gradients and in the Metropolis
> accept/reject step.
>
> But, the log densities drop constant terms (additive terms in the log density
> only involving constants and data as declared in the data block).
>
> If you really need the log density on the constrained parameters without
> the Jacobian, then you have to evaluate that with propto=false in the C++
> template to avoid dropping constant terms.  I'm not sure how to do this
> through RStan;  internally, Stan doesn't care about the constant terms.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Feb 26, 2016, at 5:46 PM, Andrew Holbrook <ahol...@uci.edu> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Everyone,
> >
> > I'm currently trying to implement an HMC experiment outside of stan but would like to use stan to evaluate the log-probability and its gradient.  I found the log_prob-methods section in the rstan manual and would like some clarification on the following excerpt from the 'Details' section before I proceed:
> >
> > However, when using the log density function for a model exposed to R, we need to be careful. For example, if we are interested in finding the mode of parameters on the constrained space, we then do not need the adjustment. For this reason, there is an argument named adjust_transform for functions log_prob and grad_log_prob.
> >
> >  At the end of the day, I would like the log-probability evaluated on the constrained parameters.  After some tooling around, I settled on first getting the unconstrained transformed parameters and then plugging them into log_prob with 'adjust_transform = FALSE'.  Here is an example with a simple exponential distribution model:
> >
> > test_model <- stan_model('log_prob_test.stan')
> > test             <- sampling(test_model, data=list(y=1), iter=1, chains=1)
> > un               <- unconstrain_pars(test, pars=list(lambda=2))
> > log_prob(test, upars=un,adjust_transform=FALSE)
> >
> > It gave me what I wanted for the simple model, but are there any issues I should know about in general?  I will be using these log-probabilities as part of the accept/reject step, so I intuit that the log-Jacobians should not be included.
> >
> >
> > Next, I want to evaluate the gradient.  After playing around I'm under the impression that
> >
> > grad_log_prob(test,upars=un,adjust_transform=TRUE)
> >
> > will give me the gradient of the log-probability plus log Jacobian.  It seems correct to take the unconstrained transformation into account in this way.  But am I wrong to use the transform when evaluating the gradient but not for the log-probability?  Keep in mind I will be using these values within HMC.

make clean-all

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
I found the problem, which was an error of mine in the model code that somehow was tolerated on windows and mac, but not on linux.

the transformed parameters block had these lines

for (m in 1:num_elements(sy)) {
    if (nzstart == 0) {
      if (sy[m] > 0) nzstart <- m;
    }
  }

and the problem was that I had not set the variable nzstart to zero before the loop.
therefore nzstart got never overwritten and kept as value a very low negative number.
in the model section of the code nzstart with a negative number was used as and index when accessing parts of a matrix.
this can of course not work.

would have been ease to catch that problem if it hadn't worked in the first place under windows,
but the fact that it did let me suspect that the problem ist not with the model code.

hope I didn't take to much of your time!

Guido

On Sunday, February 28, 2016 at 2:16:59 PM UTC-5, Dustin Tran wrote:
> Say I'm using a model with both parameters and transformed parameters. How do I find the total number of parameters in each block separately in RStan? Using the model_pars or even things like the inits attribute, it couples the two sets of parameters so you can't distinguish the two.

I don't think there is anything like that in RStan. Here is a function that returns the things in the parameters block.

get_stan_params <- function(object) {
  stopifnot(is(object, "stanfit"))
  params <- grep("context__.vals_r", fixed = TRUE, value = TRUE,
                 x = strsplit(get_cppcode(get_stanmodel(object)), "\n")[[1]])
  params <- sapply(strsplit(params, "\""), FUN = function(x) x[[2]])
  params <- intersect(params, object@model_pars)
  return(params)
}

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Awesome. In case this is useful when someone finds this thread in the future, I use the following code to count the number of local parameters—these are parameters that are not in the transformed block and are not hyperparameters given by another stan file.

get_stan_params <- function(object) {
  stopifnot(is(object, "stanfit"))
  params <- grep("context__.vals_r", fixed = TRUE, value = TRUE,
                 x = strsplit(get_cppcode(get_stanmodel(object)), "\n")[[1]])
  params <- sapply(strsplit(params, "\""), FUN = function(x) x[[2]])
  params <- intersect(params, object@model_pars)
  return(params)
}

count_params <- function(object, params) {
  stopifnot(is(object, "stanfit") || is(object, "stanmodel"))
  return(sum(sapply(object@par_dims[params], prod)))
}

full_model <- suppressMessages(stan(file, data = data, iter = 1, chains = 1))
local_model <- stan_model(local_file)
g_alpha <- vb(local_model, data=c(data,phi), iter=1)

pars_local <- get_stan_params(g_alpha)
pars_full <- get_stan_params(full_model)
pars <- sapply(pars_local, function(x) if (x %in% pars_full) return(x))
count_params(g_alpha, pars)

Dustin

> On Feb 28, 2016, at 12:24 AM, ricka...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Hello,
>
> I've been working on a categorical logit model in Stan that's trying to measure the relative ability of subjects. I have a total of ~500 subjects, but in each data point only 10 subjects are present and one is selected. So in each data point, there is a random subset of 10 of the ~500 subjects. The key part of the model looks like this:
>
>
> for (i in 1:n) {
>  vector[10] x;
>
>  for (j in 1:10) {
>     x[j] <- subject_effects[subjects[i][j]];
>  }
>
>  res[i] ~ categorical_logit(x);
> }
>

With the new vectorization, you should be able to write this as

  for (i in 1:n)

    res[i] ~ categorical_logit(subject_effects[subjects[i]]);

Assuming that you declared subject_effects as a vector.

> Because softmax is invariant under the addition of a constant, one solution the Stan manual offers is to fix a category to 0 to act as a reference category. However, in my model, I can set one of the subjects to 0 as a reference but that reference won't be present except for whichever data points include that particular subject.
>
>
> My question is: does that matter for identifiability or does it still identify the model to set one of the subjects as a reference?

If all the subjects interact, then it's technically enough.
But if there's a partition of the subjects across which they
don't interact, then no.

> If it's inappropriate, is the only solution to set strong priors on the subject effects?

You can do that.  You should have priors based on what you
know about the problem in any case.  In any case, a hierarchical
prior on subject_effects would be in order.

> Since I really only care about the relative differences between subjects, does it matter either way?

What you can't have in Stan is an unidentified model.  Putting
a prior on the subject_effects will identify it, but it's only
a soft kind of identification in the total log density.  It's usually
better to have the likelihood itself be identified as well.

- Bob

messages.subject: Estimation for a distribution whose PDF I cannot calculate (although sampling is possible)
messages.subject_clean: Estimation for a distribution whose PDF I cannot calculate (although sampling is possible)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Forgive my posting a question on here about quite a general estimation problem, but I always find the insight of the Stan community to be far superior than other fora.

I am trying to determine the performance of a yet-to-be-determined estimator of a particular aspect of a distribution, by doing Monte Carlo testing of it over a number of samples from a particular distribution. Because I am looking to evaluate the estimator's properties, I am wanting to repeat the estimation process probably tens of thousands of times. So whatever the estimation process, it needs to be fast.

The snag is that I can't determine the PDF of this distribution (it involves a mixture of a normal with a bespoke survival-type distribution). Nor can I determine the moments of this distribution; they are without-doubt, analytically intractable.

However, I can draw samples from this distribution at a reasonable pace: 100 samples in less than 0.05s, and 1000 samples in 0.15s, for example.

Up until now, I have been working with a surrogate distribution, whose moments are well-characterised, and have been using generalised method of moments to equate the sample moments, with their population equivalents. Note: I don't like method of moments, I am just using it here, because I don't see another equally-fast choice (I would prefer maximum likelihood, or even better, a Bayesian equivalent, but I can't see a way here.)

The surrogate distribution does quite well at emulating the first couple of moments of the true distribution from which I'm sampling. However, the higher moments are nowhere near. This means that the estimator shows some bias, that is undesirable for its application.

I've also tried matching the characteristic functions of the empirical and actual data, but this method is struggling to produce any accuracy at all.

Given the speed of being able to draw samples from the true distribution, I was wondering whether there was an alternative way to go. Essentially something like ABC, but it would have to be faster. This might be possible, because all I want is a point estimate. An alternative would be to construct an empirical likelihood, then maximise this. However, before jumping in, I wanted to tap the estimation-skill of the Stan community.

Does anyone have any ideas?

Best,

Ben

PS If you need details of the surrogate distribution, then look at my question here: http://mathematica.stackexchange.com/questions/108052/estimate-parameters-of-a-derived-distribution - it basically has the shape of a survival distribution, with gaussian noise added. The actual distribution is similar, but with quite different 3rd and higher moments.

messages.body_plain:
The goal is to model NBA team tendencies to perform well or poorly in a given quarter.

The most basic model to predict outcomes in a quarter is a linear regression where the margin of victory for a given quarter is predicted by the publicly available Vegas full game spread.  So for instance, if the Spurs are playing the 76ers and Vegas says Spurs win the game by 14 pts, a regression equation ignoring team tendencies would predicts that Spurs win second quarter by about 4 points.  This works OKAY.  I'm hypothesizing that I can predict quarter outcomes better by including specific team tendencies.  Spurs have a particularly great bench so maybe they outperform in the 2nd quarter.

I use this code.  It's in JAGS but I think its basically the same as STAN and okay to post right? The variable line is equal to the vegas line.  And I set the beta1[j] prior very high because I don't see any reason why the relation between full game line and quarter performance would change based on the team.  I do think the y intercept my change though...

model {
  for (i in 1:Ntotal) {
    y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], 1 / (sigma ^ 2))
    mu[i] <- beta0[team[i]] + beta1[team[i]] * line[i]
  }

  for (j in 1:Nsubj) {
    beta0[j] ~ dnorm( beta0mu, 1)
    beta1[j] ~ dnorm( beta1mu, 1000)

messages.subject: Re: Estimation for a distribution whose PDF I cannot calculate (although sampling is possible)
messages.subject_clean: Estimation for a distribution whose PDF I cannot calculate (although sampling is possible)
messages.body_plain:
Perhaps use some sort of mixture model approximation - eg draw 100 samples, and use an n=100 basis kernel density estimate as an approximation.

This will converge to the actual PDF with a sufficiently large number of samples.  The only question then is what is "sufficiently large" to be useful for you, and how to choose the bandwidth.

messages.body_plain:
Well, BUGS (more precisely Jags, nowadays..) still has its points :
discrete parameters sampling ;
(much) less type/declaration nitpicking* : a vector is the same thing as a row vector wich is the same thing as a real[], a matrix is a matrix, etc...  (OTOH, no way to declare restrictions or constraints...) ;
DAG are a "natural" form of expressing a lot of problems (in my case, medical statistics) ;
"natural" automatic handling of missing data (again, a strong point with those pesky medical datasets...) ;
Some (questionable) use of the DAG structure (e. g. automated DIC computation).
I still think that a "SuperBUGS" language, subsuming BUGS and able to use more efficient sampling methods, would have a lot of use cases...

Currently, Stan is a great language for applied mathematicians working on Bayesian statistical problems. But a lot of statistics users are biologists, physicians, engineers, etc..., looking for a valid way to think about biological, medical, engineering, etc... problems in terms of probabilities. To them, the larger technical overhead of Stan can be perceived as a hurdle.

Another possible hurdle is the availability of resources : on an "normal" Linux installation, the minimal memory needed to compile even the simplest Stan program is about 4,5 Gb (thanks to Boost, I think). This means that you can't use it on an average laptop without swapping somehow. In Windows, this means trashing (and in Linux, to a somewhat lesser extend...), and Stan gets a bad rap...

None of this reasons is sufficient, or even serious. But their conjunction steers a lot of end-users away from Stan towards Jags.

HTH,

--
Emmanuel Charpentier

* I'm starting to consider C++ as the non-conventional infectious agent (a bit like a prion) of a neurological disease, which, among other symptoms, is the alteration of the perception of practicality. Consider the discussion on the "new form of sampling statements" discussion(s) in stan-devel and tell me with a straight face that's not pathological...

> On Feb 29, 2016, at 5:49 AM, Emmanuel Charpentier <emanuel.c...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Well, BUGS (more precisely Jags, nowadays..) still has its points :
> 	• discrete parameters sampling ;

This is almost always a bad idea computationally, but
I agree that users like to be able to write it.  The models
I have that I used to struggle with in BUGS/JAGS fit in
a snap in Stan when I marginalize out the discrete parameters (two
examples you can use for comparison are in the marginalizing
discrete parameters chapter of the manual).

> 	• (much) less type/declaration nitpicking* : a vector is the same thing as a row vector wich is the same thing as a real[], a matrix is a matrix, etc...  (OTOH, no way to declare restrictions or constraints...) ;

What's best for simple models isn't necessarily what's
best for more complex models.  We really geared Stan toward
being able to write more complex models.

Also, we wanted to be able to write down linear algebra
statements naturally and do type inference at compile time
to catch potential bugs.

> 	• DAG are a "natural" form of expressing a lot of problems (in my case, medical statistics) ;

Agreed, but they're also limiting in more complex cases.

> 	• "natural" automatic handling of missing data (again, a strong point with those pesky medical datasets...) ;

It still requires modeling and a simple univariate prior on
the missing data is rarely what you want.

> 	• Some (questionable) use of the DAG structure (e. g. automated DIC computation).

> I still think that a "SuperBUGS" language, subsuming BUGS and able to use more efficient sampling methods, would have a lot of use cases...

That's what NIMBLE is trying to do.  And PyMC to some extent.

> Currently, Stan is a great language for applied mathematicians working on Bayesian statistical problems. But a lot of statistics users are biologists, physicians, engineers, etc..., looking for a valid way to think about biological, medical, engineering, etc... problems in terms of probabilities. To them, the larger technical overhead of Stan can be perceived as a hurdle.

They've told us as much themselves.  Others building complex models
have found it liberating.  It's really very hard to please everyone (and
I didn't mean that sarcastically).

> Another possible hurdle is the availability of resources : on an "normal" Linux installation, the minimal memory needed to compile even the simplest Stan program is about 4,5 Gb (thanks to Boost, I think). This means that you can't use it on an average laptop without swapping somehow. In Windows, this means trashing (and in Linux, to a somewhat lesser extend...), and Stan gets a bad rap...

We could seriously use a better C++ compiler technology!

> None of this reasons is sufficient, or even serious. But their conjunction steers a lot of end-users away from Stan towards Jags.

Agreed.

>
> HTH,
>
> --
> Emmanuel Charpentier
>
> * I'm starting to consider C++ as the non-conventional infectious agent (a bit like a prion) of a neurological disease, which, among other symptoms, is the alteration of the perception of practicality. Consider the discussion on the "new form of sampling statements" discussion(s) in stan-devel and tell me with a straight face that's not pathological...

C++ is a classic example of something that's very complex and
very useful for hard problems (like autodiff and efficient matrix
libraries and custom memory management) but overkill for a lot of
simple problems where C or Java (or even Python or R) would be just
fine.

There aren't any statements that do sampling in Stan, so we
want to try to clear up misconceptions users have to that end
(which they also have about BUGS/JAGS).  The goal's not at
all related to C++.  It's related to the fact that a Stan program
defines a log density rather than being required to lay out a generative
model a la BUGS (for better or worse).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
If you can draw samples from the distribution then that usually
means your model is intractable due to an intractable integrable.
But HMC is really good at doing that already — so you should
be able to incorporate this by adding more nuisance parameters
and just letting Stan fit the entire joint model.

> Perhaps use some sort of mixture model approximation - eg draw 100 samples, and use an n=100 basis kernel density estimate as an approximation.
>
> This will converge to the actual PDF with a sufficiently large number of samples.  The only question then is what is "sufficiently large" to be useful for you, and how to choose the bandwidth.
>
>
> On Monday, 29 February 2016 14:02:12 UTC+11, Ben Lambert wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > Forgive my posting a question on here about quite a general estimation problem, but I always find the insight of the Stan community to be far superior than other fora.
> >
> > I am trying to determine the performance of a yet-to-be-determined estimator of a particular aspect of a distribution, by doing Monte Carlo testing of it over a number of samples from a particular distribution. Because I am looking to evaluate the estimator's properties, I am wanting to repeat the estimation process probably tens of thousands of times. So whatever the estimation process, it needs to be fast.
> >
> > The snag is that I can't determine the PDF of this distribution (it involves a mixture of a normal with a bespoke survival-type distribution). Nor can I determine the moments of this distribution; they are without-doubt, analytically intractable.
> >
> > However, I can draw samples from this distribution at a reasonable pace: 100 samples in less than 0.05s, and 1000 samples in 0.15s, for example.
> >
> > Up until now, I have been working with a surrogate distribution, whose moments are well-characterised, and have been using generalised method of moments to equate the sample moments, with their population equivalents. Note: I don't like method of moments, I am just using it here, because I don't see another equally-fast choice (I would prefer maximum likelihood, or even better, a Bayesian equivalent, but I can't see a way here.)
> >
> > The surrogate distribution does quite well at emulating the first couple of moments of the true distribution from which I'm sampling. However, the higher moments are nowhere near. This means that the estimator shows some bias, that is undesirable for its application.
> >
> > I've also tried matching the characteristic functions of the empirical and actual data, but this method is struggling to produce any accuracy at all.
> >
> > Given the speed of being able to draw samples from the true distribution, I was wondering whether there was an alternative way to go. Essentially something like ABC, but it would have to be faster. This might be possible, because all I want is a point estimate. An alternative would be to construct an empirical likelihood, then maximise this. However, before jumping in, I wanted to tap the estimation-skill of the Stan community.
> >
> > Does anyone have any ideas?

> > Best,

The actual distribution is similar, but with quite different 3rd and higher moments.

It sounds as if R may just have ran out of RAM. There is now a save_warmup logical flag that you can pass to stan() or sampling(), which if FALSE will not save the warmup (which was historically the biggest runtime difference between CmdStan and RStan).

The "negative length vectors" thing has come up before, and may have to do with trying to internally pass a signed int to something expecting an unsigned int. It usually goes away if you have the latest Rcpp, RcppEigen, and rstan all using the same compiler.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Interpret Data From NBA Model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Interpret Data From NBA Model
messages.body_plain:
See comments inline.

> On Feb 28, 2016, at 10:53 PM, Daniel Ashman <dmaxa...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> The goal is to model NBA team tendencies to perform well or poorly in a given quarter.
>
> The most basic model to predict outcomes in a quarter is a linear regression where the margin of victory for a given quarter is predicted by the publicly available Vegas full game spread.  So for instance, if the Spurs are playing the 76ers and Vegas says Spurs win the game by 14 pts, a regression equation ignoring team tendencies would predicts that Spurs win second quarter by about 4 points.  This works OKAY.  I'm hypothesizing that I can predict quarter outcomes better by including specific team tendencies.  Spurs have a particularly great bench so maybe they outperform in the 2nd quarter.
>
> I use this code.  It's in JAGS but I think its basically the same as STAN and okay to post right? The variable line is equal to the vegas line.  And I set the beta1[j] prior very high because I don't see any reason why the relation between full game line and quarter performance would change based on the team.  I do think the y intercept my change though...
>
> model {
>   for (i in 1:Ntotal) {
>     y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], 1 / (sigma ^ 2))
>     mu[i] <- beta0[team[i]] + beta1[team[i]] * line[i]
>   }
>
>   for (j in 1:Nsubj) {
>     beta0[j] ~ dnorm( beta0mu, 1)
>     beta1[j] ~ dnorm( beta1mu, 1000)
>   }
>
>   beta0mu  ~ dnorm( 0, 0.01)
>   beta1mu  ~ dnorm( 0, 0.01 )
>   sigma ~ dunif( 0.01, 100 )
> }"

That 1000 is an awfully tight prior in JAGS/BUGS.

The Stan model's fully vectorizable.

model {
  y ~ normal(beta0[team] + beta1[team] .* line, sigma);
  beta0 ~ normal(beta0mu, 1);
  beta1 ~ normal(beta1mu, .03);
  beta0mu ~ normal(0, 10);
  beta1mu ~ normal(0, 10);
  sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

}

>
> Here are the results for beta[0] (where each beta[j] represents a different teams performance in the 2nd quarter.

We'd probably fit a hierarchical model of the regression coefficients
varying by quarter, probably with a multivariate normal hierarchical
prior.  What you're doing in fitting separate models to each quarter
is what Andrew calls "the secret weapon" (for
reasons that escape me, as it seems the obvious thing to do if
you can't or don't want to formulate a joint model).

> 2. Quantiles for each variable:
>
>                2.5%       25%      50%       75%   97.5%
> beta0[1]  -1.846658 -0.911965 -0.42716  0.066712  0.9764
> beta0[2]  -1.593201 -0.717900 -0.23415  0.253651  1.1870
> beta0[3]  -1.403347 -0.442260  0.04895  0.538899  1.4522
> beta0[4]  -1.022131 -0.134366  0.35487  0.847460  1.7730
> beta0[5]  -1.118993 -0.125492  0.34585  0.792129  1.7380
> beta0[6]  -1.679617 -0.750041 -0.27263  0.195049  1.1185
> beta0[7]  -1.649200 -0.714389 -0.22667  0.250890  1.1410
> beta0[8]  -1.541198 -0.590174 -0.10111  0.363645  1.2489
> beta0[9]  -1.602044 -0.697521 -0.20717  0.285829  1.2359
> beta0[10] -1.137249 -0.055353  0.50943  1.073706  2.1413
> beta0[11] -1.138886 -0.240002  0.23286  0.702269  1.6059
> beta0[12] -1.762396 -0.839376 -0.37060  0.096504  1.0471
> beta0[13] -0.985172 -0.055704  0.42922  0.906376  1.7693
> beta0[14] -0.937979  0.001158  0.50194  0.976599  1.9126
> beta0[15] -1.660372 -0.742521 -0.27773  0.182986  1.1124
> beta0[16] -1.050729 -0.104680  0.39235  0.882033  1.7564
> beta0[17] -1.358114 -0.407956  0.06367  0.561248  1.4973
> beta0[18] -1.579561 -0.638118 -0.15016  0.321270  1.2662
> beta0[19] -1.110811 -0.197150  0.27794  0.763533  1.6939
> beta0[20] -1.662329 -0.750089 -0.26170  0.244139  1.1590
> beta0[21] -1.046530 -0.162887  0.30275  0.790877  1.6816
> beta0[22] -0.798897  0.102462  0.58808  1.071479  1.9920
> beta0[23] -2.610936 -1.708306 -1.23872 -0.779827  0.1366
> beta0[24] -0.008198  0.953392  1.44733  1.943777  2.8944
> beta0[25] -1.745053 -0.831961 -0.35806  0.133408  1.0361
> beta0[26] -1.923597 -0.999055 -0.48417  0.009926  0.9732
> beta0[27] -2.135424 -1.206515 -0.72905 -0.238180  0.6819
> beta0[28] -1.079826 -0.149818  0.34418  0.819707  1.7135
> beta0[29] -1.646407 -0.649124 -0.16497  0.309218  1.2260
> beta0[30] -1.464176 -0.569695 -0.06708  0.399478  1.3437
>
> It looks like most teams have a beta where the 2.5% quantile is negative, and the 97.5% quantile is positive, which means we cannot credibly deduce that they have a tendency to outperform or under perform.

All of these terms are loaded statistical baggage.

What you have in Bayesian terms is a posterior probability
that the team's going to overperform or underperform, with
an estimate of the performance and uncertainty intervals.
The model estimates a 97.5% chance or so that team 24 is
overperforming and also a 75%+ chance team 23 is underperforming.

You can calculate these in Stan as generated quantities as follows:

generated quantities {
  int<lower=0, upper=1> overperform[30];
  for (n in 1:30)
    overperform[n] <- (beta0[n] > 0);
}

Then the posterior mean of overperform[n] is the posterior estimate
(based on model and observed data) that team overperforms in the quarter.

>  Is this a sound interpretation? What about teams 23 and 24, they seem to have statistically significant tendencies here, should I assume the mean for those two teams is correct? Any thoughts or questions are welcome! Thanks!

We don't tend to think in terms of statistical significance.
Instead, we might compare two models predictively, one in
which the performance is allowed to vary by quarter and one in
which it isn't.  And then do tests on how well these match the
in-sample or held-out data.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
If they don't all interact, then they won't be calibrated
to each other anyway!

If the lp__ is mixing that well, you should be fine given
that the other quantities of interest are mixing.

- Bob

> On Feb 28, 2016, at 10:15 PM, ricka...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Thanks for the tips - especially about vectorizing the categorical_logit statement.
>
> Unfortunately, the subjects don't all interact and there's no natural reference category, so my solution was improper.
>
> I should have mentioned that I do have a hierarchical prior on subject_effects with a half-cauchy on the variance and a zero-mean. Ideally I would reframe the problem to include a reference category but it just doesn't seem possible here.
>
> With the priors, here is the summary of lp:
> lp__                       -40896.22    3.67 46.21 -40983.73 -40928.47 -40896.32 -40864.14 -40807.07   159 1.01
>
> And the statistics:
> accept_stat__    stepsize__       treedepth__  n_leapfrog__  n_divergent__
>  Min.   :0.00   Min.   : 0.0026   Min.   : 1   Min.   :   1   Min.   :0.000
>  1st Qu.:0.81   1st Qu.: 0.0256   1st Qu.: 7   1st Qu.: 127   1st Qu.:0.000
>  Median :0.93   Median : 0.0339   Median : 7   Median : 127   Median :0.000
>  Mean   :0.84   Mean   : 0.0649   Mean   : 7   Mean   : 161   Mean   :0.044
>  3rd Qu.:0.98   3rd Qu.: 0.0445   3rd Qu.: 7   3rd Qu.: 127   3rd Qu.:0.000
>  Max.   :1.00   Max.   :14.3855   Max.   :10   Max.   :1023   Max.   :1.000
>
> Would you consider this a soft identification on the log density? I'm not sure how to interpret these to diagnose identifiability.
>
> The only other solution that comes to mind for me is to fit multiple binary logit models with 10 data points per trial and the selected subject labeled as 1 and the others as 0. Any thoughts on this approach compared to what I'm doing now?
>
> Thanks,
> Rick
>
> On Sunday, February 28, 2016 at 4:47:56 PM UTC-8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Feb 28, 2016, at 12:24 AM, ricka...@gmail.com wrote:
> >
> > Hello,
> >
> > I've been working on a categorical logit model in Stan that's trying to measure the relative ability of subjects. I have a total of ~500 subjects, but in each data point only 10 subjects are present and one is selected. So in each data point, there is a random subset of 10 of the ~500 subjects. The key part of the model looks like this:
> >
> >
> > for (i in 1:n) {
> >  vector[10] x;
> >
> >  for (j in 1:10) {
> >     x[j] <- subject_effects[subjects[i][j]];
> >  }
> >
> >  res[i] ~ categorical_logit(x);
> > }
> >
>
> With the new vectorization, you should be able to write this as
>
>   for (i in 1:n)
>     res[i] ~ categorical_logit(subject_effects[subjects[i]]);
>
> Assuming that you declared subject_effects as a vector.
>
> > Because softmax is invariant under the addition of a constant, one solution the Stan manual offers is to fix a category to 0 to act as a reference category. However, in my model, I can set one of the subjects to 0 as a reference but that reference won't be present except for whichever data points include that particular subject.
> >
> >
> > My question is: does that matter for identifiability or does it still identify the model to set one of the subjects as a reference?
>
> If all the subjects interact, then it's technically enough.
> But if there's a partition of the subjects across which they
> don't interact, then no.
>
> > If it's inappropriate, is the only solution to set strong priors on the subject effects?
>
> You can do that.  You should have priors based on what you
> know about the problem in any case.  In any case, a hierarchical
> prior on subject_effects would be in order.
>
> > Since I really only care about the relative differences between subjects, does it matter either way?
>
> What you can't have in Stan is an unidentified model.  Putting
> a prior on the subject_effects will identify it, but it's only
> a soft kind of identification in the total log density.  It's usually
> better to have the likelihood itself be identified as well.
>
> - Bob
>
